question: Are Boerne ISD schools good?
metaTitle: Are Boerne ISD schools good?
metaDescription: Boerne ISD scored 92 points with 20 distinctions in 2024-2025 and six straight A ratings, but four Kendall County elementaries graded lower.
shortAnswer: By the state's own measure, yes. Boerne ISD has earned an A rating from the Texas Education Agency for six consecutive years, scoring 92 points in the 2024-2025 ratings with 20 distinction designations. Not every campus rated A — the Boerne Star reported lower grades at four elementaries.
body:
## The record

**Six consecutive years of "A" ratings from the Texas Education Agency**, including the 2024 and 2025 rating years. In the **2024–2025 ratings, Boerne ISD scored 92 points and earned 20 distinction designations** ([Boerne Star](https://www.boernestar.com/article/11432,boerne-isd-six-straight-years-of-a-ratings); [TEA 2025 Accountability Rating System](https://tea.texas.gov/texas-schools/accountability/academic-accountability/performance-reporting/2025-accountability-rating-system)).

Six years is the number that carries weight. Any district can post one strong year. Six in a row, through a period in which the county's population grew sharply, is a durable result rather than a fluctuation.

## What an "A" actually measures, precisely

Most explanations stop at "it's a state rating." The actual arithmetic is public, and it changes how you should read a 92 ([TEA, 2025 A–F Accountability Ratings summary](https://tea.texas.gov/texas-schools/accountability/academic-accountability/performance-reporting/2025-a-f-statewide-summary-deck.pdf)).

The overall grade is built from three domains, combined this way:

- **The better of Student Achievement or School Progress, weighted 70 percent**, plus
- **Closing the Gaps, weighted 30 percent.**

And each domain measures something specific:

- **Student Achievement** — "What students know and can do." Built from **STAAR, CCMR and graduation**.
- **School Progress** — "How far students have come or how campuses have done compared to similar comparison groups." It is itself a better-of: the higher of **Academic Growth or Relative Performance**.
- **Closing the Gaps** — "How different student groups are performing."

**A is the 90–100 band.** Boerne ISD's 92 sits in the lower half of that band, not at the top of it.

There is also a floor rule worth knowing, printed in TEA's own summary: "If a campus receives a D or an F for 3 of the 4 domains listed above, their final scale score is capped at 69 and 59 (respectively), unless the campus is not scored on all four domains, or the student achievement domain is above a D or F (respectively)."

## The honest reading of a 70/30 better-of formula

Put the structure and the campus results side by side, because they explain each other.

A "better of" weighted composite means **a strong achievement score can carry a weaker growth score**. If a district's students already test well, the achievement domain can supply the 70 percent on its own, and how far those students moved this year never has to be the number that counts. The reverse is also true and is how a district serving a harder population can rate well on growth alone.

That is exactly why **Boerne ISD can hold six straight A ratings while four of its elementaries rate lower.** Both facts are real. The district composite is not an average of campus grades, and it is not a promise about any individual campus.

Neither half of that should be softened. A six-year A is a genuine, hard-to-fake result. It is also a weighted composite of standardized assessment, CCMR and graduation outcomes, and it does not measure class size, teacher retention, the arts program, athletics, special education services, counselor load, or whether a particular child will be happy in a particular building.

**Distinction designations** are a separate award layer — campuses earn them for top-quartile performance in specific areas relative to a comparison group of similar campuses. Twenty of them across a district the size of Boerne ISD is a broad result, not one flagship school carrying the average.

## The district rating is not the campus rating

**Not every Boerne ISD campus rated A.** The Boerne Star reported that **Viola Wilson, Currington, Herff and Kendall elementaries received lower grades** ([Boerne Star](https://www.boernestar.com/article/11432,boerne-isd-six-straight-years-of-a-ratings)).

That matters more to a buyer than the district average does, because a child attends one campus, not a district. Two houses a mile apart inside the same "A-rated district" can zone to campuses with different ratings, different demographics and different programs.

This is also why "we bought in the A district" is an incomplete diligence story. Look up the individual campus rating for the attendance zone of the specific address, on TEA's own reporting rather than a real estate portal's summary score, and confirm the zone with the district office. When you pull it, look at the **domain breakdown**, not just the letter — a campus rated on growth and a campus rated on achievement got there by different routes, and the routes tell you different things about what your child would walk into.

## Attendance zones move in growing districts

**Kendall County grew 20.3 percent between 2020 and 2025**, from an estimated 44,568 to 53,289 residents, mostly through domestic migration ([Community Impact](https://communityimpact.com/san-antonio/boerne-fair-oaks-ranch/government/2026/03/30/kendall-county-population-increases-by-203-from-2020-2025/)).

Districts absorbing that kind of growth rezone. New campuses open, boundaries shift, and a home that zones to one elementary this year may zone elsewhere after the next boundary study. No listing, no agent and no website can promise a future attendance zone. The district is the only source, and even the district can only tell you the current one.

If a specific campus is the reason you are buying a specific house, ask the district directly, in writing, what the current zone is and whether a boundary study is underway.

## The rating has a cost line

Building classrooms for a growing enrollment is financed with bonds, and bond debt appears on the tax rate. Boerne ISD's **2025 rate was 1.0109 per $100** of taxable value — **0.6969 maintenance and operations plus 0.3140 debt service**. Recent history: 0.9909 in 2024, 0.9932 in 2023, 1.1786 in 2022 and 1.2046 in 2021 ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/295/Boerne-ISD)).

Two things to read out of that series. First, the rate is not a straight line; it has come down substantially from 2021 while the debt component funds growth. Second, the school district is the largest single line on most Boerne-area tax bills, which is the trade a buyer makes for the rating.

Texas school districts are required to grant a **residence homestead exemption**, and Kendall AD notes that **Boerne ISD is among the local jurisdictions offering over-65 and disability tax "freezes,"** along with the City of Boerne, Comfort ISD and Kendall County ([Kendall Appraisal District](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)). Kendall AD is the office that applies those to your account.

## Who else is in Boerne ISD — and who is not

**Most of Fair Oaks Ranch is served by Boerne ISD**, even though that city's limits span Bexar, Comal and Kendall counties ([Wikipedia, Fair Oaks Ranch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Oaks_Ranch,_Texas)). So a Fair Oaks Ranch address can be in a different county from a Boerne address and still feed the same district.

**Bulverde is served by Comal ISD**, not Boerne ISD ([Wikipedia, Bulverde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulverde,_Texas)). Comal ISD is a separate district with its own rating record and its own adopted rate. Do not carry Boerne ISD's numbers across that line.

**Comfort ISD** also appears on Kendall County tax bills, serving the western part of the county ([Kendall Appraisal District](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)).

## What to actually do

1. Get the exact address, not the subdivision name.
2. Ask the district for the current attendance zone for that address, in writing.
3. Pull that campus's own TEA rating, and read the domain breakdown, not just the letter.
4. Tour the campus. A rating cannot tell you whether the principal is any good.
5. Confirm the taxing units on the parcel's appraisal record with Kendall AD before you build a payment estimate around them.

## Related questions

- [Is Boerne, Texas a good place to live?](/answers/is-boerne-texas-a-good-place-to-live)
- [Why are homes in Boerne, Texas so expensive?](/answers/why-are-homes-in-boerne-so-expensive)
- [Boerne vs. Fair Oaks Ranch vs. Bulverde: which should I buy in?](/answers/boerne-vs-fair-oaks-ranch-vs-bulverde)
- [What are property taxes like in Boerne, Texas?](/answers/what-are-property-taxes-like-in-boerne)
- [Is Boerne, Texas growing?](/answers/is-boerne-texas-growing)

## Questions about a specific property?

Call or text **[830-446-3847](tel:+1-830-446-3847)** · Email **[heath.shepard@kw.com](mailto:heath.shepard@kw.com)**

question: Are property taxes prorated at closing in Texas?
metaTitle: Are property taxes prorated at closing in Texas?
metaDescription: TREC 20-19 Paragraph 13 prorates taxes through the Closing Date, lets an exemption change count, and leaves buyer and seller to true up later.
shortAnswer: Yes. Under Paragraph 13 of the TREC 20-19 contract, taxes for the current year are prorated through the Closing Date. The title company allocates the year between seller and buyer on the settlement statement, the proration may take a change in exemptions into account, and the parties must adjust it once the actual tax statements are available.
body:
## The exact language, because paraphrases of it are wrong

Proration is not a custom or a title company convention. It is a paragraph in the promulgated contract. Here is **Paragraph 13 of the One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), TREC form 20-19**, in full ([TREC 20-19](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)):

> "Taxes for the current year, interest, rents, and regular periodic maintenance fees, assessments, and dues (including prepaid items) will be prorated through the Closing Date. The tax proration may be calculated taking into consideration any change in exemptions that will affect the current year's taxes. If taxes for the current year vary from the amount prorated at closing, the parties shall adjust the prorations when tax statements for the current year are available. If taxes are not paid at or prior to closing, Buyer shall pay taxes for the current year."

Four sentences. Each one does something, and three of them routinely surprise people. Note also that taxes are not the only thing ¶13 prorates — interest, rents, and regular periodic maintenance fees, assessments and dues are in the same sentence, which matters on an HOA property or a home with a tenant in place.

Form 20-19 is the current resale contract, carrying a **05-04-2026** form date ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/forms/one-four-family-residential-contract-resale)). Condominiums, builder new construction and farm and ranch each use a different promulgated form, and the proration language should be read in the form actually being used.

## Why proration exists: the calendar does not line up with the closing

A Texas property tax bill covers a **calendar year**, and the statement for that year does not arrive until late in it. Nobody is paying in January for the year ahead.

So a June closing splits a year whose bill has not been issued yet. The seller owned part of the year; the buyer will own the rest; and whoever owns the property when the statement lands is the one who pays it. That is what the last sentence of ¶13 is doing: "If taxes are not paid at or prior to closing, **Buyer shall pay taxes for the current year.**"

The practical mechanic: the seller's share of the year is **credited to the buyer on the settlement statement**, and the buyer pays the full-year bill when it comes. In an ordinary resale the seller does not write a check to the tax office at closing.

## "Prorated through the Closing Date"

The split point is the **Closing Date** as defined in the contract, not the effective date, not the funding date, not the day the movers arrive. Everything ¶13 lists is divided at that line.

Because the current year's rates and values are frequently not final at closing, the figures used are estimates. Taxing units adopt rates in late summer and fall; appraisal districts certify values on their own schedule. A March closing is prorating a year nobody has finished calculating.

Rates do move. Boerne ISD adopted **1.0109 per $100** of taxable value for 2025 after 0.9909 in 2024 ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/295/Boerne-ISD)). The City of Boerne held at **0.4716** for both 2024 and 2025 ([Kendall County](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/297/Boerne-City-of)). Kendall County adopted **0.377** for 2025 and **0.373** for 2026 ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/306/Kendall-County)). Rates drift by small amounts. Appraised values in a fast-growing county move far more, which is where most of the variance comes from.

Ask the title company which year's rates and values they used. That is a fair, ordinary question and they will answer it.

## The exemption sentence is the one that bites

"The tax proration **may be calculated taking into consideration any change in exemptions that will affect the current year's taxes**."

Read that carefully. It is permissive — *may* — and it points at a real problem: the seller's exemptions and the buyer's exemptions are not the same, and the current year's taxes can change because of the sale itself.

Where this hurts:

- **Buying from an over-65 seller.** That seller's school district taxes may have sat under a [school tax ceiling](/answers/texas-over-65-property-tax-exemption-and-school-tax-ceiling), frozen at the amount for the year they qualified, plus an additional $60,000 school exemption. None of that belongs to the buyer.
- **Buying from a disabled veteran.** A qualifying veteran can hold a [total exemption on the residence homestead](/answers/texas-disabled-veteran-property-tax-exemption) — the entire appraised value. A proration run off that seller's tax picture can start from nearly nothing.
- **Buying from anyone with a long-held homestead.** The 10% homestead cap can hold the seller's taxable value well below market. The cap does not transfer.

And the buyer's own exemption does not fill the gap in year one. A residence homestead exemption requires the owner to have **owned and occupied the home as a principal residence on January 1** of the tax year ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)). A buyer who closes in June did not. Their own [homestead exemption](/answers/what-is-the-texas-homestead-exemption) — **$140,000** at the school district for 2026 — generally starts the following January 1, with the application due before May 1.

So the current year can be a gap year: the seller's exemptions are gone and the buyer's have not started. That is precisely the situation ¶13's exemption sentence contemplates, and precisely the situation a proration built on last year's bill fails to capture.

Tell the title company, before closing, what exemptions the seller holds and what you will and will not qualify for. They cannot take something into consideration that nobody mentioned.

## The true-up obligation runs between the parties, and nothing triggers it

"If taxes for the current year vary from the amount prorated at closing, **the parties shall adjust the prorations when tax statements for the current year are available.**"

There is a contractual obligation to adjust. This is stronger than most people assume — it is not a courtesy.

It is also weaker than it sounds in practice, for one reason: **it runs between buyer and seller, not through the title company.** The file is closed. Nobody is holding funds. No system sends a reminder in December when the tax statements come out. The obligation sits in a contract in a drawer while both parties have moved on, and in most transactions nobody ever raises it.

If the variance is large enough to matter — and on a property where exemptions changed, it can be — the practical steps are to calendar the tax statement date, run the actual numbers, and raise it in writing with the other party. How to enforce that obligation if the other side declines is a question for a **Texas real estate attorney**. The contract itself says so: ¶23 of form 20-19 states that "TREC rules prohibit real estate brokers and sales agents from giving legal advice" and provides fields for each party's attorney.

## Where taxes actually appear on the settlement statement

Two other paragraphs in the same contract put taxes on the closing statement in places people do not expect ([TREC 20-19](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)):

- **¶12A(1) Seller's Expenses** includes "**tax statements or certificates**." The seller pays for the tax certificate that establishes what is owed.
- **¶12A(2) Buyer's Expenses** includes "all prepaid items, including required premiums for flood and hazard insurance, **reserve deposits for insurance, ad valorem taxes and special governmental assessments**." That is the escrow reserve — money collected up front so the lender can pay the tax bill later.

The reserve deposit is not the proration. They are two different lines doing two different jobs, and confusing them is a common reason a settlement statement looks like it double-charges for taxes. Ask the title company to walk you through both lines.

## The escrow shortfall arrives later, and it is not a mistake

If taxes are escrowed, an under-estimated first year does not stay quiet. The servicer collects based on the estimate, the real bill arrives higher, the escrow account runs short, and when the servicer re-analyzes the account the monthly payment goes up to cover both the shortfall and the higher going-forward amount.

That adjustment lands well after closing, and it is almost always traceable to a first-year estimate built on the seller's exemptions. The number to budget from is an estimate built on the **purchase price**, the **current adopted rates for the actual taxing units on that parcel**, and the **exemptions the buyer personally will qualify for**. Kendall Appraisal District publishes adopted rates and exemptions entity by entity ([kendallad.org](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)).

Boerne property is in **Kendall County**, not Bexar County and not the City of San Antonio, so Bexar CAD figures and San Antonio rates do not describe a Boerne bill.

## Situations to raise before the option period ends

- **Ag-valued or wildlife-valued land.** A change of use triggers a three-year rollback, a separate liability from the year's proration, allocated by the contract's own terms.
- **New construction.** A property that was a vacant lot on January 1 may be appraised as a lot for the current year. The following year looks nothing like the proration.
- **A seller whose exemption status is changing mid-year** — a death, a trust transfer, a move.
- **MUD, PID or special district assessments.** Not all of it is ad valorem tax, and ¶13 handles assessments and dues in the same breath as taxes without making them the same thing.
- **A tenant in place**, since ¶13 also prorates rents.

If the appraised value itself looks wrong after closing, the protest deadline is **May 15, or 30 days after the district mails the notice of appraised value, whichever is later** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/protests/)).

## What to actually do

1. Read ¶13 in your own contract and confirm it is the resale form.
2. Ask the title company which year's rates and values they used, and whether exemption changes were taken into consideration.
3. Ask what the seller's exemptions are. Get the answer before closing.
4. Estimate your own first full-year bill from purchase price, current rates and your own exemptions.
5. Calendar the date current-year tax statements become available, and check the variance against the proration.
6. Keep the settlement statement.

The proration calculation and the funds are the title company's. What ¶13 requires of you in your specific deal is a question for a Texas real estate attorney, values and exemptions are determined by the appraisal district, and tax consequences belong with a CPA.

## Related questions

- [What happens at a Texas closing?](/answers/what-happens-at-a-texas-closing)
- [Who pays closing costs in Texas?](/answers/who-pays-closing-costs-in-texas)
- [Why did my Texas property taxes go up?](/answers/why-did-my-texas-property-taxes-go-up)
- [What is the Texas homestead exemption in 2026?](/answers/what-is-the-texas-homestead-exemption)
- [What is the Texas over-65 property tax exemption and school tax ceiling?](/answers/texas-over-65-property-tax-exemption-and-school-tax-ceiling)

## Questions about a specific property?

Call or text **[830-446-3847](tel:+1-830-446-3847)** · Email **[heath.shepard@kw.com](mailto:heath.shepard@kw.com)**

---

*This page explains how property tax proration works under the TREC contract. It is not legal or tax advice. Paragraph 23 of the contract states that TREC rules prohibit brokers and sales agents from giving legal advice — take contract interpretation to a Texas real estate attorney, the calculation to the title company, and tax consequences to a CPA.*

question: Boerne vs. Fair Oaks Ranch vs. Bulverde: which should I buy in?
metaTitle: Boerne vs. Fair Oaks Ranch vs. Bulverde: which should I buy in?
metaDescription: Fair Oaks Ranch spans Bexar, Comal and Kendall counties; Bulverde is Comal ISD on US 281; Boerne is the Kendall County seat on I-10.
shortAnswer: Boerne is the Kendall County seat on I-10, with city utilities and Boerne ISD. Fair Oaks Ranch incorporated in 1988 and spans Bexar, Comal and Kendall counties, so your appraisal district depends on the lot. Bulverde is Comal County, incorporated 1999, Comal ISD, on US 281.
body:
## The side-by-side

| | Boerne | Fair Oaks Ranch | Bulverde |
|---|---|---|---|
| County | Kendall (county seat) | **Bexar, Comal and Kendall** | Comal |
| Incorporated | Long-established city; county seat | **1988** | **1999** |
| 2020 census population | **18,084** | **9,833** | **5,692** |
| School district | Boerne ISD | **Most of the city is Boerne ISD** | **Comal ISD** |
| Main highway | **I-10** | Between I-10 and US 281 | **US 281** |
| Distance to San Antonio | ~31 miles NW on I-10 | Adjacent to northwest Bexar County | North of San Antonio on 281 |

Sources: [City-Data, Boerne](https://www.city-data.com/city/Boerne-Texas.html); [World Population Review](https://worldpopulationreview.com/us-cities/texas/boerne); [Wikipedia, Fair Oaks Ranch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Oaks_Ranch,_Texas); [Texas State Historical Association](https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/fair-oaks-ranch-tx); [Wikipedia, Bulverde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulverde,_Texas); [City of Bulverde](https://www.bulverdetx.gov/304/About-Bulverde).

## The one fact that surprises everybody: Fair Oaks Ranch is in three counties

**Fair Oaks Ranch city limits span Bexar, Comal and Kendall counties** ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_Oaks_Ranch,_Texas); [TSHA](https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/fair-oaks-ranch-tx)). Two houses on the same street can sit in different counties.

That is not trivia. County determines:

- **Which appraisal district values your home and takes your homestead exemption and protest.** A Kendall County parcel files with [Kendall Appraisal District](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/). A Bexar County parcel files with Bexar CAD. A Comal County parcel files with Comal CAD. Filing with the wrong one is a real and common relocation mistake, and the exemption deadline is before May 1.
- **Which county line items appear on your tax bill,** and at which rates.
- **Which county offices you deal with** for recording, permits outside the city, and emergency services districts.

So "Fair Oaks Ranch taxes" is not one answer. It is three, depending on the lot. Pull the specific parcel's appraisal record before you assume.

The compensating simplicity: **most of Fair Oaks Ranch is served by Boerne ISD**, so the school variable is usually stable across the city even when the county variable is not. Confirm the specific address with the district.

## Boerne: city services and the county seat

Boerne is the **county seat of Kendall County**, about 31 miles northwest of San Antonio on I-10. Inside the city limits you get municipal utilities and a city government that regulates what happens on your block and, for some ordinances, out into the extraterritorial jurisdiction.

The 2025 adopted rates for a city-limits home in Boerne ISD, per $100 of taxable value:

- **Boerne ISD: 1.0109** — 0.6969 M&O plus 0.3140 debt, up from 0.9909 in 2024 ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/295/Boerne-ISD)).
- **City of Boerne: 0.4716** — also 0.4716 in 2024, 0.4766 in 2023, 0.4510 in 2022 ([Kendall County](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/297/Boerne-City-of)).
- **Kendall County: 0.377** — 0.317976 M&O plus 0.059024 debt, down from 0.3827 in 2024 ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/306/Kendall-County)).

Kendall County's rate applies countywide, so a Fair Oaks Ranch home on the Kendall side pays it too — while one on the Bexar or Comal side pays that county's rate instead.

Sales tax in Boerne is **8.25 percent**: 6.25 state, 1.50 city, 0.50 county ([City of Boerne](https://www.ci.boerne.tx.us/646/Current-Tax-Rates)).

Buy in Boerne when you want walkable downtown access, I-10 as your commute, city water and sewer, and Boerne ISD without a county-line question.

## The school district line is the largest single number on the bill

Compare the layers rather than the towns. For 2025, per $100 of taxable value:

| Taxing unit | 2025 adopted rate |
|---|---|
| **Comal ISD** | **1.0748** — 0.7248 M&O plus 0.3500 debt ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/299/Comal-ISD)) |
| **Boerne ISD** | **1.0109** — 0.6969 M&O plus 0.3140 debt ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/295/Boerne-ISD)) |
| **Comfort ISD** | **0.9328** — down from 0.9603 in 2024 and 0.9626 in 2023 ([Kendall County](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/300/Kendall-County)) |
| City of Boerne | 0.4716 ([Kendall County](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/297/Boerne-City-of)) |
| Kendall County | 0.377 ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/306/Kendall-County)) |

Read the column, not the rows. Every school district rate on that list is **larger than the city and county rates combined**. In Boerne city limits, the 1.0109 school line is more than the 0.4716 city line and the 0.377 county line added together, and the same holds for a Comal ISD parcel.

Which means the practical version of this comparison is simple: **which ISD a parcel sits in moves the monthly payment more than which city name is on the mailing address.** A Bulverde home in Comal ISD carries 1.0748 where a Boerne-area home in Boerne ISD carries 1.0109 — on the same taxable value, that gap is a real line in a lender's escrow calculation, separate from any difference in price.

Comal ISD's own recent trend, per $100: **1.0748 in 2025**, down from **1.0869 in 2024** and **1.0892 in 2023**, with the debt component holding at 0.3500 each of those years ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/299/Comal-ISD)). Kendall County publishes it because part of the county falls inside Comal ISD.

Rates are adopted annually by each taxing unit and they move independently. Pull the current year for the specific parcel before building a payment around any of these, and take the payment math to your **lender**.

## Bulverde: the 281 side, and a different ISD

**Bulverde is in Comal County, incorporated in 1999, with a 2020 census population of 5,692, and US 281 runs through the east side** ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulverde,_Texas); [City of Bulverde](https://www.bulverdetx.gov/304/About-Bulverde)).

The defining differences from Boerne:

- **Comal ISD, not Boerne ISD.** Different rating record, different bond history, different tax rate. Comal ISD adopted **1.0748 per $100 for 2025** — 0.7248 M&O plus 0.3500 debt — after 1.0869 in 2024 and 1.0892 in 2023 ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/299/Comal-ISD)). That is the single largest line on the bill, and it is higher than Boerne ISD's 1.0109.
- **Comal Appraisal District, not Kendall AD.**
- **US 281 rather than I-10.** That is a different commute into a different part of San Antonio, and it serves the north-central employment corridor better than I-10 does.
- **A younger, smaller municipality.** Incorporated in 1999 versus Fair Oaks Ranch's 1988 and Boerne's long history as the county seat. Newer cities have less accumulated infrastructure and fewer accumulated ordinances — read that as a pro or a con depending on what you want.

## How to actually choose

Work the decision in this order:

1. **Which employment center do you drive to?** I-10 favors Boerne and Fair Oaks Ranch. US 281 favors Bulverde. Drive the route on a weekday at your real departure time before anything else.
2. **Which school district, and which campus?** Boerne ISD has held a **Texas Education Agency "A" rating for six consecutive years** ([Boerne Star](https://www.boernestar.com/article/11432,boerne-isd-six-straight-years-of-a-ratings)), but campus-level grades vary within it, and Comal ISD is a separate system entirely. Verify the attendance zone with the district for the exact address.
3. **City limits, ETJ, or unincorporated?** That decides whether you get city water and sewer or a well and septic, whether city ordinances apply, and which taxing entities bill you.
4. **Pull the parcel's appraisal record last, and use it to confirm county, district, and every taxing unit on the bill.** Do not reconstruct that from a listing sheet.

## What none of the three escapes

Groundwater. Kendall County groundwater is regulated by the **Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District**, which sets drought stages and pumping rules ([ccgcd.org](https://ccgcd.org/)), and Comal and Bexar county wells fall under their own districts. Any acreage property on a private well in this region carries well-yield and drought-rule due diligence that a city tap does not.

question: Can an HOA ban short-term rentals in Texas?
metaTitle: Can an HOA ban short-term rentals in Texas?
metaDescription: Tarr v. Timberwood Park (Tex. 2018) only construed a bare residential-purposes covenant. An amended Texas HOA declaration can still bar Airbnb.
shortAnswer: Often yes. Texas has no statewide short-term rental preemption statute, and an HOA declaration is a private contract that can be amended to restrict or prohibit short-term rentals. Tarr v. Timberwood Park (Tex. 2018) held only that a bare residential-purposes-only covenant does not by itself bar short stays.
body:
## What Tarr actually decided

**Tarr v. Timberwood Park Owners Association**, No. 17-0088 (Tex. 2018), is the case every investor hears about and almost nobody reads. The Texas Supreme Court held, unanimously, that where renters use a single-family home for a residential purpose, the rental does not violate a bare "residential purposes only" covenant — regardless of how short the stay is ([Texas Municipal League, *Short-Term Rentals*](https://www.tml.org/DocumentCenter/View/4951/Short-Term-Rentals---4-2024-PDF)).

Read the scope of that carefully, because the scope is the whole point:

- It is a case about **interpreting a specific covenant**. The declaration in Timberwood Park said "residential purposes" and did not define the term, did not set a minimum lease length, and did not address transient occupancy.
- It is **not a holding that HOAs cannot restrict short-term rentals**.
- It says **nothing about city zoning, city permits or licensing**. A municipal ordinance is a separate body of law and Tarr does not touch it.

The useful way to state the rule: a Texas HOA that wants to stop short-term rentals generally needs language that actually does that. A generic "residential use only" clause, standing alone, does not.

## How an HOA gets to yes anyway

Deed restrictions are private contracts among the owners. Most Texas declarations include an amendment mechanism, typically requiring some supermajority of owners. If the membership amends the declaration to define a minimum lease term, prohibit transient occupancy, or ban short-term rentals outright, the analysis changes — and **Texas appellate courts have upheld amended restrictions that restrict short-term rentals** ([Silberman Law Firm](https://silblawfirm.com/real-estate-law/texas-appeals-court-supports-hoas-new-rules-restricting-short-term-rentals/), [analysis of the Tarr ruling](https://legalclarity.org/texas-supreme-court-ruling-on-short-term-rentals/)).

That is the exposure nobody prices in. A buyer can close on a property whose current declaration is silent, run it as a short-term rental profitably, and then watch the association amend the declaration two years later. Whether a particular amendment binds a particular owner — and whether any grandfathering applies — depends on the amendment language, the declaration's own amendment provision, and the facts. **That is a question for a Texas real estate attorney, not for a real estate agent and not for a forum post.**

## There is no state law overriding any of this

Texas does **not** have a statewide short-term rental preemption statute. **HB 2127 (2023) does not specifically cover short-term rental regulation**, so cities retain their authority to license and restrict them ([Texas Municipal League](https://www.tml.org/DocumentCenter/View/4951/Short-Term-Rentals---4-2024-PDF)).

The practical result is that a Texas short-term rental sits under two independent sets of rules that do not talk to each other:

1. **Public law** — the city ordinance, zoning, permitting, and hotel occupancy tax.
2. **Private law** — the recorded declaration, deed restrictions and any POA rules.

Either one can stop the business. Neither one cures the other.

## A city permit is not HOA permission, and HOA permission is not a city permit

This is the sentence to remember. In Boerne, for example, the city issues a short-term rental permit under [Ordinance No. 2023-09](https://www.ci.boerne.tx.us/2444/Short-Term-Rentals) with a fee, an inspection, an insurance minimum and a block-face separation rule. Holding that permit says nothing about whether the subdivision's declaration allows the use. And a friendly HOA board says nothing about whether the city will issue the permit.

A buyer underwriting a short-term rental needs **both cleared, independently, before the option period expires.** Clearing one and assuming the other is how a deal closes and then cannot operate.

Note also that Boerne is in **Kendall County** and is not governed by San Antonio's ordinance. Whatever city the property sits in, read that city's rules.

## How to actually check the private side before you close

The declaration is a recorded document. It can be pulled and read.

- **Get the full recorded declaration and every recorded amendment**, not the HOA's summary sheet and not the listing agent's description. Amendments are where the restriction usually lives.
- **Order the subdivision information, including the resale certificate.** Under [Texas Property Code Chapter 207](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-207-003/), a property owners' association must provide subdivision information on proper written request, including assessments, unpaid amounts, certain known violations, insurance, certain pending litigation and transfer restrictions. Delivery is within 10 business days of a written request, and the certificate must be prepared no earlier than 60 days before delivery.
- **Read the minutes and any pending amendment notices.** An amendment already circulating for a vote is the clearest possible warning, and it will not show up in the covenants themselves.
- **Ask whether the association has enforced against short-term rentals before.** Enforcement history is a fact; assurance is not.
- **Have a Texas real estate attorney read the declaration** if the investment thesis depends on the answer. Interpreting covenants is legal work.

The TREC forms that carry the HOA side of a Texas transaction are the **Addendum for Property Subject to Mandatory Membership in a Property Owners Association (form 36-11, effective 07/01/2026)** and **Subdivision Information, Including Resale Certificate (form 37-5)**.

## The condominium wrinkle

Condominium regimes operate under their own declaration and rules, and a condo association can carry rental restrictions, minimum lease terms and registration requirements that read nothing like a single-family HOA's covenants. Tarr involved a single-family subdivision. Do not port its reasoning onto a condo declaration without an attorney reading the actual document.

## The short version for an investor

- A bare "residential purposes only" covenant, by itself, probably does not stop a short-term rental in Texas, under Tarr.
- Nearly anything more specific than that probably does.
- The declaration can be amended later, and amended restrictions have been upheld.
- The city can regulate independently, because no state statute preempts it.
- Both boxes have to be checked before closing, and the declaration is the box people skip.

question: Can I defer my property taxes in Texas if I'm over 65?
metaTitle: Can I defer my property taxes in Texas if I'm over 65?
metaDescription: Texas over-65 property tax deferral: Form 50-126, how it stops foreclosure, the 5 percent annual interest under Tax Code 33.06, and what happens when it ends.
shortAnswer: Yes. A Texas homeowner 65 or older can defer property taxes on their residence homestead by filing Comptroller Form 50-126 with the appraisal district. Deferral stops foreclosure and delinquency penalties while it is in effect, but the taxes keep accruing at 5 percent annual interest under Tax Code 33.06 and eventually come due.
body:
## Deferral is a pause, not a discount

This is the single most important thing to understand before filing, and it is the thing that gets lost when the option is described as tax relief.

A deferral does not reduce, forgive or cancel anything. The taxes are still assessed. They still accrue. What the deferral does is **stop collection activity on the residence homestead** while it is in place — no foreclosure on the homestead for those taxes, and the ordinary delinquency penalties do not pile up in the usual way during the deferral period.

The balance grows the entire time. At some point it is paid, in full, with interest.

## The interest rate is 5%, and it is in the statute

**Texas Tax Code §33.06(d)**: "The annual interest rate during the deferral or abatement period is five percent instead of the rate provided by Section 33.01" ([Tax Code §33.06](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/tax-code/tax-sect-33-06/)).

Five percent annually, substituted for the ordinary delinquent-tax rate. That is a real benefit relative to standard delinquency, and it is still compounding growth on a balance that is not being paid down.

Run the arithmetic honestly before deciding. On a Boerne-area homestead where the combined rate across the school district, city and county runs well above 1.8 per $100 of taxable value, a deferred year is a meaningful sum, and five deferred years at 5% is a number worth putting on paper — alongside what the property is likely to be worth when the bill comes due.

## How to file, and where

File **Comptroller Form 50-126, Tax Deferral Affidavit**, with the **appraisal district** for the county where the property sits. Not the tax office, not the city.

For a Boerne or Kendall County homestead, that is the **Kendall Appraisal District** ([kendallad.org](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)). Boerne is the county seat of Kendall County. It is not in Bexar County and not in the City of San Antonio, so Bexar CAD's forms and procedures are not the ones that apply.

The deferral applies to the **residence homestead**. It is not a tool for a rental, a second home or acreage held for investment.

## Exhaust the exemptions first

Deferral is the option of last resort, and a surprising number of people reach for it while leaving the free benefits unclaimed. Before deferring, confirm every one of these is actually posted on the account:

- The general residence homestead exemption — **$140,000** at the school district for 2026, raised from $100,000 by **Proposition 13**, approved by voters in **November 2025** and implemented through **SB 4, 89th Legislature** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)).
- The **additional $60,000** school district exemption for owners 65 or older or disabled, plus any local option of at least $3,000 that other taxing units have adopted ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)).
- The **school tax ceiling**, which freezes school district taxes at the amount for the year the owner qualified.
- Any **local freeze**. Kendall Appraisal District names the **City of Boerne, Boerne ISD, Comfort ISD and Kendall County** as jurisdictions offering over-65 and disability freezes ([Kendall AD](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)).
- Any **disabled veteran exemption**, which for a qualifying veteran can be a total exemption on the homestead.

Also check whether the **value** is right. A protest is free and the deadline is **May 15, or 30 days after the district mails the notice of appraised value, whichever is later** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/protests/)).

An exemption that was never filed, or a value that was never challenged, is a cheaper fix than borrowing against the house at 5%.

## What ends a deferral

The deferral is tied to the owner and the homestead. When the qualifying owner no longer owns and occupies the property as a residence homestead — on a sale, a move, or a death — the deferral ends and the accumulated taxes and interest become payable. The statute provides a period for payment after the deferral ends before ordinary delinquency consequences resume; the exact timing and mechanics for a specific situation are a question for a **Texas real estate attorney**.

Practical consequences that follow from that:

- **Selling the house pays it off.** A deferred balance is settled out of the sale, which reduces the seller's proceeds. Anyone planning to downsize should know the number before they price the house.
- **Heirs inherit the obligation, not a forgiveness.** A family expecting a clear house may be looking at a substantial balance against it.
- **It affects the estate's options.** Whether the heirs can keep the property often turns on whether they can pay or refinance that balance.

Nobody should file a deferral without the family knowing it exists.

## The mortgage problem

If the property carries a mortgage, this is not automatically available in practice.

Most loan agreements require the borrower to keep property taxes current, and many loans escrow taxes and pay them directly. A deferral can conflict with those terms, and the servicer may advance the taxes anyway and bill the borrower. Whether a deferral is compatible with a particular loan is a question for the **lender or servicer**, in writing, before filing.

The homeowners who use deferral most cleanly are the ones who own the home free and clear.

## The honest way to think about it

A deferral converts a current cash problem into a growing lien on the house. For a homeowner on a fixed income with substantial equity and no intention of moving, that trade can be entirely rational — the equity is there precisely to be used, and 5% is far better than the alternatives available to someone who cannot pay.

For anyone planning to sell within a few years, or who wants to leave the house unencumbered, it usually is not. The balance simply arrives at the moment the equity was going to be used for something else.

Eligibility, the current form and the deferred balance on an account are all determined by the appraisal district and the tax office. The estate and title consequences belong with a **Texas real estate attorney**, the financial and tax consequences with a **CPA**, and loan compatibility with the **lender**.

question: Conventional vs. FHA vs. VA loan in Texas: which one should I use?
metaTitle: Conventional vs. FHA vs. VA loan in Texas: which one should I use?
metaDescription: Conventional, FHA and VA compared for Texas buyers on verifiable terms: 2026 loan limits, VA entitlement and funding fee exemption, and Texas 50(a)(6).
shortAnswer: Conventional loans follow the 2026 conforming limit of $832,750 for one unit. FHA uses a nationwide floor of $541,287 and a ceiling of $1,249,125, set by county. VA loans have no loan limit for a veteran with full entitlement, and the funding fee is waived for service-connected disability compensation. Ask a lender to price all three.
body:
## Start with the part that is fixed, not the part that is marketed

Most comparisons of these three programs lead with down payment percentages, credit minimums and mortgage insurance rates. Those are the parts that move — by lender overlay, by borrower, by month. Lead instead with the structural facts that are published, dated and the same for everyone. They are what actually determine which programs are on the table for a given purchase price.

## How much each program will lend

**Conventional.** For 2026, the Federal Housing Finance Agency set the conforming loan limit for a one-unit property at **$832,750**, up $26,250 from 2025's $806,500. The high-cost area ceiling is **$1,249,125**. FHFA announced the increase after third-quarter 2025 house price index data showed prices up 3.26% year over year ([FHFA](https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/fhfa-announces-conforming-loan-limit-values-for-2026)). A loan above the applicable conforming limit is a **jumbo** — Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will not buy it, so it is priced and underwritten by the individual lender or its investor, on their terms.

**FHA.** For 2026, per **Mortgagee Letter 2025-23**, the nationwide one-unit **floor is $541,287** and the **ceiling is $1,249,125**, effective for case numbers assigned **January 1 through December 31, 2026** ([HUD Mortgagee Letter 2025-23](https://www.hud.gov/sites/dfiles/hudclips/documents/2025-23hsgml.pdf), [HUD announcement](https://www.hud.gov/news/hud-no-25-145)). FHA limits are set county by county between those two numbers. Each county's actual limit is published on HUD's lookup tool, and that lookup — not a third-party article — is the number a lender will use ([HUD FHA mortgage limits lookup](https://entp.hud.gov/idapp/html/hicostlook.cfm)).

**VA.** Veterans with **full entitlement have no VA loan limit**, and the VA guaranty does not exceed **25%** ([U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs](https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/loan-limits/)). That is a real structural advantage, and it is the one most often misunderstood: no VA limit is not the same as no limit. The VA is not capping the loan. The lender still underwrites the file, and the appraisal still governs value.

Entitlement can be partial — a veteran with an existing VA loan, or a prior VA foreclosure, may not have full entitlement. The Certificate of Eligibility answers it, and the lender pulls it.

## The VA funding fee, and the exemption most eligible borrowers do not ask about

VA loans carry a one-time funding fee paid to the VA, calculated as a percentage of the loan amount. Certain borrowers do not pay it at all. The exemptions include **veterans receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability**, veterans who would be **eligible to receive that compensation but are taking retirement or active-duty pay instead**, certain recipients of **Dependency and Indemnity Compensation**, and **Purple Heart recipients still serving on active duty** ([U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs](https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/funding-fee-and-closing-costs/)).

Documentation is **VA Form 26-8937 (Verification of VA Benefits)**, a **current award letter dated within the last 12 months**, or a letter from a **Veteran Service Center Manager**. The second category on that list is the one that gets missed: a veteran who is entitled to compensation but elected retirement pay instead can still be exempt. That is a file question for the lender, raised at application, not at closing.

## What none of these three programs does in Texas

All three are federal loan products. Texas layers its own constitutional rules on top of the homestead — the home you actually live in — and those rules survive whichever program you choose.

A cash-out refinance or home equity loan on a Texas homestead is governed by the **Texas Constitution, Section 50(a)(6)**: total borrowing against the homestead cannot exceed **80% of fair market value** at closing, so at least 20% equity must remain; closing cannot occur until at least **12 days** after the later of the application or your receipt of the required notice; fees other than the appraisal, land survey, title insurance premium and title search/exam cannot exceed **2%** of loan principal; the loan is generally **non-recourse**; and only **one** such loan may exist on the homestead at a time, with **12 months** required between home equity closings. A Texas HELOC on a homestead is also a 50(a)(6) loan and carries the same limits ([Texas cash-out rules summarized](https://hurstlending.com/texas-cash-out-refinance-rules-50a6-guidelines/)).

This is why the purchase decision and the refinance plan should be made together. If the strategy is minimum down now and a cash-out in two years, 80% is the hard ceiling in Texas no matter which of the three programs you used to buy. Investment property in Texas is **not** governed by 50(a)(6).

## Where these programs actually differ for a real buyer

The differences that decide it are file-specific, and a lender can price them on your numbers in an afternoon. The dimensions worth asking about by name:

- **Mortgage insurance structure.** Conventional and FHA handle it differently, and one is cancellable under conditions while the other is not. VA has no monthly mortgage insurance. Ask what the monthly amount is, how long it lasts, and what makes it go away.
- **Appraisal standards.** FHA and VA appraisals include minimum property condition requirements that a conventional appraisal does not. On an older home, a rural property, or anything with deferred maintenance, that can turn into required repairs before closing — a real risk on Hill Country properties with wells, septic systems, outbuildings or peeling paint on pre-1978 construction.
- **Seller concessions.** Each program caps what a seller can contribute toward the buyer's costs, and the caps differ. This shapes what you can negotiate.
- **Property eligibility.** Condominiums in particular have program-specific approval requirements that can eliminate a building outright.
- **Assumability.** FHA and VA loans have assumption mechanics conventional loans do not. Relevant when rates move.
- **Speed and certainty.** How long the lender's own underwriting queue runs matters more to a seller than the program name.

## The comparison to ask for, in writing

"Price this file as conventional, FHA and VA. Give me the rate, the monthly payment including taxes, insurance and any mortgage insurance, the cash to close, and what my mortgage insurance does over time in each case."

That single request gets you a decision you can defend. It also surfaces the case buyers miss most often, where the program with the lower entry cost carries the higher lifetime cost, or the reverse.

## What the seller's side is reading

A Texas buyer whose purchase depends on a mortgage uses the **Third Party Financing Addendum, TREC form 40-11, effective 01/03/2025** ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)). TREC promulgates these forms and license holders are required to use them; a license holder cannot draft contract language.

The listing side reads that addendum together with the preapproval letter. Some sellers have opinions about loan programs — usually about appraisal condition requirements and timelines rather than about the buyer. A loan officer who will take a listing agent's call and speak to the file is worth more at that moment than a fractionally better rate.

## Who to ask

Program eligibility, pricing, mortgage insurance, overlays and which loan is cheapest over your actual holding period are **lender** questions. Entitlement and funding fee exemption status run through the **VA** and your lender. County-level FHA limits come from **HUD's lookup tool**. How the Texas homestead rules apply to your ownership or title situation is a question for a **Texas real estate attorney**.

question: Do I need a real estate attorney to buy a house in Texas?
metaTitle: Do I need a real estate attorney to buy a house in Texas?
metaDescription: Texas does not require an attorney to buy a house. Here is why, and the specific situations where hiring a Texas real estate attorney is the right call anyway.
shortAnswer: No. Texas does not require a real estate attorney to buy a house. The title company handles escrow, title search and closing documents, and license holders use TREC promulgated forms. An attorney is the right call for title defects, probate or estate sales, deed drafting, deed restriction questions, and any custom contract language.
body:
## The contract itself tells you to hire one

Before anything else: the promulgated contract does not treat a lawyer as optional advice from a website. It says so on its own face, twice.

**Paragraph 23 is titled CONSULT AN ATTORNEY BEFORE SIGNING.** Its text: "**TREC rules prohibit real estate brokers and sales agents from giving legal advice. READ THIS CONTRACT CAREFULLY.**" The form then provides printed fields for Buyer's Attorney and Seller's Attorney, with phone numbers ([TREC form 20-19, ¶23](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

**Paragraph 6E(1)** goes further and names the specific job: "**Broker advises Buyer to have an abstract of title covering the Property examined by an attorney of Buyer's selection**, or Buyer should be furnished with or obtain a Title Policy. If a Title Policy is furnished, the **Commitment should be promptly reviewed by an attorney of Buyer's choice due to the time limitations on Buyer's right to object**."

Read that second one closely. It is not generic caution. It identifies the single highest-value hour a real estate attorney will ever spend on an ordinary residential purchase: reading the title commitment inside the objection window. The contract flags it because that window closes fast and closes permanently.

So the honest answer to "do I need an attorney" is: not to close, and the state built a system so you would not have to. But the contract you are signing has a paragraph whose entire purpose is to tell you to get one, and the reason is title.

## Why Texas works this way

Texas is a title company state. In a residential purchase, the title company acts as **escrow agent**, runs the title search, issues the title commitment and the title policy, prepares the closing documents, and disburses funds at closing. That is the function an attorney performs in the states that require one.

The second half of the system is the TREC promulgated contract. The Texas Real Estate Commission writes the forms, and license holders are required to use them ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)). A REALTOR is not drafting your contract — they are filling blanks on a form the state wrote.

That is not a convenience. It is the reason the system works without a lawyer in every deal. **Drafting contract language is the practice of law, and a real estate license does not authorize it** — which is exactly what ¶23 means by "TREC rules prohibit real estate brokers and sales agents from giving legal advice." The promulgated forms exist precisely so a license holder can paper a transaction without crossing that line. TREC does not write custom contracts.

So the framing is not "you do not need a lawyer in Texas." It is: the routine case has been pre-lawyered by the state, and the non-routine case still needs one.

## The limits of what your agent can do

A Texas license holder can explain how a promulgated form works, fill in the negotiated terms, and advise on price, condition, market and strategy. That covers most of what a buyer needs.

A license holder cannot draft contract language, interpret a deed restriction for you as a legal matter, advise you on how to take title, tell you what a title exception means for your legal rights, or opine on the effect of a divorce decree or a will on the chain of title.

When a client asks a question that lands past that line, the correct answer is a referral, not a guess. An agent who freelances a special provision to solve a problem is creating a bigger one.

## When an attorney is the right call

These are the situations where paying for an hour of a real estate attorney's time is cheap relative to the exposure.

**A title defect the commitment flagged.** A break in the chain of title, an unreleased lien, a judgment, a probate that was never completed, a missing heir, a boundary discrepancy the survey exposed. The title company will tell you it cannot insure over something. It will not tell you how to fix it.

This is the ¶6E(1) situation, and it is on a clock. Under **¶6D** the buyer must object in writing by the earlier of the closing date or a stated number of days after receiving the commitment, exception documents and survey, and "failure to object within the time allowed **will constitute a waiver** of Buyer's right to object" — with only the Schedule C requirements surviving ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6D](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). If the seller does not cure a timely objection within the **15-day cure period**, the buyer gets **5 days** to terminate with earnest money refunded or waive, and silence waives.

A buyer who sends the commitment to a lawyer the week of closing has usually already waived. The hour costs the same either way; only the timing determines whether it was worth anything.

**Probate and estate sales.** An estate selling a property raises questions about the authority of the person signing, whether the will was probated, whether an independent administration exists, and whether all heirs have joined. This is one of the most common reasons a Texas residential deal goes sideways late.

**Deed drafting.** If the transaction needs a deed prepared for something beyond the ordinary conveyance — a transfer into a trust or an entity, a correction deed, a deed with a reserved life estate, a gift deed between family — a lawyer drafts it. Nobody else may.

**Custom contract language.** Any term the promulgated forms and addenda do not accommodate. Seller financing structured beyond the addendum, a leaseback longer than the promulgated temporary lease contemplates, a right of first refusal, an option tied to rezoning or platting, a seller carryback with unusual terms. A license holder may not write these.

**Deed restriction interpretation.** Whether a "residential purposes only" covenant permits a short-term rental, whether a restriction is enforceable after a subdivision amendment, whether a use is grandfathered. Deed restrictions are private contracts, and their interpretation is legal work.

**Partition.** Co-owners who cannot agree on selling, or inherited property split among siblings.

**Marital property.** Texas is a **community property** state. How a married person takes title, whether a non-purchasing spouse must join, what a divorce decree did to the property, and how separate property is characterized are all legal questions with real consequences.

**An entity or trust buying.** The formation, the authority to sign, and the operating documents the title company will demand.

**A 1031 exchange.** The attorney works alongside a CPA and a qualified intermediary. The tax answer is not the real estate agent's to give.

**Any dispute.** A contested earnest money release, an alleged default, a non-disclosure claim after closing, a seller refusing to close. Escrowed funds cannot be released without mutual agreement or a court order, and once the other side is dug in, the next move is legal.

## What an attorney will not change

An attorney will not make the title policy cheaper. Texas title insurance premium rates are **promulgated by the Texas Department of Insurance**, so the premium for a given policy amount is the same at every title company in the state ([TDI](https://tdi.texas.gov/title/titlerates2026.html)).

An attorney will not rewrite a promulgated form into something better for routine terms. The forms are good, and the negotiation happens in the blanks.

An attorney will not sit at the closing table and improve a closing that was already going to work.

## The pieces that already protect you without one

The TREC contract and its addenda build in more protection than most buyers realize.

**Paragraph 5B** gives an unrestricted right to terminate for any reason, which functions as a due diligence window. **Paragraph 6B** returns the earnest money if the title commitment never shows up in time. **Paragraph 6D** gives a title objection and cure process. **Paragraph 7B(2)** lets a buyer who never received the seller's disclosure notice terminate at any time prior to closing, and gives a fresh 7 days after the notice finally arrives ([TREC form 20-19](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf); [Texas Property Code §5.008](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-5-008/)). **Paragraph 14** handles casualty loss. **Paragraph 15** sets the default remedies both ways.

Outside the base form, the **Third Party Financing Addendum, form 40-11, effective 01/03/2025** supplies a financing exit, and the **Addendum Concerning Right to Terminate Due to Lender's Appraisal, form 49-1** addresses a low appraisal ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

The current resale contract is **TREC form 20-19, effective 07/01/2026** — 12 pages, footer-dated 05-04-2026 ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/forms/one-four-family-residential-contract-resale)).

Use those, and the ordinary purchase does not need a lawyer. Ignore them and no lawyer hired at closing will fix it.

question: Do I need flood insurance in Boerne, Texas?
metaTitle: Do I need flood insurance in Boerne, Texas?
metaDescription: Flood insurance in Boerne and Kendall County: when a lender requires it, what Texas seller's disclosure asks about flooding, and the option-period deadline.
shortAnswer: If the property is in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area and you are using a federally backed loan, the lender will require flood insurance. Outside that zone it is optional but not unnecessary — a map line is not a risk assessment. Boerne is in Kendall County; get a flood quote during the option period.
body:
## When it is required, and who is doing the requiring

Flood insurance is not required by the State of Texas. The requirement comes from the lender, and it is triggered by two conditions together: the structure sits in a **Special Flood Hazard Area** on the FEMA flood map, and the loan is **federally backed or federally regulated**, which covers conventional loans sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac as well as FHA, VA and USDA loans.

Meet both conditions and coverage is mandatory for the life of the loan. The lender orders a flood zone determination early, the requirement lands in your closing conditions, and it does not get negotiated away. If the policy is not in place, the loan does not fund.

Meet only one — an SFHA property bought with cash, or a financed property outside the SFHA — and nobody requires anything. That is where the real decision lives.

## The zones, and what the percentages actually mean

Texas Property Code §5.008 uses FEMA's two categories, and the statutory notice defines them precisely:

- **100-year floodplain**, which is the **Special Flood Hazard Area**: Zones **A, V, A99, AE, AO, AH, VE or AR**. These carry a **1% annual chance** of flooding.
- **500-year floodplain**, a moderate flood hazard area: **shaded Zone X**. A **0.2% annual chance**.

([Texas Property Code §5.008](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-5-008/))

"100-year flood" is the phrase that misleads people most. It is not an event that happens once a century. It is a 1% chance in any given year, every year, independently. Over a thirty-year mortgage, that compounds into something a homeowner should take seriously, and it says nothing about whether one occurred last year.

## A map line is not a risk assessment

This is the part that matters more than the zone designation itself. FEMA flood maps are engineering products with real limits. They are drawn on data of varying vintage, they are updated on a schedule that lags development, and in Hill Country terrain the topography changes over short distances. Upstream construction, new impervious cover, an undersized culvert or a low-water crossing can all move real-world risk without moving a line on a map.

The result is straightforward: a property outside the SFHA can still flood, and properties outside mapped flood zones do flood. Being in Zone X is a reason your lender will not require a policy. It is not evidence that water cannot reach the structure.

Two things worth doing regardless of the zone, both during the option period: look at the actual FEMA flood map for the parcel on the [FEMA Flood Map Service Center](https://msc.fema.gov/portal/home) — the official public source for flood hazard information produced in support of the National Flood Insurance Program, searchable by address — rather than a summary someone typed into a listing, and ask an **insurance agent** for a quote even if nothing requires one. Outside the SFHA the premium is frequently far lower than buyers assume, and a quote costs nothing to obtain.

## What the seller has to disclose about flooding in Texas

A seller of residential real property of **not more than one dwelling unit** must give the buyer the written notice prescribed by **Texas Property Code §5.008**, or one substantially similar ([Texas Property Code §5.008](https://texas.public.law/statutes/tex._prop._code_section_5.008)). The flood questions in that notice were added by **SB 339, 86th Legislature**, and are mandatory for contracts executed **on or after September 1, 2019** ([SB 339 enrolled text](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/86R/billtext/pdf/SB00339F.pdf)).

The notice asks the seller, in substance, whether:

- The property is located wholly or partly in a **100-year floodplain** (Special Flood Hazard Area).
- The property is located wholly or partly in a **500-year floodplain** (moderate flood hazard area).
- The property has **flooded at least once in the past 5 years**.
- The property is located in a **reservoir flood pool**.
- The property has been **repaired for flood damage**.
- The seller has **received assistance or flood insurance proceeds** for flood damage.

The current TREC version of the form is the **Seller's Disclosure Notice, form 55-1, effective 05/28/2026** ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

Read those answers carefully, and read the blanks carefully too. A seller answers to the best of their knowledge, and a seller who bought the house three years ago may not know what happened before that. "Unknown" is a common and often honest answer that tells you to go verify independently.

Note also that some sellers are **exempt from providing the form** — transfers pursuant to court order, foreclosures, transfers by a trustee in bankruptcy, transfers between co-owners, transfers to a spouse or descendant, transfers by a fiduciary administering an estate, and new residences not previously occupied. The exemption is from the form. It does not license misrepresentation. If the contract is signed before the seller has given the notice, the buyer may **terminate for any reason within 7 days after receiving it**.

## Boerne is Kendall County, and the property may not be in the city at all

Boerne is the county seat of **Kendall County**, in the Texas Hill Country. It is **not** in Bexar County and it is not the City of San Antonio. San Antonio's ordinances do not apply here, and neither do Bexar County's floodplain administration procedures.

Properties in and around Boerne fall into three regulatory situations: inside Boerne city limits, inside Boerne's extraterritorial jurisdiction, and in unincorporated Kendall County outside both. Floodplain development permitting, elevation requirements and the local floodplain administrator differ across those. Before assuming which set of rules applies, confirm the jurisdiction the parcel actually sits in with the **City of Boerne** or **Kendall County**.

## Get the quote during the option period, because it is a deadline

The option period is the window in which a Texas buyer can terminate for any reason. It is finite, it is negotiated rather than set by law, and it runs on **calendar days** from the effective date. The termination right expires at **5:00 p.m. local time** on the last day, whether or not your insurance quote came back.

The option fee is delivered to the escrow agent — the title company, not the seller — **within three days after the effective date**, rolling to the next business day if day three is a weekend or legal holiday ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/article/changes-delivery-option-fee-0)). Miss that delivery and there is no termination right to exercise.

So the flood work belongs on the same schedule as the inspection: pull the flood map for the parcel, read the seller's disclosure flood answers, and get a written quote from an insurance agent. A flood premium that arrives after the option period has closed is information you can no longer act on. On a financed purchase in an SFHA, an unexpected annual premium can also change the debt-to-income picture your lender approved, which is a reason to get the number in front of the loan officer early rather than late.

## Who to ask

Coverage, premiums, elevation certificates and whether a policy makes sense outside a mapped zone are questions for a **licensed insurance agent**. Whether your loan requires coverage is a **lender** question and depends on the flood zone determination they order. Floodplain designations, permitting and local elevation requirements come from the **City of Boerne** or **Kendall County**, depending on where the parcel sits. Disputes about what a seller disclosed or should have disclosed are for a **Texas real estate attorney**.
