question: Does Boerne, Texas flood?
metaTitle: Does Boerne, Texas flood?
metaDescription: FEMA zone codes, the five flood questions Texas form 55-1 asks under SB 339, and the option-period order for checking a Boerne address.
shortAnswer: Flood risk in Boerne is address-specific, not city-wide. Whether a particular property floods is determined by its FEMA flood zone, the seller's disclosure under Texas Property Code 5.008, and an insurance quote. A property outside the mapped Special Flood Hazard Area can still flood; the map is not a risk assessment.
body:
**This page does not assert a flood history for any specific Boerne property, street or subdivision.** Anyone who tells you a neighborhood "floods" or "never floods" without naming a map panel, a disclosure or a claims history is guessing. What follows is how to get the real answer on the address you care about, and the order to do it in.

## Step one: the FEMA flood map, and what the zone codes mean

Every property in the United States sits somewhere on a FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map. You find a specific address on the [FEMA Flood Map Service Center](https://msc.fema.gov/portal/home), which is the official public source for flood hazard information produced in support of the National Flood Insurance Program and searches by address, place or coordinates. The answer comes back as a zone designation.

Texas law builds its flood disclosure on the same two categories, defined in the statutory seller's notice ([Texas Property Code §5.008](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-5-008/)):

- **100-year floodplain — the Special Flood Hazard Area.** Zones **A, V, A99, AE, AO, AH, VE or AR**. These carry a **1% annual chance** of flooding.
- **500-year floodplain — moderate flood hazard.** **Shaded Zone X**, a **0.2% annual chance**.

Two things people misread. "100-year flood" is not a flood that happens once a century; it is the 1%-per-year event, and it can happen in consecutive years. And a zone is assigned to a mapped area, not measured on your slab — two houses on the same street can sit in different zones, and the line can run through a single lot.

If the property is in a Special Flood Hazard Area and there is a federally backed mortgage on it, flood insurance is generally a lender requirement, not a choice. That is a question for the lender and an insurance agent on the specific address.

## Step two: the seller's disclosure asks five flood questions, and it is statutory

Since **SB 339 of the 86th Legislature**, mandatory for contracts executed **on or after September 1, 2019**, the Texas statutory seller's disclosure notice includes explicit flood items ([SB 339](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/86R/billtext/pdf/SB00339F.pdf); [Texas Property Code §5.008](https://texas.public.law/statutes/tex._prop._code_section_5.008)).

The notice asks whether the property:

1. is located wholly or partly in a **100-year floodplain** (Special Flood Hazard Area);
2. is located wholly or partly in a **500-year floodplain** (moderate flood hazard area);
3. **has flooded at least once within the past 5 years**;
4. is located in a **reservoir flood pool**; and
5. **has been repaired for flood damage**, or whether the seller has **received assistance or flood insurance proceeds** for flood damage.

That third and fifth items are the ones that matter most, because they are history rather than mapping. A property can sit outside every mapped zone and still have a disclosed flood and a repair.

Two mechanics on the disclosure itself are worth knowing. The current TREC version of the form is **55-1, effective 05/28/2026** ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)). And if a contract is signed without the seller having delivered the notice, the **buyer may terminate for any reason within 7 days after receiving it** — a separate exit from the option period, on its own clock.

The disclosure is what the seller knows. Certain transfers are exempt from the form — foreclosure, court-ordered transfers, transfers by a trustee in bankruptcy, transfers between co-owners, transfers to a spouse or descendant, transfers by a fiduciary administering an estate, and new residences not previously occupied. On an exempt transfer you get no notice at all, which means the mapping and insurance work carries the entire load.

Renters have their own version: TREC publishes a **Landlord's Floodplain and Flood Notice, form 54-1, effective 11/26/2025**.

## Step three: a map designation is not a risk assessment

This is the part that gets people hurt.

FEMA maps are engineering products with a revision date, built on the drainage and development conditions that existed when the study was done. They do not model every creek, every low-water crossing, every undersized culvert, or the parking lot that got paved upstream after the map was drawn. **Property outside a Special Flood Hazard Area can and does flood.**

Boerne sits in the Hill Country, where **Cibolo Creek** runs. The Hill Country's combination of thin soil over limestone, steep relief and intense rainfall produces fast-rising water in creek and draw bottoms. The **[Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District](https://ccgcd.org/)** maintains stream gauges on **Cibolo Creek and the Guadalupe River**, along with roughly 42 monitor wells and more than 100 rain gauge sites — which is a reminder that surface water here is monitored in real time for a reason.

On a specific property, the questions that actually predict water are physical: where is the lot relative to the creek and to the nearest draw, where does the slab sit relative to the street, where does the neighborhood drain, and is there a low-water crossing between the house and the way out. Walk it, and walk it after a rain if you can.

## Step four: do the flood work inside the option period, because it has a deadline

The **option period** is the window in which a Texas buyer has an **unrestricted right to terminate** ([Texas Real Estate Research Center](https://trerc.tamu.edu/article/option-period-basics-2360/)). It is also the only window in which the flood questions can be answered in time to act on them.

The flood checklist for that window:

- **Pull the FEMA zone for the exact address**, not the subdivision.
- **Get an actual insurance quote** — not an estimate, a quote, on this address, from an insurance agent. Premium and availability are the market's own risk assessment, and they tell you things a map will not.
- **Ask whether an elevation certificate exists**, and whether one would change the rating. This is a surveyor question.
- **Read the seller's disclosure flood answers**, and ask follow-up questions in writing about anything checked or left blank.
- **Ask the City of Boerne** about drainage, floodplain development permits and any local floodplain information for the address. Boerne is in **Kendall County**, not Bexar County, and it is not in the City of San Antonio — San Antonio's floodplain pages and ordinances do not govern Boerne. City of Boerne: 201 East San Antonio Avenue, Boerne, TX 78006, 830-249-9343. For an address in unincorporated Kendall County, that question goes to the county.
- **Check the survey** for the floodplain line, if the survey shows one.

The mechanical trap is the one that catches every Texas buyer: the option fee must reach the **title company within three days of the effective date** or there is no termination right at all, no matter what the option period says ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/article/changes-delivery-option-fee-0)). Insurance quotes and elevation certificates take time. Start them on day one, not day seven.

## What an honest answer sounds like

"Does Boerne flood?" is the wrong shape of question. "Does 000 Example Street sit in Zone AE, has it flooded in the last five years per the seller's disclosure, and what will an insurer charge to write it?" is answerable, in about three business days, for the price of a phone call.

## Who answers which question

- **An insurance agent** — availability, premium, what the carrier's own model says, whether an elevation certificate changes the rate.
- **A surveyor** — elevation certificate, where the floodplain line falls on the lot.
- **The City of Boerne** (or Kendall County for unincorporated property) — drainage, floodplain development permits, local map information.
- **A lender** — whether flood insurance is required for the loan.
- **A Texas real estate attorney** — anything involving a disclosure that turns out to have been wrong.

question: Does Boerne have enough water?
metaTitle: Does Boerne have enough water?
metaDescription: Boerne draws on Canyon Lake water, City Lake and Trinity wells, while Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District sets Kendall County pumping limits.
shortAnswer: Boerne draws from three sources — Canyon Lake surface water purchased through the Guadalupe-Blanco River Authority, Boerne City Lake, and local wells in the Trinity Group aquifers. Supply is actively managed, not unlimited: the Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District sets drought stages and pumping rules countywide. Check ccgcd.org for the current stage.
body:
## Where the city's water actually comes from

Three sources, not one ([City of Boerne](https://www.ci.boerne.tx.us/FAQ.aspx?QID=315)):

1. **Canyon Lake surface water**, purchased through the **Guadalupe-Blanco River Authority**.
2. **Boerne City Lake.**
3. **Local wells in the Trinity Group aquifers.**

Diversification is the point. A city drawing from one source is exposed to whatever happens to that source. Boerne can lean on surface water when the aquifer is stressed and on groundwater when surface supply is short. That is a meaningfully better position than a single-source system, and it is also why "does Boerne have enough water" has no yes-or-no answer — it depends on which source, which year and which stage.

## Who regulates the groundwater

The **Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District** regulates groundwater in Kendall County and sets drought stages. It does that with real instrumentation: roughly **42 monitor wells**, stream gauges on **Cibolo Creek and the Guadalupe River**, and more than **100 rain gauge sites** ([Cow Creek GCD](https://ccgcd.org/)).

Drought stages in the district have moved between **Stage 2, Stage 3 and Stage 4** in recent years ([Boerne Star](https://www.boernestar.com/article/1520,cow-creek-moves-into-stage-3-drought)). Stage 4 emergency rules have been reported to carry a **mandatory reduction in allowable well pumping**.

This page does not state a current stage, on purpose. Stages change with conditions, and a number printed in any article — including this one — goes stale. **[ccgcd.org](https://ccgcd.org/) is the source.** Check it before you rely on a stage, and check it again before closing.

Cow Creek GCD is also a taxing entity that can appear on a Kendall County tax bill, alongside Kendall County WCID #1 and two MUDs ([Kendall Appraisal District](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)). Groundwater management here is a funded local government function, not an advisory committee.

## Growth is the pressure

**Kendall County grew 20.3 percent between 2020 and 2025**, from an estimated 44,568 to 53,289 residents, mostly through domestic migration ([Community Impact](https://communityimpact.com/san-antonio/boerne-fair-oaks-ranch/government/2026/03/30/kendall-county-population-increases-by-203-from-2020-2025/)).

More rooftops on a finite aquifer is the core tension in every Hill Country water conversation. It is why groundwater regulation exists here, why drought stages have teeth, and why a development that cannot document water does not get built at the density its plan assumed. Water availability is one of the quiet reasons Hill Country supply stays constrained and prices stay firm.

## A city tap and a well are two different purchases

This is the part that costs buyers money, and it has nothing to do with the city's overall supply.

**Inside the city limits**, you are a City of Boerne utility customer. The city manages source, treatment, distribution and drought restrictions. Your obligation is to follow watering restrictions and pay the bill. Supply risk is the city's problem to solve.

**On acreage outside the city**, the well is yours. Everything below is your diligence:

- **Yield.** Gallons per minute, tested — not "the seller says it's always been fine." A well that serves two people may not serve six with irrigation and livestock.
- **Depth, casing and pump condition.** Age, materials, and whether the pump is near end of life. Replacement is a five-figure conversation.
- **Which formation it draws from**, and how that formation has behaved through recent drought stages.
- **Shared wells.** A well serving more than one tract is governed by an agreement, and the quality of that agreement is a legal question.
- **District rules.** Permitting, registration and pumping limits under Cow Creek GCD, including what happens to your allowable pumping in a high drought stage.
- **Water quality testing**, separately from yield.
- **Storage and rainwater collection**, which many Hill Country properties use to buffer a low-yield well.

A general home inspection is not a well evaluation. A qualified water well contractor tests the well; **Cow Creek GCD** answers the permitting and pumping-rule questions; a **Texas real estate attorney** reads a shared-well agreement or a water-rights reservation in the chain of title.

## What the contract paperwork does and does not tell you

TREC promulgates a **Seller's Disclosure about Groundwater and Surface Water Rights, form 61-0, effective 07/01/2026** ([TREC contracts](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)). Its existence is the tell: water rights in Texas are separable from the surface estate and are worth disclosing on their own form.

The standard **Seller's Disclosure Notice** under Texas Property Code §5.008 covers property condition as the seller knows it ([Tex. Prop. Code §5.008](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-5-008/)). A seller cannot disclose an aquifer trend they do not know about, and there is no box on any form that certifies future yield. Disclosure is a floor, not a diligence plan.

## The realistic answer

Boerne has a managed, three-source supply and an active groundwater district with instrumentation and enforcement. That is better infrastructure than most Hill Country towns of its size, and it is the reason growth here has not run into a hard wall.

It is not an unlimited supply, and nobody local pretends otherwise. Drought stages have reached Stage 4 with mandatory pumping cuts. Landscaping expectations formed somewhere wetter do not survive here. And a buyer on a private well carries the risk personally, in a way a city utility customer does not.

Buy accordingly: check the current stage at [ccgcd.org](https://ccgcd.org/), confirm whether the address is on city water or a well before you write the offer, and put a real well evaluation inside the option period if it is a well.

question: Does Texas really have no state income tax, and what do I pay instead?
metaTitle: Does Texas really have no state income tax, and what do I pay instead?
metaDescription: Texas has no state income tax. What you pay instead: annual market-value reappraisal, a stacked local property tax bill, and 8.25% sales tax in Boerne.
shortAnswer: Yes. Texas has no state individual income tax. It funds local government mostly through property tax, and sales tax runs 6.25% state plus local add-ons to a maximum 8.25%, which is what Boerne charges. Texas property is reappraised at market value annually, subject to a 10% homestead cap.
body:
## The no-income-tax part is real

There is no asterisk on it. Texas does not levy a state individual income tax, so there is no state return to file on wages, and no state withholding line on a Texas paycheck. Federal tax obligations are unchanged.

What is misleading is the way the fact usually gets used. "No income tax" is presented as though the money simply is not collected. It is collected — it is collected locally, from property, and the mechanism it runs on is different enough from most states that a new resident should understand it before closing on a house.

## What replaces it: a stacked local property tax bill

A Texas property tax bill is not one rate set by the state. It is the **sum of every taxing entity whose boundary covers the parcel**, each of which adopts its own rate every fall.

For a home inside the Boerne city limits, in Boerne ISD, the 2025 stack looked like this, per $100 of taxable value:

| Entity | 2025 rate |
|---|---|
| Boerne ISD | **1.0109** (M&O 0.6969 + debt 0.3140) |
| City of Boerne | **0.4716** |
| Kendall County | **0.377** (M&O 0.317976 + debt 0.059024) |
| **Combined** | **1.8595** |

Sources: [Boerne ISD rates](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/295/Boerne-ISD), [City of Boerne rates](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/297/Boerne-City-of), [Kendall County rates](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/306/Kendall-County).

That 1.8595 is **before any special district on the parcel and before any exemption**. It is not a universal Boerne number. Depending on the address, the bill may also carry Kendall County MUD, Miralomas MUD, the Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District, or Kendall County WCID #1 ([Kendall AD](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)). Part of Kendall County is in **Comfort ISD**, whose 2025 rate was **0.9328** ([Kendall County](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/300/Kendall-County)).

The county rate has drifted down: 0.377 in 2025, 0.3827 in 2024 and 2023, 0.38770 in 2022, 0.412700 in 2021. **Kendall County's 2026 adopted rate is 0.373** (M&O 0.325765 + debt 0.047235). A falling rate does not automatically mean a falling bill, because the other half of the equation is the value.

Pull the entity list for your specific parcel from [kendallad.org](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/). Boerne is in **Kendall County**, not Bexar County, so the appraisal district is Kendall AD and not Bexar CAD, and San Antonio's rates and ordinances have nothing to do with it.

## The value side is the part that catches people

Texas appraisal districts value property at **market value and reappraise annually**. Once a homestead exemption is on the property, the increase in net appraised value is **capped at 10% per year** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)).

Two things follow.

First, the cap governs the rate of climb, not the ceiling. In a county where values are rising, a capped property can go up 10% a year for several years running, and the taxable value converges on market over time.

Second, **the cap only exists once the homestead exemption exists.** A property without one has no cap at all. That is why the first reappraisal after a purchase can move a long way, especially when the prior owner held it for years under a capped value.

## The exemptions that pull the number back down

- **School district residence homestead exemption: $140,000**, raised from $100,000 by **Proposition 13**, approved by Texas voters in **November 2025** and implemented by **SB 4, 89th Legislature**, effective for tax year 2026 ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)). Since the school rate is the biggest line, this is the largest single reduction on most bills.
- **Local option exemption**: taxing units may offer up to **20%** of appraised value, minimum $5,000.
- **Age 65 or older, or disabled**: school districts must grant an **additional $60,000**; other taxing units may adopt a local option of at least $3,000. Kendall AD notes that the City of Boerne, Boerne ISD, Comfort ISD and Kendall County offer over-65 and disability tax freezes ([Kendall AD](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)).
- **Counties collecting a farm-to-market or flood-control tax** must give a **$3,000** residence homestead exemption.

**The January 1 rule decides when any of it starts.** You must have **owned and occupied the home as your principal residence on January 1** of the tax year, and the application deadline is **before May 1** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)).

Close in February and the exemption takes effect the following year. The first year is the unexempted bill, on an uncapped value. If a lender builds the escrow estimate off that first bill, the payment is higher than the one you will settle into — and if the lender builds it off the *seller's* old exempted bill, it is lower, and the escrow shortage shows up a year later. Ask the lender which number they used.

Nobody files the exemption for you. Not the seller, not the title company, not the agent. It is a form filed with the appraisal district.

## Sales tax, and the other things that are not property tax

Texas state sales tax is **6.25%**, with local add-ons to a combined maximum of **8.25%**. **Boerne is at the maximum**: 6.25% state + 1.50% City of Boerne + 0.50% Kendall County ([City of Boerne](https://www.ci.boerne.tx.us/646/Current-Tax-Rates)).

For short-term rental operators, **hotel occupancy tax in Boerne is 13% total** — 6% state plus 7% city, remitted through the city portal.

## If the value looks wrong, there is a process and a deadline

The appraisal notice must be sent by **May 1**, or by **April 1** for a residence homestead, "or as soon as practical thereafter." The protest deadline is **May 15, or 30 days after the district mails the notice of appraised value, whichever is later** — counted from the **mailing** date, not the day it lands in your mailbox. If that falls on a weekend or holiday it rolls to the next business day ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/protests/)).

The notice of protest form is **Comptroller Form 50-132**, and a protest is sufficient if it identifies the property, the owner and a subject showing dissatisfaction, in writing. The appraisal review board must give **at least 15 days** notice of the hearing, and an owner may appear in person, by phone or videoconference, or by written affidavit.

## Who answers which question

- **Kendall Appraisal District** — exemptions, appraised value, which entities tax your parcel, protests.
- **A CPA or tax advisor** — whether the overall trade works in your favor, and anything involving a sale in your prior state. Nobody should give you a single "effective rate" comparison between two states as a reason to move; price your actual address.
- **A lender** — how the first-year tax figure is being used in your escrow estimate.

## Related questions

- [What should I know about moving from California to the Texas Hill Country?](/answers/moving-from-california-to-the-texas-hill-country)
- [What are property taxes like in Boerne?](/answers/what-are-property-taxes-like-in-boerne)
- [What is the Texas homestead exemption?](/answers/what-is-the-texas-homestead-exemption)

- [Why did my Texas property taxes go up?](/answers/why-did-my-texas-property-taxes-go-up)

question: How are rental properties taxed differently from a homestead in Texas?
metaTitle: How are rental properties taxed differently from a homestead in Texas?
metaDescription: A Texas rental gets no homestead exemption and no 10 percent cap, only the 20 percent circuit breaker under Tax Code 23.231, expiring December 31, 2026.
shortAnswer: A Texas rental gets no residence homestead exemption and no 10 percent homestead appraisal cap. It is instead covered by the separate 20 percent circuit breaker on non-homestead property under Tax Code Section 23.231, which applies to tax years 2024 through 2026 and expires December 31, 2026 unless the Legislature renews it.
body:
## The first difference: no homestead exemption

Texas homestead exemptions attach to a **residence homestead** — a property the owner owned and occupied as a principal residence on **January 1** of the tax year. A rental is not that, so none of the following apply to it ([Texas Comptroller, *Property Tax Exemptions*](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)):

- The **$140,000 school district residence homestead exemption**, raised from $100,000 by **Proposition 13**, approved by Texas voters in **November 2025** and implemented by **SB 4 of the 89th Legislature**, effective for tax year 2026.
- The **additional $60,000** school district exemption for owners **age 65 or older or disabled**.
- The **local option** homestead exemption of up to **20 percent** of appraised value that a taxing unit may offer, with a $5,000 minimum.
- The **$3,000** residence homestead exemption required from counties that collect a farm-to-market or flood-control tax.

On a rental, the taxable value is the appraised value. Nothing comes off the top.

The over-65 school tax ceiling is in the same category — it freezes school taxes on a **residence homestead** for a qualifying owner, and it has nothing to offer a rental. In Kendall County, several jurisdictions offer over-65 and disability tax freezes, named by [Kendall Appraisal District](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/) as the City of Boerne, Boerne ISD, Comfort ISD and Kendall County — all of which are homestead-linked.

## The second difference: no 10 percent cap

The **10 percent annual cap** on increases in net appraised value applies to properties that already have a homestead exemption. It is the mechanism that keeps a homeowner's taxable value from tracking a fast-rising market in real time.

A rental does not get it. On a non-homestead property the appraised value can move with the market, subject only to the circuit breaker below.

That difference compounds over a hold period. Two identical houses on the same street, one owner-occupied and one rented, can drift meaningfully apart in taxable value over several years of appreciation — and the gap runs against the investor.

## The third difference: the circuit breaker, and its expiration date

**Tax Code Section 23.231** caps the appraised value of **non-homestead real property** at or below an annually indexed threshold, limiting increases to **20 percent** per year. It was created by **SB 2 (2023)** as a pilot covering tax years **2024, 2025 and 2026**, and it **expires December 31, 2026 unless the Legislature renews it** ([Travis CAD](https://traviscad.org/circuitbreaker), [summary of the 2023 Texas property tax law changes](https://resolutepts.com/texas-property-tax-law-changes/)).

It excludes land receiving agricultural special appraisal and homesteads already covered by the 10 percent cap.

The threshold is indexed annually and published sources disagree on the current figure, so confirm it with the appraisal district for any property anywhere near it. For most residential rentals in Kendall County the threshold is not the operative question anyway; the expiration date is.

**That sunset is the single most actionable fact on this page for an investor.** A multi-year pro forma written in 2026 that assumes 20 percent as a permanent ceiling on appraised value is assuming a statute with a scheduled end date. Model the hold both with and without it, and watch the 2027 legislative session.

## What does not change: the protest right

An investor has the same right to protest as a homeowner, and on a property with no exemptions and no meaningful cap, the protest is doing more work.

- **Deadline: May 15, or 30 days after the appraisal district mails the notice of appraised value, whichever is later.** The clock runs from the **mailing** date, not from when the notice arrives. A deadline falling on a weekend or holiday rolls to the next business day.
- The notice of appraised value must be sent by **May 1**, or by **April 1** for a residence homestead, "or as soon as practical thereafter" under Tax Code Section 25.19. A rental is on the later schedule.
- The notice of protest is **Comptroller Form 50-132**, and a protest is sufficient if it identifies the property, the owner, and a subject showing dissatisfaction, in writing.
- The appraisal review board must give **at least 15 days** notice of the hearing, and an owner may appear in person, by phone or videoconference, or by written affidavit.

Source: [Texas Comptroller, *Property Tax Protests*](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/protests/).

For a Boerne or Kendall County rental, the protest goes to **Kendall Appraisal District (kendallad.org)**. **Boerne is in Kendall County — not Bexar County and not the City of San Antonio**, so Bexar CAD deadlines, notices and portals are the wrong ones.

## The income-tax side belongs to a CPA

Property tax is only half of what changes. A rental also becomes an income-producing asset on the owner's federal return, and that brings in a set of questions this page will not answer because they are decided filer by filer:

- **Depreciation** — the recovery period, the method, and what portion of basis is depreciable versus allocated to land.
- **Depreciation recapture** on sale.
- **Passive activity loss rules** and whether losses are currently deductible, suspended, or usable against other income.
- **Which expenses are deductible**, and the line between a repair and a capital improvement.
- **The interaction with a [1031 exchange](/answers/what-is-a-1031-exchange)** and the basis that carries forward.
- **Hotel occupancy tax** if the property is operated as a short-term rental — 13 percent combined in Boerne, 6 percent state and 7 percent city.

Every one of those is **a CPA or tax advisor's** work. Texas has no state individual income tax, which changes the arithmetic but not the questions.

## The conversion moment, which people get wrong

Two timing traps are worth naming.

**January 1 governs.** Homestead qualification depends on owning and occupying the property as a principal residence on January 1 of the tax year. A property converted to a rental mid-year does not lose its homestead treatment retroactively for that year — but the following January 1 is a hard line.

**Keeping an exemption you are no longer entitled to is not a savings strategy.** An exemption that stays on a property after it stops being the owner's residence is an exposure, and appraisal districts do check. **Kendall Appraisal District** is the right place to sort out what applies to a specific property and what has to be removed.

## The short version

| | Homestead | Rental |
|---|---|---|
| School district exemption | $140,000 | none |
| Over-65 additional school exemption | $60,000 | none |
| Local option exemption up to 20 percent | available | none |
| Annual appraisal cap | 10 percent | 20 percent circuit breaker, through tax year 2026 |
| Over-65 school tax ceiling | yes | no |
| Protest right | yes | yes |

## Related questions

- [What is the Texas homestead exemption?](/answers/what-is-the-texas-homestead-exemption)
- [What is the 10 percent homestead cap in Texas?](/answers/what-is-the-10-percent-homestead-cap-in-texas)
- [What is a 1031 exchange?](/answers/what-is-a-1031-exchange)
- [What is the BRRRR method, and does it work in Texas?](/answers/what-is-the-brrrr-method-and-does-it-work-in-texas)
- [What are property taxes like in Boerne?](/answers/what-are-property-taxes-like-in-boerne)

question: How do I file for a homestead exemption in Kendall County, Texas?
metaTitle: How do I file for a homestead exemption in Kendall County, Texas?
metaDescription: File with Kendall Appraisal District, not Bexar CAD: own and occupy by January 1, apply free before May 1, and take the $140,000 school exemption.
shortAnswer: File with the Kendall Appraisal District at kendallad.org, not Bexar CAD. Boerne is in Kendall County. You must have owned and occupied the home as your principal residence on January 1, and the application is due before May 1. There is no fee to file directly with the district.
body:
## Start with the district, because this is where people go wrong

Boerne is the county seat of **Kendall County**. It is not in Bexar County and it is not in the City of San Antonio. A Boerne homeowner files a homestead exemption with the **Kendall Appraisal District** ([kendallad.org](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)).

This trips up relocating buyers constantly, because "San Antonio" is the metro name, the airport, the MLS region and the way most people describe where they live. None of that changes jurisdiction. Bexar Appraisal District appraises property in Bexar County. It does not appraise property in Kendall County, and an application sent there for a Boerne home does not get forwarded into a different county's roll.

The same logic applies in reverse. Parts of Fair Oaks Ranch sit in Bexar and Comal counties as well as Kendall, because the city's limits span all three. The appraisal district is set by which county the **parcel** is in, not which city mails your water bill.

## Where to actually file

This is the office. It is in Boerne, and it is not Bexar CAD ([Kendall Appraisal District](https://kendallad.org/)).

| | |
|---|---|
| Address | **118 Market Avenue, Boerne, TX 78006** |
| Phone | **(830) 249-8012** |
| Email | **requestinfo@kendallad.org** |
| Appraisal and Operations hours | Monday to Friday, **8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.** |
| Tax Collection hours | Monday to Friday, **8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.** |
| Property search | **[esearch.kendallad.org](https://esearch.kendallad.org/)** |
| Taxpayer Portal — exemptions and protests | **[eprotest.kendallad.org](https://eprotest.kendallad.org/)** |

Two of those are worth separating, because people conflate them. **esearch** is the public property search — use it to pull the account for a specific parcel and see which taxing units are on it and what exemptions are currently posted. **The Taxpayer Portal at eprotest.kendallad.org is the transactional side** — it is where exemption applications and protests are handled online. The name says "eprotest," but exemptions run through it too, which is why homeowners who only want to file a homestead exemption sometimes skip past it.

Note the two different closing times. Appraisal and Operations runs to 5:00 p.m.; Tax Collection closes at 4:00 p.m. If you are driving to Boerne to pay something rather than to ask something, the earlier clock is the one that governs.

## The two qualifying facts

You must have **owned** the home and **occupied it as your principal residence on January 1** of the tax year ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)). Both, on that date. Not "closed in January." Not "moved in over the holidays and finalized later."

If you bought in the middle of the year, you were not the January 1 owner-occupant of that property. That is the ordinary rule, and it is the reason a first tax bill on a new purchase so often looks different from what the listing or the prior owner's bill suggested. Whether any exception applies to a specific purchase is a question for the appraisal district.

## The deadline, and what happens if you miss it

The exemption application is due **before May 1**, which is generally described as April 30 ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)). The appraisal district publishes its current forms and filing instructions on its site.

Filing is **free** when you do it directly with the appraisal district. Newly closed buyers in Kendall County reliably get official-looking mail offering to file the homestead exemption for a fee. That is a paid service for a form you can submit yourself, and the letters are not from the county.

## What the exemption stack looks like on a Kendall County bill

Your bill is not one tax. It is the sum of every taxing unit that covers your parcel, and each one handles exemptions separately. In Kendall County, the entities that appear on tax bills include **Boerne ISD, Comfort ISD, City of Boerne, Kendall County, Kendall County MUD, Miralomas MUD, Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District and Kendall County WCID #1** ([Kendall Appraisal District](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)).

The mandatory piece is the school district's **$140,000** residence homestead exemption for 2026, raised from $100,000 by **Proposition 13**, approved by voters in **November 2025** and implemented through **SB 4, 89th Legislature** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)). On top of that, any taxing unit may adopt a **local option exemption of up to 20% of appraised value** with a $5,000 minimum, and a county collecting a farm-to-market road or flood control tax must give **$3,000**.

Which local options each Kendall County entity has actually adopted, and at what amount, is published on the appraisal district's [adopted tax rates and exemptions page](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/). Read that page rather than assuming — adopted exemptions are a local decision made entity by entity, and they can change year to year.

## The over-65 and disability freezes, by entity

Kendall Appraisal District notes that some jurisdictions offer **over-65 and disability tax "freezes."** The ones it names are the **City of Boerne, Boerne ISD, Comfort ISD and Kendall County** ([Kendall Appraisal District](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)).

That is a meaningful local detail. The school district tax ceiling for owners 65 and older is required statewide, but a city or county freeze is a local option, and not every Texas city or county has one. If you are 65 or older and moving into Boerne from somewhere else in Texas, the entity-by-entity picture here is different from what you left, and the appraisal district is the place to confirm what applies to your parcel.

Owners 65 or older or disabled also get an **additional $60,000** school district exemption on top of the general homestead amount, and other taxing units may adopt a local option of at least $3,000 ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)).

## What filing also turns on

Once a homestead exemption is in place, the property gets the **10% cap** on annual increases in net appraised value. In a county that grew 20.3% between 2020 and 2025, that cap does real work over time — and it resets to market value when the property sells, which is why a new owner's bill can jump well past what the seller was paying.

## Where the tax rates actually come from

The appraisal district sets **value** and administers **exemptions**. It does not set tax rates. Rates are adopted by each taxing unit's own governing body, and they move independently.

For context on scale: the **City of Boerne rate was 0.4716 per $100 of taxable value for 2025**, the same as 2024, after 0.4766 in 2023 and 0.4510 in 2022 ([Kendall County](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/297/Boerne-City-of)). **Boerne ISD adopted 1.0109 for 2025** — 0.6969 maintenance and operations plus 0.3140 debt — after 0.9909 in 2024, 0.9932 in 2023, 1.1786 in 2022 and 1.2046 in 2021 ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/295/Boerne-ISD)). Current adopted rates for every Kendall County entity are posted on the [county's tax rate information page](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/184/Tax-Rate-Information) and on the [appraisal district's page](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/).

## Practical sequence after you close

1. Confirm the parcel is in Kendall County, not Bexar or Comal.
2. Wait until the deed is recorded and the appraisal district shows you as owner. Look the account up at [esearch.kendallad.org](https://esearch.kendallad.org/) to check.
3. File the residence homestead application directly with Kendall AD, free — through the [Taxpayer Portal](https://eprotest.kendallad.org/), by mail or in person at 118 Market Avenue.
4. If you are 65 or older, disabled, or a disabled veteran, file for those exemptions at the same time — they are separate from the general homestead exemption.
5. Check the following year's notice of appraised value to confirm the exemption actually posted.

Step 5 gets skipped, and it is the one that catches a filing that never landed.

Eligibility, the current application form and the status of your exemption are all determined by the Kendall Appraisal District. For how an ownership change, a trust, an LLC or an inheritance affects your exemption, talk with a Texas real estate attorney, and take the tax consequences to a CPA.

## Related questions

- [What is the Texas homestead exemption in 2026?](/answers/what-is-the-texas-homestead-exemption)
- [What is the Texas over-65 property tax exemption and school tax ceiling?](/answers/texas-over-65-property-tax-exemption-and-school-tax-ceiling)
- [How do I protest my property taxes in Texas?](/answers/how-do-i-protest-my-property-taxes-in-texas)
- [What are property taxes like in Boerne?](/answers/what-are-property-taxes-like-in-boerne)
- [What is the 10 percent homestead cap in Texas?](/answers/what-is-the-10-percent-homestead-cap-in-texas)

## Questions about a specific property?

Call or text **[830-446-3847](tel:+1-830-446-3847)** · Email **[heath.shepard@kw.com](mailto:heath.shepard@kw.com)**

---

*This page explains how homestead exemption filing works in Kendall County. It is not tax or legal advice. Exemption eligibility is determined by the Kendall Appraisal District, and tax consequences should go to a CPA.*

question: How do I protest my property taxes in Texas?
metaTitle: How do I protest my property taxes in Texas?
metaDescription: The Texas protest deadline is May 15 or 30 days after the district mails your notice. File Form 50-132; the ARB owes you 15 days hearing notice.
shortAnswer: File a written notice of protest with your appraisal district by May 15, or 30 days after the district mails your notice of appraised value, whichever is later. Comptroller Form 50-132 works. The appraisal review board must give at least 15 days notice of the hearing, which you may attend in person, by phone, by video or by affidavit.
body:
## You are not protesting the tax. You are protesting the value.

This distinction decides whether a protest goes anywhere. The appraisal district determines **value** and administers **exemptions**. Tax **rates** are set by each taxing unit's governing body — the school board, the city council, the commissioners court. The appraisal review board cannot lower a rate, and arguing at a hearing that your bill is too high is arguing to the wrong body.

What you can protest at the appraisal district is the district's work: the appraised value, whether it is unequal compared with similar properties, whether the district has your property's characteristics right, whether an exemption was wrongly denied, and other determinations that affect your liability ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/protests/)).

## The deadline, stated exactly

**May 15, or 30 days after the appraisal district mails the notice of appraised value, whichever is later** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/protests/)).

Three details inside that sentence do real work:

- **"Whichever is later."** A late-mailed notice extends your deadline. It does not shorten it. If the district mails on May 20, you get 30 days from May 20, not until May 15.
- **Counted from mailing, not delivery.** The clock starts when the district drops it in the mail. Mail that sits in a forwarded box or a vacation hold is still running. Ask the district for the mailing date if the postmark is gone.
- **Weekends and holidays roll forward.** A deadline that lands on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday moves to the next business day.

The district is required to send the notice of appraised value by **May 1**, or by **April 1 for a residence homestead**, or as soon as practical after ([Tax Code §25.19, via the Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/protests/)). Homesteads get the earlier notice, which in practice means homeowners have more runway than owners of other property types.

## Filing it is simpler than people expect

A protest is sufficient if it is **in writing** and identifies:

- the property,
- the property owner, and
- a subject showing the owner is dissatisfied with some determination of the appraisal district.

([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/protests/))

That is the whole bar. There is a standard form — **Comptroller Form 50-132, Notice of Protest** — and most districts accept online filing, but the statute does not require a specific format. A letter that identifies the property and says what you disagree with works.

Because the bar is that low, there is no strategic reason to skip filing while you decide whether to pursue it. File, then work the case. Withdrawing later costs nothing.

For a Boerne or Kendall County property, this goes to the **Kendall Appraisal District** ([kendallad.org](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)). Boerne is in Kendall County, not Bexar County and not in the City of San Antonio, so Bexar CAD's deadlines, portals and procedures are not yours.

## What happens next

The **appraisal review board must give you at least 15 days notice** of the hearing date, time and place ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/protests/)).

You may appear:

- **in person**,
- **by telephone or videoconference**, or
- **by written affidavit**.

The affidavit option gets overlooked. An owner who cannot take a weekday morning off, or who has moved out of state, can still put evidence in front of the board in writing. It is a real option, not a formality.

Many districts also offer an informal conference with an appraiser before the formal hearing. A large share of protests resolve there. It is worth asking whether the district offers one and taking it.

## What evidence actually moves a value

The board decides on evidence. The arguments that carry weight are the ones that attack the district's own inputs:

- **Condition.** Foundation movement, a roof at end of life, failed septic, deferred maintenance, an unpermitted addition. Photographs and contractor bids, not descriptions.
- **Characteristics that are wrong.** Square footage, year built, bathroom count, pool that is not there, a second structure that was demolished. Districts appraise from records, and records go stale.
- **Comparable sales.** What similar properties actually sold for around January 1 of the tax year. Not asking prices.
- **Unequal appraisal.** Your value compared with the appraised values of comparable properties in the district. This is a separate ground from market value and sometimes the stronger one.
- **An exemption that was denied or never posted.** Check the notice for the exemptions you expect to see; a missing homestead exemption is its own problem and often a bigger number than a value argument.

Hill Country acreage has its own set of issues that districts frequently miss: usable versus unusable slope, actual road access, whether the well produces, whether a floodplain crosses the buildable area, and whether an ag or wildlife valuation is being applied correctly.

## After the ARB

If you disagree with the board's determination, Texas provides appeal routes beyond the ARB, including judicial appeal and, for some matters, binding arbitration or an appeal to the State Office of Administrative Hearings. Each has its own deadline, filing requirement and cost, and the right route depends on the property type and what is being disputed. That is a question for a Texas real estate attorney or a licensed property tax consultant, not something to work out from a web page.

## Two things worth checking before you protest

**Is the homestead cap already holding your value down?** A homesteaded property's net appraised value cannot rise more than **10% per year**. If the cap is already limiting what you are taxed on, the market value shown on the notice may be well above your taxable value, and the protest math is different from what the headline number suggests.

**Do you own non-homestead property?** A separate **20% circuit breaker** under **Tax Code §23.231** limits annual appraised value increases on qualifying non-homestead real property valued at or below a threshold that is **indexed annually** — confirm the current figure with your appraisal district. It was created by **SB 2 (2023)** as a pilot for tax years **2024, 2025 and 2026**, and it **expires after the 2026 tax year** unless the Legislature renews it. No application is required; the district applies it automatically, and the owner must have held the property for at least one full calendar year to qualify ([Travis Central Appraisal District](https://traviscad.org/circuitbreaker)). Check your notice to see whether it was applied, and plan for the possibility that it is gone in 2027.

## The honest expectation

A protest is not a negotiation over what you want to pay. It is an evidentiary argument about what the property was worth on January 1 and whether the district appraised it the way it appraised similar property. Owners who bring documents win more than owners who bring opinions.

Value, exemptions and hearing procedure are all determined by the appraisal district and its review board. For appeal strategy beyond the ARB, talk to a Texas real estate attorney or a licensed property tax consultant, and take any tax consequences to a CPA.

question: How do I terminate a real estate contract in Texas?
metaTitle: How do I terminate a real estate contract in Texas?
metaDescription: The real exits: the option period, the financing addendum, the 7-day disclosure right under 5.008, and why escrow release is a separate event.
shortAnswer: You terminate a Texas contract by exercising a right the contract gives you and delivering written notice — most commonly during the option period using TREC form 38-8. Terminating the contract and getting the earnest money back are two separate events: escrowed funds cannot be released without mutual agreement or a court order.
body:
## The rule underneath all of it

A signed contract is binding. You do not get out of it because you changed your mind. You get out of it because the contract, or a statute, gave you a right to get out of it — and you exercised that right the way it says to, before it expired.

So the first question is never "how do I cancel." It is "which right do I have, and when does it die."

## Route one: the option period

This is the clean exit, and it is the one most terminations use.

Paragraph 5B of the contract grants the buyer "the **unrestricted right to terminate** this contract by giving notice of termination to Seller within [blank] days after the Effective Date of this contract (Option Period)," and specifies that "Notices under this paragraph must be given **by 5:00 p.m. (local time where the Property is located)** by the date specified" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶5B](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). No justification required, no inspection report needed, no argument with the seller.

Paragraph 5B also states the outcome: "(i) **the option fee will not be refunded** and Escrow Agent shall release any option fee remaining with Escrow Agent to Seller; and (ii) **any earnest money will be refunded to Buyer**."

TREC publishes the form for the notice: **Notice of Buyer's Termination of Contract, form 38-8, effective 04/01/2025** ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

Days are counted as **calendar days**, with the effective date as day zero. A ten-day option period on a contract with a November 1 effective date expires at 5:00 p.m. on November 11.

Three things kill this route, and ¶5D names the first two:

> "If **no dollar amount is stated** as the option fee or if Buyer fails to deliver the option fee within the time required, **Buyer shall not have the unrestricted right to terminate** this contract under this paragraph 5."

**Late option fee delivery.** Paragraph 5A requires delivery to the Escrow Agent — the title company, not the seller — within **3 days after the Effective Date**. Paragraph 5A(2) extends that only if the last day is a Saturday, Sunday or Legal Holiday, defined by reference to Texas Government Code Sections 662.003(a) and 662.003(b)(4) and (6). Paragraph 5E: "**Time is of the essence** for this paragraph and strict compliance with the time for performance is required."

**A blank option fee.** Nothing to do with timing. A contract with an option period filled in but the option fee dollar blank left empty confers no unrestricted right to terminate at all. Read your own executed ¶5A and confirm a dollar figure is in it.

**The 5:00 p.m. deadline.** Not a soft deadline. An inspector who could not get out until the following Tuesday does not extend it. If more time is needed, the option period is extended in writing on the **Amendment to Contract, form 39-11, effective 07/01/2026**, signed by both parties before the current period expires ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

## Route two: the financing addendum

Once the option period ends, the financing exit is usually the most important one left standing.

The **Third Party Financing Addendum, form 40-11, effective 01/03/2025** governs it ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)). It creates a right to terminate tied to the buyer's ability to obtain approval for the financing described in the addendum, with its own deadline running from the effective date.

The failure mode is specific and it is common: the buyer assumes "my loan fell through" is self-executing. It is not. The right has a deadline, and it requires written notice. A buyer whose loan dies after the addendum's deadline has passed is in a contract with no financing exit and earnest money exposed.

Related exits with their own forms and their own clocks:

- **Addendum Concerning Right to Terminate Due to Lender's Appraisal, form 49-1** — the low-appraisal exit.
- **Addendum for Sale of Other Property by Buyer, form 10-6** — the home-sale contingency.
- **Addendum for Property Subject to Mandatory Membership in a Property Owners Association, form 36-11, effective 07/01/2026** — HOA subdivision information and resale certificate.

There is one more financing-adjacent trap worth naming. If the buyer elected to obtain the survey under **¶6C(2)** and then failed to, the contract says the buyer "**may not terminate** the contract under Paragraph 2B of the Third Party Financing Addendum because the survey was not obtained" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6C(2)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). A forgotten survey order can close the financing exit.

Read the deadline on every addendum attached to your contract the day it is signed, not the week it expires.

## Route three: the seller's disclosure right under §5.008 and ¶7B

This one surprises people because it can outlive the option period entirely, and the contract version is stronger than most buyers realize.

Texas Property Code §5.008 requires a seller of residential real property of **not more than one dwelling unit** to give the buyer a written notice of the property's condition ([Texas Property Code §5.008](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-5-008/), [statute text](https://texas.public.law/statutes/tex._prop._code_section_5.008)).

Paragraph 7B of the contract implements it as a **check one box only** election, and option (2) is the one that creates the right:

> "If Buyer does **not receive** the Seller's Disclosure Notice, **Buyer may terminate this contract at any time prior to the closing** and the earnest money will be refunded to Buyer. If Seller delivers the Seller's Disclosure Notice, **Buyer may terminate this contract for any reason within 7 days after Buyer receives** the Seller's Disclosure Notice **or prior to the closing, whichever first occurs**, and the earnest money will be refunded to Buyer."

([TREC form 20-19, ¶7B(2)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf))

Two distinct rights in one paragraph. While the notice is outstanding, the buyer can terminate **at any time prior to closing** — an open-ended exit with earnest money refunded. Once it is delivered, that collapses into **7 days after receipt, or prior to closing, whichever comes first**.

"For any reason" is the same unrestricted standard as the option period, and the seven days run from **receipt**, not from the effective date. A seller who delivers the disclosure two weeks into the contract has just handed the buyer a fresh seven-day window. A seller who never delivers it has left the exit open until the closing table.

Option (3) of ¶7B is the exemption box — the seller is not required to furnish the notice under the Texas Property Code. The statutory exemptions include transfers pursuant to court order, foreclosure, a trustee in bankruptcy, transfers between co-owners, transfers to a spouse or a descendant, transfers by a fiduciary administering an estate, and new residences not previously occupied. Exemption from the form is not a license to misrepresent the property.

The current TREC version of the notice is **Seller's Disclosure Notice, form 55-1, effective 05/28/2026** ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

## Route four: title — ¶6B and ¶6D

Two title-side exits, both easy to miss because they run on the title company's timeline rather than the buyer's.

**The commitment never arrives.** Paragraph 6B requires the seller to furnish the title commitment "**within 20 days after the Title Company receives a copy of this contract**." If it is late, delivery is "automatically extended up to **15 days or 3 days before the Closing Date, whichever is earlier**." If it still has not been delivered within the time required, "**Buyer may terminate this contract and the earnest money will be refunded to Buyer**" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6B](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

**Objections are not cured.** Under ¶6D the buyer may object in writing to defects, exceptions or encumbrances disclosed on the survey or in the commitment, by the earlier of the closing date or a stated number of days after receiving the commitment, exception documents and survey. Then:

- Failure to object in time "**will constitute a waiver** of Buyer's right to object," except that Schedule C requirements are not waived.
- Provided the seller is not obligated to incur expense, the seller cures timely objections within a **15-day Cure Period**, with the closing date extended as necessary.
- If the objections are not cured, the buyer has **5 days after the end of the Cure Period** to terminate with the earnest money refunded, or to waive. **Silence is a waiver.**

That last line is the whole point. The 5-day window is not a grace period — it is a decision deadline, and the default outcome of doing nothing is that the buyer takes the property with the defect.

A revised commitment, revised survey or new exception document restarts the same objection window as to the new matter.

## Route five: casualty — ¶14

If the property is damaged or destroyed by fire or other casualty after the effective date, ¶14 requires the seller to restore it "as soon as reasonably possible, but in any event by the Closing Date."

If the seller fails to do so due to factors beyond the seller's control, the buyer may (a) **terminate and have the earnest money refunded**, (b) extend the time for performance up to **15 days**, or (c) accept the property in its damaged condition with an assignment of insurance proceeds if the carrier permits, plus **a credit from the seller at closing in the amount of the deductible** ([TREC form 20-19, ¶14](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

## Route six: the seller terminates

Sellers have far fewer exits. TREC publishes a **Notice of Seller's Termination of Contract, form 50-0**, but the form does not create a right — it papers one the contract already gave the seller ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

The two that exist in the base form:

**Late earnest money, under ¶5C.** If the buyer fails to timely deliver the earnest money, the seller may terminate the contract, exercise the remedies under ¶15, or both — but only "by providing notice to Buyer **before Buyer delivers the earnest money**" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶5C](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). That is a narrow window. A seller who sits on it until the wire lands has lost it.

**Buyer default, under ¶15.** The seller may "(a) enforce **specific performance**, seek such other relief as may be provided by law, or both, or (b) terminate this contract and **receive the earnest money as liquidated damages**, thereby releasing both parties from this contract."

A seller who simply wants out because a better offer arrived does not have a termination right, and acting as though they do creates real exposure. That conversation belongs with a Texas real estate attorney before anything is sent.

## Route seven: both parties agree

Anything the parties both sign is enforceable between them. A mutual termination and release, signed by buyer and seller, ends the contract and directs where the earnest money goes. This is how most messy situations actually resolve, and it is the fastest path when both sides want out.

## Terminating and getting your money back are two different things

This is the part that generates almost all of the frustration.

Termination is unilateral when you hold the right. Notice goes out, the contract ends.

**Release of escrowed earnest money is not unilateral.** It requires both parties to sign a release, or a court order ([Texas Real Estate Research Center](https://trerc.tamu.edu/article/option-period-basics-2360/)). The title company is neutral. It does not adjudicate who was right. If the seller declines to sign — out of disagreement, or out of pique — the money sits in escrow while the contract is already dead.

The option fee behaves differently and worse for the buyer. Under ¶5A(4) the buyer authorizes the escrow agent to release it to the seller "at any time without further notice to or consent from Buyer" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶5A(4)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). It may already be gone.

The practical consequence is that your leverage is the quality of your paperwork. A termination that was timely, in writing, on the right form, delivered the way the contract requires, and documented, leaves a refusing seller with nothing to stand on. A sloppy one gives them an argument, and an argument is all it takes to freeze the money.

If a release stalls, the next step is a Texas real estate attorney and the contract's dispute provisions. There is no version of this where the title company breaks the tie for you.

## A short checklist before you send anything

1. Identify the exact right you are exercising — ¶5B option period, the Third Party Financing Addendum, the appraisal addendum, ¶7B(2) for the seller's disclosure, ¶6B or ¶6D on title, ¶14 casualty, or mutual agreement.
2. Confirm the deadline for that right, counted from the correct effective date.
3. Use the correct promulgated form.
4. Deliver it the way the contract specifies delivery, to the party it specifies, before the time it specifies — and for ¶5B, before 5:00 p.m. local time where the property is located.
5. Keep proof of delivery.
6. Send the earnest money release request as a separate, parallel action — and expect it to take longer.

The contract this all runs on is the **One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), TREC form 20-19, effective 07/01/2026** — 12 pages, footer-dated 05-04-2026 ([TREC form 20-19 PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf), [TREC form page](https://www.trec.texas.gov/forms/one-four-family-residential-contract-resale)) — or the corresponding promulgated form for a condo, new home, land or farm and ranch transaction, where the paragraph numbers differ.

One last thing worth saying plainly: ¶23 of the contract is titled **CONSULT AN ATTORNEY BEFORE SIGNING** and states that "TREC rules prohibit real estate brokers and sales agents from giving legal advice." Your agent can tell you what the deadline is and send the form. Whether you have a right to terminate in a contested situation is a legal question, and it goes to a Texas real estate attorney.

## Related questions

- [What is earnest money in Texas, and is it refundable?](/answers/what-is-earnest-money-in-texas-and-is-it-refundable)

question: How does the option fee work in Texas?
metaTitle: How does the option fee work in Texas?
metaDescription: How the Texas option fee works: who it goes to, the three-day delivery deadline, the combined-payment trap, release to the seller, and the credit at closing.
shortAnswer: The option fee is a negotiated amount the buyer delivers to the escrow agent — the title company, not the seller — within three days after the effective date. It pays for the unrestricted right to terminate. If the sale closes, the fee is credited to the sales price. If the buyer terminates, the seller keeps it.
body:
## What the money actually buys

The option fee is consideration. It is not a deposit, it is not part of the down payment, and it is not held for the buyer's benefit. It is payment for a contractual right.

Paragraph 5B of the current contract says it directly: "For nominal consideration, the receipt of which Seller acknowledges, and Buyer's agreement to pay the option fee within the time required, Seller grants Buyer the **unrestricted right to terminate** this contract by giving notice of termination to Seller within [blank] days after the Effective Date of this contract (Option Period)" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶5B](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

Unrestricted means unrestricted. Not "if the inspection is bad." Not "if the appraisal is low." Any reason, or none.

That distinction matters because it changes how everything downstream behaves. Earnest money is the buyer's money sitting in escrow. The option fee is the seller's money the moment the right is purchased — the escrow agent is just the delivery point.

## The amount is negotiated, not set by law

There is no statutory option fee in Texas, and TREC does not set one. Paragraph 5A of form 20-19 is a fill-in-the-blank: "$____ as earnest money and $____ as the option fee." The number is whatever the buyer and seller agree to, the same way they agree to the sales price ([TREC form 20-19, ¶5A](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

In practice the amount tracks the length of the option period and the competitiveness of the offer. A buyer asking for a longer window generally pays more for it. A buyer trying to win a multiple-offer situation may put up a larger non-refundable fee as a signal of seriousness. Commonly reported figures sit in the low hundreds of dollars, but that is market convention reported by practitioners, not a rule — the number is whatever the parties write down.

## Where the fee goes, and by when

Paragraph 5A: "**Within 3 days after the Effective Date**, Buyer must deliver to [blank] (**Escrow Agent**) at [blank] (address): $____ as earnest money and $____ as the option fee" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶5A](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

It goes to the escrow agent — the title company. Not the seller, not the listing agent, not the listing brokerage.

Paragraph 5A(2) handles the weekend. If the last day to deliver the earnest money, option fee or additional earnest money falls on a **Saturday, Sunday or Legal Holiday**, the time extends to the end of the next day that is none of those. The contract does not leave "legal holiday" to interpretation — it defines it by reference to **Sections 662.003(a) and 662.003(b)(4) and (6) of the Texas Government Code**.

Paragraph 5E closes the door on flexibility: "**Time is of the essence** for this paragraph and strict compliance with the time for performance is required."

Delivery is the thing that activates the right. A buyer who negotiated a ten-day option period and then delivered the fee on day four does not have a ten-day option period — that buyer has no termination right at all. The contract survives, the earnest money is still at risk, and the seller has no obligation to let the buyer out. This is the single most avoidable failure in a Texas contract.

Because the deadline runs from the effective date, an incorrect effective date poisons it. The effective date is when the last party signs and that signature is delivered, not the day the offer was written and not the day the seller said yes on the phone.

## Two ways to lose the right, and one of them is a blank

Paragraph 5D is the exact answer to "what happens if I miss it," and it names two failures, not one:

> "If **no dollar amount is stated** as the option fee or if Buyer fails to deliver the option fee within the time required, **Buyer shall not have the unrestricted right to terminate** this contract under this paragraph 5."

([TREC form 20-19, ¶5D](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf))

The late wire is the failure everyone talks about. The blank is the one that actually gets missed, because it happens at the drafting stage where nobody is watching a clock.

A contract that names an option period — ten days, fifteen days, whatever was negotiated — but leaves the option fee dollar blank empty gives the buyer **no unrestricted right to terminate**. The option period paragraph is filled in. The fee amount is not. Under ¶5D the right does not exist. A $0 or blank entry is not a free option period; it is no option period at all.

This is why a buyer should read ¶5A on their own executed contract, not just the summary their agent gave them. Confirm there is a dollar figure in the option fee blank, confirm the escrow agent and address are filled in, and confirm the delivery went out within three days.

## The combined-payment trap

Paragraph 5A says the earnest money and option fee are made payable to the escrow agent and "**may be paid separately or combined in a single payment**." Most buyers now send one wire or one check covering both.

Paragraph 5A(3) then fixes the order: amounts received are applied "**first to the option fee, then to the earnest money, and then to the additional earnest money**" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶5A(3)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). That order is what creates the trap. Suppose the contract calls for a $300 option fee and $3,000 in earnest money, and the buyer wires $3,000 by mistake. The first $300 satisfies the option fee — so the termination right is intact — and the remaining $2,700 lands as earnest money. The earnest money is now $300 short of what the contract requires, which is a buyer default, not a rounding error.

Paragraph 5A(1) adds a third bucket, **additional earnest money**, delivered within a stated number of days after the effective date. If the contract uses it, that is one more amount and one more deadline in the waterfall.

The failure is quiet. Nobody gets an error message. It usually surfaces when someone reconciles escrow, which can be days or weeks later. Sending the two amounts as two separate payments removes the problem entirely, and it also makes the escrow receipt unambiguous if the option fee delivery is ever questioned.

## The escrow agent can hand the fee to the seller without asking

The buyer agrees to this in the contract itself. Paragraph 5A(4):

> "Buyer authorizes Escrow Agent to release and deliver the option fee to Seller **at any time without further notice to or consent from Buyer**, and releases Escrow Agent from liability for delivery of the option fee to Seller. **The option fee will be credited to the Sales Price at closing.**"

([TREC form 20-19, ¶5A(4)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf))

"Without further notice to or consent from Buyer" is signed by the buyer at the moment the offer is made. This is a real difference from earnest money, which sits in escrow and cannot be paid to anyone without mutual agreement or a court order. A buyer who assumes both amounts are sitting untouched at the title company until closing is wrong about half of it. The option fee may already be in the seller's account.

That is also why "just get my option fee back" is not a request the title company can grant after the fact.

## What happens to the fee at closing

Paragraph 5A(4) again: "The option fee will be credited to the Sales Price at closing." The buyer does not pay it twice. It shows up as a credit on the buyer's side of the settlement statement and reduces the cash needed at closing by that amount.

So the economics are simple. Close, and the fee is effectively returned as a credit. Terminate, and the seller keeps it — which is exactly what the buyer paid for.

Out-of-state buyers frequently expect Texas to work like a "due diligence fee" state where the fee is a pure sunk cost, or like an earnest-money state where everything comes back. Texas is neither. The fee is non-refundable and creditable at the same time.

## Which contract this lives in

All of the above is **Paragraph 5, EARNEST MONEY AND TERMINATION OPTION**, of the **One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), TREC form 20-19, effective 07/01/2026** — a 12-page form carrying a 05-04-2026 footer date ([TREC form 20-19 PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf), [TREC form page](https://www.trec.texas.gov/forms/one-four-family-residential-contract-resale)). Condominium resales, builder new construction and farm and ranch each use a different promulgated form with its own number ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

License holders are required to use the promulgated forms and may not draft contract language — Paragraph 23 of the contract is titled **CONSULT AN ATTORNEY BEFORE SIGNING** and states that "TREC rules prohibit real estate brokers and sales agents from giving legal advice." If a deal needs a custom option structure — an extended option tied to a rezoning, for instance, or an option fee that applies to something other than the sales price — that is a job for a Texas real estate attorney.

- [Is the option fee refundable in Texas?](/answers/is-the-option-fee-refundable-in-texas)
- [What is earnest money in Texas, and is it refundable?](/answers/what-is-earnest-money-in-texas-and-is-it-refundable)
