*This page explains how the effective date works in a Texas real estate contract. It is not legal advice. If deadlines have run against an incorrect effective date, talk with a Texas real estate attorney.*

question: What happens at a Texas real estate closing?
metaTitle: What happens at a Texas real estate closing?
metaDescription: The title company runs it, no attorney required, and signing is not closing. Funding and recording are, plus what paragraph 13 prorates.
shortAnswer: At a Texas closing the title company acts as escrow agent. The parties sign the deed, note and closing disclosure, the buyer wires funds, the lender funds the loan, and the title company records the deed. Signing is not closing — the deal closes when it funds and records. No attorney is required.
body:
## The title company runs it

In Texas, residential closings happen at a title company, and the title company does the work that in some other states falls to an attorney. It serves as **escrow agent**, runs the title search, issues the title commitment and then the title policy, prepares the closing documents, collects and disburses funds, and records the deed.

Hiring an attorney is optional, not required. Nothing about a Texas residential closing depends on one being present.

The title company is neutral. It represents neither buyer nor seller. It cannot give either side legal advice and it cannot decide a dispute between them — which is exactly why escrowed earnest money cannot be released without mutual agreement or a court order.

## Before the signing appointment

The closing is the last step of a chain that has been running since the effective date.

The title company opens the file and orders the title search, then issues the **title commitment** — which lists what the policy will cover, what it excepts, and what has to be cleared before it will insure.

That has a deadline. Paragraph 6B of the contract requires the seller to furnish the commitment "**within 20 days after the Title Company receives a copy of this contract**," along with legible copies of the exception documents at the buyer's expense. If it is not delivered in time, delivery is "automatically extended up to **15 days or 3 days before the Closing Date, whichever is earlier**." If it still has not arrived, "**Buyer may terminate this contract and the earnest money will be refunded to Buyer**" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6B](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

Once it arrives, the buyer's objection clock under ¶6D starts. Objections are due by the earlier of the closing date or a stated number of days after receiving the commitment, exception documents and survey, and failure to object in time "**will constitute a waiver**" of the right, except as to the Schedule C requirements. If the seller does not cure timely objections within the **15-day cure period**, the buyer has **5 days** after that period ends to terminate with earnest money refunded, or waive.

Liens get payoff statements ordered. Tax certificates get pulled. The survey question gets resolved under ¶6C — either the seller's existing survey plus a **T-47 Affidavit or T-47.1 Declaration** is accepted, or a new survey is ordered ([TDI T-47](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/formT-47.pdf)). The HOA is contacted for the resale certificate and transfer amounts if there is one.

On the lender's side, underwriting finishes, the appraisal comes in, and the loan gets a clear to close. The lender issues the **Closing Disclosure**, which itemizes the final loan terms and costs and must reach the borrower in advance of consummation under federal rules — your lender will tell you the exact timing for your loan.

The buyer's side has its own tasks: homeowner's insurance bound and the binder delivered to the lender, the wire set up, a government-issued photo ID ready, and the final walkthrough scheduled.

Any one of these can move the closing date. The one that moves it most often is the lender.

## What gets signed

The stack varies with the loan, but the core documents are consistent.

**Seller signs**
- The **deed** conveying title to the buyer
- The settlement statement
- Affidavits required by the title company, which may include a T-47 or T-47.1 and a no-lien affidavit
- Tax and identity forms, including IRS reporting forms where applicable
- Any FIRPTA-related certification

**Buyer signs**
- The **promissory note** — the promise to repay
- The **deed of trust** — the lien securing the note against the property
- The **Closing Disclosure**
- The settlement statement
- Loan affidavits and disclosures, occupancy certification, and the tax authorization forms

A deed and a deed of trust require notarization. Whoever is signing has to have valid identification and has to be present, physically or by an accepted remote method the title company offers.

Sellers and buyers frequently sign separately, hours or days apart. There is no requirement that everyone sit at the same table, and on many transactions nobody does.

## Signing is not closing

This is the single most misunderstood part of a Texas closing, and it is where people get caught.

Signing is the buyer and seller executing documents. **Closing is when the transaction funds and records.** The deal is not done when the pen goes down.

The sequence after signing:

1. The title company confirms it has every required item — all signatures, the buyer's funds, the seller's payoff figures, the lender's loan package.
2. The lender reviews the executed package and **funds** — wires the loan proceeds.
3. The title company **records** the deed and the deed of trust with the county clerk in the county where the property sits. For Boerne that is **Kendall County**, not Bexar County.
4. Only then does the title company **disburse** — payoff to the existing lender, proceeds to the seller, commissions, the county's recording fees, and any credits.

**Funds are not disbursed and documents are not recorded until all required items are received.** A missing signature page, a payoff that arrived short, a wire that has not landed, or a lender that did not release funding will hold everything. The file sits signed and unclosed.

This is why the answer to "can I get the keys right after I sign?" is no. Possession transfers at closing and funding, per the contract, unless the parties agreed otherwise in writing — a temporary residential lease, for instance, using the promulgated forms 15-7 or 16-7 ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

It is also why Friday afternoon closings are structurally risky. If anything stalls after signing, the title company and the lender are closed until Monday and the money sits in limbo across the weekend.

## Money movement

**The buyer wires.** Large closing funds come by wire, not by personal check. Confirm wire instructions by calling the title company at a number you looked up independently — never from the email containing the instructions. Wire fraud in real estate closings is a persistent, active problem, and a wire sent to a fraudulent account is generally not recoverable.

**Prorations settle.** Paragraph 13 governs, and it is worth reading in full: "**Taxes for the current year, interest, rents, and regular periodic maintenance fees, assessments, and dues (including prepaid items) will be prorated through the Closing Date. The tax proration may be calculated taking into consideration any change in exemptions that will affect the current year's taxes. If taxes for the current year vary from the amount prorated at closing, the parties shall adjust the prorations when tax statements for the current year are available. If taxes are not paid at or prior to closing, Buyer shall pay taxes for the current year**" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶13](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

Two consequences people miss. The tax number on your settlement statement is an estimate — the parties **shall adjust** once the real statements come out, which can mean a check months after closing. And if the property's exemptions are changing, the proration may be computed with that in mind, so a seller's homestead or over-65 exemption does not automatically follow the property to the buyer.

**Expenses split per ¶12.** Paragraph 12A(1) assigns the seller lien releases with prepayment penalties and recording fees, release of seller's loan liability, tax statements or certificates, preparation of deed, and one-half of the escrow fee. Paragraph 12A(2) assigns the buyer the loan costs, the loan title policy with lender endorsements, one-half of the escrow fee, prepaid flood and hazard insurance premiums and reserves, and PMI, the VA Loan Funding Fee or FHA MIP as required by the lender ([TREC form 20-19, ¶12](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

**Brokerage compensation is separate.** Paragraph 12B: "Brokerage compensation is not set by law and is fully negotiable," and each party pays their own broker under separate written agreements.

**The option fee shows as a credit.** Paragraph 5A(4): "The option fee will be credited to the Sales Price at closing." Earnest money is credited to the buyer as well.

**The seller nets.** Payoff, compensation and seller-side costs come off the sales price, and the remainder is wired or issued to the seller after funding.

## If the house burns down before closing

Paragraph 14, CASUALTY LOSS, covers damage by fire or other casualty after the effective date. The seller must restore the property "as soon as reasonably possible, but in any event by the Closing Date."

If the seller cannot, due to factors beyond the seller's control, the buyer has three options ([TREC form 20-19, ¶14](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)):

1. **Terminate** and have the earnest money refunded.
2. **Extend** the time for performance up to **15 days**, with the closing date extended as necessary.
3. **Accept** the property in its damaged condition with an assignment of insurance proceeds, if the carrier permits — **plus a credit from the seller at closing in the amount of the deductible**.

Option three is the one worth knowing about. A buyer taking the insurance proceeds is not also stuck eating the seller's deductible; the contract makes the seller credit it. That single clause can be worth a few thousand dollars on a hail claim, and it is routinely forgotten in Hill Country storm season.

## The title policy

The owner's title policy is issued after closing. It insures the buyer's title against covered defects — liens, undisclosed heirs, forgery, errors in the public record, and, if the survey exception was amended, matters a survey would disclose.

Texas title insurance premium rates are **promulgated by the Texas Department of Insurance**, so the premium for a given policy amount is identical at every title company in the state. The current schedule is "Texas Title Insurance Premium Rates, Rates Effective March 1, 2026" ([TDI](https://tdi.texas.gov/title/titlerates2026.html), [rate table](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/titlerates2026.pdf)). Which title company you use changes the service and the escrow fee, not the premium.

## When you do want an attorney

The contract says so itself. Paragraph 6E(1): "**Broker advises Buyer to have an abstract of title covering the Property examined by an attorney of Buyer's selection**, or Buyer should be furnished with or obtain a Title Policy. If a Title Policy is furnished, the **Commitment should be promptly reviewed by an attorney of Buyer's choice due to the time limitations on Buyer's right to object**" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6E(1)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

And Paragraph 23 is titled **CONSULT AN ATTORNEY BEFORE SIGNING**: "TREC rules prohibit real estate brokers and sales agents from giving legal advice. READ THIS CONTRACT CAREFULLY." The form provides printed fields for the buyer's attorney and the seller's attorney.

The title company is neutral and does not advise either side. If the transaction involves a title defect the commitment flagged, a probate or estate sale, an entity or trust taking title, a boundary dispute, a deed restriction question, community property or a divorce decree, or custom contract language, a **Texas real estate attorney** is the right person — and specifically during the ¶6D objection window, not at the closing table.

question: What is a 1031 exchange?
metaTitle: What is a 1031 exchange?
metaDescription: The 45-day identification and 180-day receipt clocks, why a year-end closing shortens them, qualified intermediaries, Form 8824 and TREC form 60-0.
shortAnswer: A 1031 exchange lets an owner defer capital gain on real property held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment by exchanging it for like-kind real property. You have 45 days to identify replacement property in writing and 180 days to receive it. A personal residence does not qualify.
body:
## What qualifies, after the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act

Section 1031 of the Internal Revenue Code now applies **only to real property**. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act removed personal property and intangible property from the section, so exchanges of equipment, vehicles, artwork or franchise rights no longer qualify ([IRS, *Like-Kind Exchanges — Real Estate Tax Tips*](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/like-kind-exchanges-real-estate-tax-tips)).

The property has to be **held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment** — both the property given up and the property received. A **personal residence does not qualify.** Neither does property held primarily for resale.

"Like-kind" is broader than most people expect within real property. Real property is generally like-kind to other real property regardless of grade or quality — raw land, a rental house, a retail building. What matters is how the property was held, not what type of building sits on it. Whether a particular property was held in a qualifying way is a facts-and-circumstances question, and it is a **CPA's** call, not an agent's.

## Deferral is not forgiveness

A 1031 exchange defers gain. It does not erase it. The deferred gain generally carries forward into the basis of the replacement property, which is why a chain of exchanges can push a large embedded gain forward for years and why the eventual taxable event, if there is one, can be much larger than the gain on any single sale.

That is the part worth understanding before anyone builds a strategy on it. It is also exactly where a **CPA or tax advisor** earns their fee, because the basis carryover, any boot received, depreciation recapture and the interaction with the taxpayer's other holdings are all specific to the filer.

## The two clocks, and the one that surprises people

Both clocks start at the **transfer of the relinquished property** — the day the old property closes.

**45 days to identify.** Replacement property must be identified **in writing, signed by the taxpayer, and delivered** to a person involved in the exchange, such as the qualified intermediary or the seller of the replacement property ([IRS](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/like-kind-exchanges-real-estate-tax-tips)). Identification is a formal written act with a deadline, not a conversation with an agent.

**180 days to receive** the replacement property — **or the due date of the tax return, including extensions, for the year of the transfer, whichever is earlier.**

That "whichever is earlier" is the rule that catches people, and it catches them in one specific situation: **a relinquished property that closes late in the calendar year.** Sell in November, and 180 days runs into May — but the return due date arrives first unless the taxpayer files an extension. The fix is usually mechanical and usually involves an extension, and it has to be handled by the CPA before the deadline, not discovered after it.

These deadlines are strict. If the timing fails, the gain may be taxable in the year of the transfer.

## The qualified intermediary is not optional in practice

A **qualified intermediary** structure is what allows a deferred exchange — one where the sale and the purchase happen on different days — to be treated as a like-kind exchange rather than a sale followed by a purchase ([IRS](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/like-kind-exchanges-real-estate-tax-tips)).

The practical rule that flows from that: **the seller cannot take receipt of the proceeds.** Money that lands in the seller's account, or in an account the seller controls, generally blows the exchange. The intermediary has to be engaged **before the relinquished property closes** — not after the funds move, and not "we'll set it up next week."

This is the single most common way a 1031 fails in the field. The deal closes normally, the title company wires the seller, and the exchange is over before the CPA hears about it. Engage the intermediary while the property is still under contract.

Choosing an intermediary is a diligence exercise of its own. They hold the money, they are not federally licensed in the way a bank is, and the taxpayer bears the counterparty risk. A CPA or attorney can point to ones they have used.

## How it shows up in a Texas contract

TREC publishes an **Addendum for Section 1031 Exchange, form 60-0, effective 01/03/2025** ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)). It is the promulgated way to put the other side on notice that the transaction is part of an exchange and to address cooperation.

Two things it does not do. It does not make the exchange work — the intermediary and the deadlines do that. And it is not a substitute for the exchange documents themselves, which the qualified intermediary prepares.

TREC license holders may not draft contract language. If the situation needs something the promulgated addendum does not cover, that is a **Texas real estate attorney's** work.

## Reporting

The exchange is reported to the IRS on **Form 8824** ([IRS Instructions for Form 8824](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i8824)). It gets filed with the return for the year the relinquished property was transferred, which means a 1031 shows up on a return even though no tax is being paid on the gain.

## What this page deliberately does not tell you

There are specific IRS rules governing **how many** replacement properties a taxpayer may identify within the 45 days and at what aggregate value. Those rules exist and they matter, and the version of them circulating on real estate blogs is frequently stated wrong. Ask the qualified intermediary and the CPA for the current identification rules in writing before the 45th day.

Likewise, nothing here addresses whether a 1031 is the right move at all. Deferring gain has a cost — the replacement property is chosen under a 45-day clock, which is not a condition anyone would choose for a major acquisition. Sometimes paying the tax and buying the right asset in ninety days beats deferring it into the wrong one in forty-five.

## Who decides what

- **CPA or tax advisor**: whether the property qualifies, whether the exchange makes sense, basis and boot, depreciation recapture, the extension needed to protect the 180 days.
- **Qualified intermediary**: the exchange documents, holding the proceeds, the identification mechanics and the current identification rules.
- **Texas real estate attorney**: entity and title questions, any contract language beyond the promulgated addendum.
- **Real estate agent**: finding and contracting the replacement property inside the 45-day window, which is the part that actually runs out first.

question: What is a MUD or a PID in a Texas subdivision?
metaTitle: What is a MUD or a PID in a Texas subdivision?
metaDescription: MUD notice is Water Code 49.452, PID notice is Property Code 5.014, each has its own TREC form, and both land on the monthly payment.
shortAnswer: A MUD is a municipal utility district and a PID is a public improvement district. Both fund water, sewer, roads and amenities in a Texas subdivision, and both add a line to the property tax bill that can change the monthly payment. Each has a TREC notice form that goes to the buyer in the transaction.
body:
## Why these exist at all

Texas grows at the edges. A developer buys raw land outside a city's utility system and has to put in water lines, wastewater treatment, drainage, streets and sometimes parks before a single house sells. That infrastructure costs real money up front, and the buyers who will use it do not exist yet.

A special district solves the timing problem. The district issues debt to build the infrastructure, and the property owners inside the district pay it back over time through a tax or an assessment on their property. The cost lands on the people who use it, spread over years, instead of entirely on the lot price at closing.

That is the honest case for them. The honest cost is that the buyer's tax bill is higher than an identical house outside the district, often by enough to change what the buyer can afford.

## MUD and PID are not the same thing

**MUD — municipal utility district.** A political subdivision with its own board. It typically owns and operates water, wastewater and drainage infrastructure, and it **levies a property tax** the same way a city or school district does. It appears as its own taxing-entity line on the tax bill, with its own rate, and that rate can change year to year as the district's debt is paid down or new debt is issued.

**PID — public improvement district.** Created by a city or county to fund specified improvements in a defined area. A PID does not levy a property tax in the MUD sense; it imposes an **assessment** against the properties within it. TREC's own form language reflects the distinction — the form is titled an "Obligation to Pay Improvement District Assessment."

Two practical consequences follow from that difference.

1. A PID assessment often has a **payoff** — an outstanding principal balance attributable to the lot that can, in many districts, be paid off in a lump sum. Ask whether it can be, and what the balance is. A MUD tax generally cannot be prepaid away; it goes with the district.
2. Because a MUD levies a tax and a PID levies an assessment, they can show up differently on a tax statement and in a lender's escrow calculation. Confirm both with the tax office and the lender rather than assuming they are interchangeable.

Related special districts appear on Texas tax bills too — water control and improvement districts, groundwater conservation districts, emergency services districts. Same principle: another entity, another line, another rate.

## The MUD notice is a statute, and its timing is the whole point

Disclosure of a MUD is not a courtesy. It is **Texas Water Code Section 49.452**, and the timing requirement is where the leverage sits.

The seller of property inside a qualifying district must give the purchaser **written notice prior to execution of a binding contract of sale and purchase**, either separately or as part of the contract, and the **purchaser signs** the notice — or the contract containing it — to evidence receipt ([Texas Water Code 49.452](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/water-code/water-sect-49-452/)).

Now the part that matters to a buyer. If the notice was **not** given before the contract, the seller may give it **at closing** instead — but a purchaser who proceeds at that point **waives termination rights**. The exit exists only in the gap between learning about the district and signing. Discovering the MUD in a closing package and signing anyway is a decision, whether or not it felt like one at the table.

The statute reaches districts providing **water, sewer, drainage or flood control** services that are financed by district bonds or standby fees and that cover **less than all the territory in at least one county**. The content of the notice itself is prescribed by **Section 49.4521**.

The section also carries an exemption list, quoted from the statute: "transfers of title under any type of lien foreclosure; transfers of title by deed in cancellation of indebtedness secured by a lien upon the property conveyed; transfers of title by reason of a will or probate proceedings; transfers of title to a governmental entity; or transfers of title for the purpose of qualifying a director." A foreclosure buyer, an heir and a governmental grantee do not get this notice, which means they do not get this warning.

How any of that applies to a specific transaction — particularly whether an exemption applies or whether a right was waived — is a question for a **Texas real estate attorney**, not an agent.

## The PID notice is a different statute, with different words

PID disclosure runs through **Texas Property Code Section 5.014**. The **seller** must give the purchaser written notice **before the effective date of a binding contract** for the purchase of the property, and the buyer acknowledges receipt ([Texas Property Code 5.014](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-5-014/)).

The notice says three things a buyer should read slowly:

- The buyer is **obligated to pay assessments** to the municipality or county for the cost of a portion of a public improvement undertaken for the benefit of the property.
- "**AN ASSESSMENT HAS BEEN LEVIED AGAINST YOUR PROPERTY.**" Past tense. The obligation already exists; the buyer is inheriting it, not being offered it.
- Failure to pay "**may result in penalties and interest being added to what you owe or in a lien on and the foreclosure of your property.**"

That last clause is the reason this is not paperwork. An unpaid PID assessment is not a late utility bill. It is secured against the house.

Section 5.014 also carries exemptions, including foreclosure sales, bankruptcy transfers, transfers to family members, and transfers involving only groundwater rights or mineral interests.

Note the difference in the two trigger points. The MUD notice under 49.452 is keyed to **execution of a binding contract**; the PID notice under 5.014 is keyed to the **effective date** of a binding contract. They are drafted in different codes for different district types, and neither one is satisfied by a verbal mention at a showing.

## The TREC forms that carry these notices

Two promulgated forms carry this in a transaction ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)):

- **Addendum Containing Notice of Obligation to Pay Improvement District Assessment, form 53-0, effective 09/01/2021.** This is the PID side — the form that delivers the Property Code 5.014 notice, including the levied-assessment language and the foreclosure warning.
- **Notice to Purchaser of Special Taxing or Assessment District, form 59-0, effective 02/12/2024.** The notice given to a purchaser of property inside a special taxing or assessment district, which is the vehicle for the Water Code notice on the MUD side.

Read them. They are short, they are specific to the property, and they exist precisely because buyers were closing without understanding the obligation. A signed notice that nobody read is still a signed notice — and under 49.452, signing it at closing is what extinguishes the termination right.

## The money is not a rounding error

Look at how the base stack already works before adding a district on top. In Kendall County, per $100 of taxable value:

- **Boerne ISD, 2025: 1.0109** — maintenance and operations 0.6969 plus debt 0.3140 ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/295/Boerne-ISD))
- **City of Boerne, 2025: 0.4716** ([Kendall County](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/297/Boerne-City-of))
- **Kendall County, 2025: 0.377**, and **0.373 for 2026** ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/306/Kendall-County))
- **Comfort ISD, 2025: 0.9328**

A district rate stacks on top of whichever of those apply to the parcel. That is why two houses with the same list price, the same square footage and the same school district can carry meaningfully different monthly payments. The difference is not in the house. It is on the tax bill, and it is permanent for as long as the district's obligation runs.

Do not take a district's rate from a listing, a builder's flyer or an old article. Pull it from the appraisal district and the tax office for the specific parcel, for the current year.

## Districts in Kendall County

Kendall Appraisal District lists the taxing entities that appear on bills in the county. Among them are a **Kendall County MUD** and a **Miralomas MUD**, along with **Kendall County WCID #1** and the **Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District**, in addition to the county, the cities and the school districts ([Kendall AD](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)).

Boerne is in **Kendall County**, not Bexar County, and the appraisal district is **Kendall Appraisal District** — not Bexar CAD. That matters for this question because the entity list, the exemptions and the rates all come from Kendall AD.

The reliable way to find out what applies to a specific house: **look the parcel up at [kendallad.org](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/) and read the entity list attached to that account.** Not the subdivision. Not the neighborhood. The parcel. District boundaries do not follow subdivision marketing names, and two lots across a street from each other can sit in different districts.

For rate documents the county publishes, start at [Kendall County tax rate information](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/184/Tax-Rate-Information).

## What to ask before you are under contract

- Is this parcel in a MUD, a PID, a WCID or any other special district? Confirm from the appraisal district account, not from a seller's recollection.
- Has the statutory notice been delivered **before** the contract binds, rather than in the closing package? Under 49.452, that timing is the difference between having a termination right and waiving one.
- What is the current rate or assessment, and what was it the last three years? A declining MUD rate and a rising one tell different stories.
- For a PID: is there a payoff amount for this lot, and can it be prepaid?
- Is the district's debt still being issued, or is it in repayment?
- Does the lender's payment estimate include the district line? A pre-approval built on the wrong tax figure produces a monthly payment that changes at closing.
- What does the district actually deliver — water and sewer, or amenities? Owners pay either way.

## Where the line is

An agent can find the entity list, pull the rates and flag the notice forms. Questions about how a district assessment affects your tax position, deductibility or an investment analysis go to a **CPA or tax advisor**. Questions about the statutory notice, the lien, the district's debt instruments, a waiver of termination rights or the enforceability of an assessment go to a **Texas real estate attorney**. Exemption and valuation questions on the parcel go to **Kendall Appraisal District**. The payment math goes to your **lender**.

## Related questions

- [What are property taxes like in Boerne?](/answers/what-are-property-taxes-like-in-boerne)
- [Why did my Texas property taxes go up?](/answers/why-did-my-texas-property-taxes-go-up)
- [Should I buy in Boerne city limits or unincorporated Kendall County?](/answers/should-i-buy-in-boerne-city-limits-or-unincorporated-kendall-county)
- [How do I protest my property taxes in Texas?](/answers/how-do-i-protest-my-property-taxes-in-texas)
- [What is the TREC 1-4 Family Residential Contract?](/answers/what-is-the-trec-1-4-family-residential-contract)

## Questions about a specific property?

Call or text **[830-446-3847](tel:+1-830-446-3847)** · Email **[heath.shepard@kw.com](mailto:heath.shepard@kw.com)**

---

For the tax consequences of a district assessment, talk with a CPA; for the statutory notice, the lien or a waiver of termination rights, talk with a Texas real estate attorney; for what applies to a specific parcel, contact Kendall Appraisal District.*

question: What is a T-47 affidavit in Texas?
metaTitle: What is a T-47 affidavit in Texas?
metaDescription: The Texas T-47 affidavit and the T-47.1 declaration in lieu, both effective November 1 2024: what they do, who signs, and how they amend the survey exception.
shortAnswer: A T-47 is a notarized affidavit in which a Texas seller states that nothing has changed on the property since the existing survey. With it, the lender and title company can often accept that survey instead of requiring a new one. A T-47.1 declaration does the same job without notarization; both took effect November 1, 2024.
body:
## The problem the form solves

A survey shows where the improvements sit relative to the boundary lines, the easements and the setbacks. It is what the title company relies on to insure against boundary and encroachment problems, and it is what the lender relies on to know the collateral is where it is supposed to be.

The existing survey in the seller's file might be five years old, or twenty. The title company has no way to know whether a shed, a fence, a pool, a driveway extension or an addition went in after the surveyor left. A stale survey plus an unknown five years of construction is an uninsurable gap.

The T-47 closes that gap with a sworn statement from the person who would know: the seller.

## What the seller is actually swearing to

The **T-47 Residential Real Property Affidavit** is a form published by the Texas Department of Insurance ([TDI T-47](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/formT-47.pdf)). The seller identifies the existing survey, states that they are the owner, and states that there have been no changes to the property since that survey was made — no new construction, no additions, no new improvements, no changes to boundary lines or fence lines, no encroachments added.

It is signed and **notarized**. The form itself identifies the title insurance company as the party issuing the policy in reliance on the statements in it.

That is the weight of the document, and it is why "just sign the T-47, it's routine" is bad advice. It is a sworn statement made to induce an insurer to issue a policy. A seller who put in a fence or a covered patio since the survey needs to say so, and then the survey probably needs updating. A Texas real estate attorney is the right person to advise a seller who is not sure what counts as a change.

The current TDI form carries the notation "Sec. V Effective November 1, 2024."

## The T-47.1 alternative

The **T-47.1 Residential Real Property Declaration in Lieu of Affidavit** was introduced effective **November 1, 2024** ([TDI T-47.1](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/form-t-47-1.pdf)).

It makes the same substantive statements. The difference is that it is **signed by the seller but not notarized**.

That difference is entirely practical. Getting a notary in front of an out-of-state seller, an estate representative, a seller mid-relocation, or two sellers in two different cities used to add days to a transaction for what was otherwise a routine form. The declaration removes the notary bottleneck.

Which one to use is not the buyer's or seller's call alone. The title company and the lender decide what they will accept, and they may still require the notarized T-47 on a given file.

## The purchase contract names both forms

This is not a side agreement between the title company and the seller. It is written into the promulgated contract.

Paragraph 6C of the One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), TREC form 20-19, is the survey paragraph, and it carries the instruction "**Check one box only**." The first of its three options has the seller furnish, within a stated number of days, the existing survey together with a "**T-47 Affidavit or T-47.1 Declaration**" — both named explicitly on the face of the form ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6C(1)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

Then comes the consequence that makes the form worth taking seriously, and it falls on the seller:

> If Seller fails to furnish **both** the existing survey and the affidavit or declaration within the time required, "Buyer shall obtain a new survey **at Seller's expense** no later than 3 days prior to Closing Date."

The operative word is *both*. A seller who emails the old survey but never gets around to signing the T-47 has not partially complied — they have failed ¶6C(1), and they are paying for a new survey. There is no checkbox and nothing to negotiate at that point; the contract already decided it.

A separate and different branch handles the case where the seller did furnish both but the package is not good enough: "If the Title Company or Buyer's lender **does not accept** the existing survey, or the affidavit or declaration, Buyer shall obtain a new survey at [ ] Seller's [ ] Buyer's expense no later than 3 days prior to Closing Date." That one is an election the parties make when the contract is written, and it is frequently left blank.

Seller's fault, seller pays. Nobody's fault, whichever box got checked.

## What the form buys

Two things.

**The buyer may not need to pay for a new survey.** If the title company and the lender accept the existing survey together with a T-47 or T-47.1, no new survey is ordered ([TDI T-47](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/formT-47.pdf)). That is the cost saving people are usually after.

**The survey exception in the title policy can be amended.** Every Texas owner's title policy contains a standard exception for matters a survey would disclose. Paragraph 6A(8) of the contract describes it as the exception "as to discrepancies, conflicts, shortages in area or boundary lines, encroachments or protrusions, or overlapping improvements," and gives the parties a choice: it "(i) **will not be amended or deleted** from the title policy; or (ii) **will be amended to read, 'shortages in area'** at the expense of [ ] Buyer [ ] Seller" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6A(8)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

Option (ii) is what an acceptable survey plus a T-47 or T-47.1 unlocks. It shrinks the exception down to shortages in area alone, so encroachments, conflicts, protrusions and overlapping improvements are covered by the policy instead of carved out of it.

The second one is the more valuable half, and it is the half buyers usually do not know they are getting. A cheap deal that ends with an unamended survey exception is not actually cheaper — it just moved the risk onto the buyer.

Texas title insurance premium rates are promulgated by the Texas Department of Insurance, so the cost of coverage does not vary by title company. The current schedule is "Texas Title Insurance Premium Rates, Rates Effective March 1, 2026" ([TDI](https://tdi.texas.gov/title/titlerates2026.html)). Ask your title company what the amendment costs on your file.

## Where it goes wrong

**The seller does not have the survey.** No survey means nothing for the affidavit to reference. The buyer is buying a new one, or the deal has no survey at all.

**The seller forgot the improvement.** A pool put in three years ago, a detached garage, a fence moved to the neighbor's apparent line. The affidavit is signed anyway and the change surfaces later. That is the scenario the form's sworn character is designed to deter.

**The lender says no regardless.** Some lenders require a current survey as a matter of policy, whatever the title company will accept. That is a lender decision and not something the parties can negotiate around.

**The parties assumed instead of checking.** Who furnishes the existing survey, and who pays for a new one if the existing one is not acceptable, is ¶6C of the TREC contract — a check-one-box-only election with a nested expense checkbox inside the first option ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6C](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). It is a negotiated term. Read it before assuming the seller is handling it.

**The T-47 arrived, but too late to object to what the survey showed.** Under ¶6D the buyer's right to object in writing to matters disclosed on the survey expires at the earlier of the closing date or a stated number of days after receiving the commitment, exception documents and the survey, and "failure to object within the time allowed **will constitute a waiver** of Buyer's right to object." A survey delivered at the last minute is a survey with nothing left to do about it.

## In the Hill Country specifically

Acreage tracts in Kendall County and the surrounding Hill Country are where survey issues actually bite. Fence lines that have never matched deed lines, easements for a shared drive, wells and septic systems whose locations matter for setbacks, and platted lots that were split informally years ago. An older survey on a rural tract is more likely to be genuinely out of date than one on a subdivision lot, and the cost of finding out after closing is higher.

A licensed Texas surveyor is who determines where the lines actually are. The T-47 is a statement about change since the last survey, not a substitute for one.

question: What is a Texas cash-out refinance under Section 50(a)(6)?
metaTitle: What is a Texas cash-out refinance under Section 50(a)(6)?
metaDescription: Texas Section 50(a)(6) caps all homestead liens at 80 percent of value, requires a 12-day wait, limits fees to 2 percent, and allows one per year.
shortAnswer: A Texas cash-out refinance is a home equity loan under Article XVI, Section 50(a)(6) of the Texas Constitution. All loans against the homestead combined cannot exceed 80 percent of fair market value, the loan cannot close until 12 days after the later of application or notice, and fees are capped at 2 percent.
body:
## Why this lives in the constitution

Most states regulate home equity lending by statute, which a legislature can change in a session. Texas put its homestead protections in the **state constitution**, and for most of the state's history it did not permit home equity lending against a homestead at all. What exists today is a carefully bounded exception, and the boundaries are the reason a Texas cash-out looks different from a cash-out anywhere else.

The practical consequence for a homeowner: some of the terms below are not negotiable with a lender, because the lender cannot waive them either.

## The rules, plainly

**80 percent loan-to-value ceiling.** All loans secured by the homestead, combined, cannot exceed **80 percent of the home's fair market value** at closing. At least 20 percent equity must remain in the property. This is a combined test — a first lien plus a second lien plus the new loan all count toward the same 80 percent.

**A 12-day waiting period.** The loan cannot close until at least **12 days** after the later of two events: the date of the application, or the date the borrower receives the required notice. This is a cooling-off period built into the process. It is the most common reason a Texas cash-out takes longer to close than a borrower expects, and it cannot be compressed by paying a rush fee.

**A 2 percent cap on fees.** Fees charged in connection with the loan cannot exceed **2 percent of the loan principal** — **excluding** the appraisal fee, the land survey fee, the title insurance premium and title search or examination charges. Those four sit outside the cap.

**Generally non-recourse.** The lender generally cannot pursue the borrower personally for a deficiency. If the home is foreclosed and the sale does not cover the balance, the borrower is generally not on the hook for the shortfall. This is a meaningful protection and it is a real reason some Texas borrowers choose this product knowingly.

**One at a time.** Only **one** Section 50(a)(6) loan may be secured by the homestead at any given time.

**12 months between closings.** At least **12 months** must pass between home equity closings.

Sources: [Rocket Mortgage](https://www.rocketmortgage.com/learn/home-equity-loan-cash-out-refinance-texas) and [Hurst Lending](https://hurstlending.com/texas-cash-out-refinance-rules-50a6-guidelines/).

## A Texas HELOC on a homestead is also a 50(a)(6) loan

This surprises people who assume a line of credit is a lighter-touch product. **A home equity line of credit secured by a Texas homestead is a Section 50(a)(6) loan and carries the same limits** — the same 80 percent combined ceiling, the same notice and waiting period, the same one-at-a-time rule.

That last point has a specific consequence worth spelling out. An open HELOC on the homestead is a 50(a)(6) loan. So a homeowner with a HELOC in place who wants a 50(a)(6) cash-out refinance generally has to deal with the existing line first, because only one such loan can be secured by the homestead at a time. Anyone planning a refinance while carrying an open equity line should raise it with the lender at application, not at underwriting.

## The math the 80 percent rule actually produces

The ceiling is on the **combined** balance against the homestead, which means the available cash is the difference between 80 percent of value and everything already owed.

A home appraised at $500,000 has an 80 percent ceiling of $400,000. If the existing mortgage balance is $340,000, the maximum new combined debt is $400,000 — and the gross proceeds before costs are $60,000, not $160,000. Subtract closing costs from there.

Two things follow. First, a borrower with a large existing balance may find there is no usable cash-out at all, regardless of how much the house appreciated. Second, **the appraisal is the whole deal.** Fair market value at closing sets the ceiling, and the borrower does not get to pick the number. A cash-out plan built on a hoped-for value is a plan with one input nobody controls.

## What this does not cover

**Investment property.** Section 50(a)(6) governs the **homestead**. A rental property held as an investment in Texas is not the homestead and is not governed by these rules — which is why investor cash-out strategies are structured on the investment side. The limits there come from the lender's own loan-to-value, seasoning and reserve requirements, not from the constitution. See [what is the BRRRR method, and does it work in Texas](/answers/what-is-the-brrrr-method-and-does-it-work-in-texas).

**Rate-and-term refinances.** A refinance that only changes the rate or the term, with no cash to the borrower, is a different transaction from a 50(a)(6) cash-out. Whether a particular restructuring counts as cash-out, and whether a loan that was once a 50(a)(6) loan keeps that character when it is refinanced later, are questions for the **lender** and, where the answer matters legally, a **Texas real estate attorney.**

**Homestead character itself.** Whether a specific property is the borrower's homestead — including in a house-hack, a property held in an entity, or a home the borrower moved out of — is a legal question, not a form field.

## Questions to put to a lender at application

- What is the combined balance against the homestead today, and what does 80 percent of the expected appraised value leave available?
- When does the 12-day clock start for this loan, and what date does that produce for closing?
- Which fees fall inside the 2 percent cap and which are the excluded appraisal, survey, title premium and title search charges?
- Is there an existing home equity loan or HELOC on the property, and what has to happen to it?
- Was there a home equity closing on this homestead in the last 12 months?

A **lender** is the right professional for qualification, rates, products and whether a specific transaction qualifies. Nothing on this page is a loan approval or a rate quote, and rates and lender overlays change.

## Related questions

- [What is the BRRRR method, and does it work in Texas?](/answers/what-is-the-brrrr-method-and-does-it-work-in-texas)
- [What is the Texas homestead exemption?](/answers/what-is-the-texas-homestead-exemption)

question: What is a title commitment in Texas?
metaTitle: What is a title commitment in Texas?
metaDescription: Schedules A through D in plain language, the 20-day delivery rule in Paragraph 6B, and how the objection and Cure Period mechanics work.
shortAnswer: A title commitment is the title company's written promise to issue a title policy on stated terms. It comes in four schedules: A is the deal facts, B is what the policy will not cover, C is what must be fixed before closing, and D discloses who gets paid. Reading it is a task with a deadline.
body:
## The commitment is a conditional offer, not a report

People call it a title report. It is not a report. It is a **commitment to insure**, conditioned on the items in Schedule C being satisfied, subject to the exceptions in Schedule B, in favor of the party named in Schedule A.

Every word of that sentence has consequences. Change the buyer's entity name after the commitment issues and Schedule A is wrong. Skip a Schedule C requirement and the policy does not issue. Ignore a Schedule B exception and the policy issues, closing happens, and the thing you were worried about is simply not covered.

Title insurance in Texas is regulated by the **Texas Department of Insurance**, which prescribes the forms and sets the premium rates ([TDI title rates](https://tdi.texas.gov/title/titlerates2026.html)). The commitment form is a promulgated form. The title company fills it in; it does not write it.

## When it has to arrive — Paragraph 6B

The contract puts a hard deadline on delivery. **Paragraph 6B** of the One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale) requires that **within 20 days after the Title Company receives a copy of the contract**, the seller furnish the buyer a commitment for title insurance and, at the buyer's expense, legible copies of the restrictive covenants and the documents evidencing exceptions in the commitment — the **Exception Documents** — other than the standard printed exceptions ([TREC form 20-19, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

If it is not delivered on time, delivery is "automatically extended up to **15 days or 3 days before the Closing Date, whichever is earlier**." If it is still not delivered within the time required, "**Buyer may terminate this contract and the earnest money will be refunded to Buyer**."

Two practical notes. The 20 days runs from **when the title company receives the contract**, not from the effective date — so a file that sits unopened for a week has already eaten a week. And the Exception Documents are furnished **at the buyer's expense** and are the part buyers routinely fail to request. The commitment names the recorded instruments; the instruments are where the restriction actually lives.

## Schedule A — the deal facts

The boring schedule, and the one with the most costly typos.

Schedule A states the **effective date of the commitment**, the **policy amount**, the **proposed insured**, the **current record owner**, the **estate or interest** being insured, and the **legal description** of the land.

Check four things:

1. **The proposed insured name** is exactly how the buyer will take title. "John and Jane Smith" is not the same as "Smith Family Trust" or "Smith Holdings LLC," and changing it later means re-issuing documents.
2. **The legal description** matches the property being bought. On acreage, a metes-and-bounds description that does not match the survey has to be resolved before closing.
3. **The record owner** is the person signing your contract. Probate, divorce, an unreleased partner interest, a dissolved entity — all real, all fixable, none fast.
4. **The policy amount** is the sales price for an owner's policy and the loan amount for a lender's policy.

## Schedule B — what the policy will not cover

Schedule B is the exceptions list, and everything on it is excluded from coverage. Recorded **restrictive covenants**, **easements** of record, mineral and royalty interests previously reserved, **taxes for the current and subsequent years**, rights of parties in possession, and the **survey exception**.

This is where the property's actual encumbrances live. A pipeline easement. A shared driveway. A deed restriction limiting use. A prior **mineral reservation**, which in much of Texas means the surface owner does not own what is underneath — and which TREC addresses with its own promulgated form, the **Addendum for Reservation of Oil, Gas, and Other Minerals, form 44-3, effective 02/01/2023** ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

Ask for the documents. A one-line reference to a recorded instrument tells you nothing; the instrument tells you everything.

## Schedule C — what must be cured before closing

Schedule C is the schedule that moves your closing date.

It lists the **requirements** the title company must see satisfied before it will issue the policy: releases of existing liens, payoff of the seller's mortgage, a death certificate and affidavit of heirship, probate documents, a corrected legal description, a missing signature from a spouse under Texas homestead and community property rules, a judgment lien to be released, unpaid taxes, an old unreleased deed of trust from a lender that no longer exists.

Some of these are routine and clear in days. Some take weeks and depend on a third party who has no stake in your closing date — a court, an out-of-state heir, a defunct lender's successor servicer.

The operational rule is simple and widely ignored: **read Schedule C the day the commitment arrives, and ask the escrow officer which items are already in hand and which are not.** A Schedule C item that nobody starts working until the week of closing is the most common reason a Texas closing slips.

Curing a title defect is legal work. A Texas real estate attorney handles what the title company cannot cure administratively.

## Schedule D — disclosure

Schedule D discloses the underwriter, the title agent's ownership, and how the premium and fees are to be distributed among the parties involved in issuing the policy. It is a transparency schedule required by regulation. Most buyers skim it. It is worth a look if you want to know who actually underwrites the policy behind the local office.

## The survey exception, and how it gets amended

The standard exception covers "discrepancies, conflicts, shortages in area or boundary lines, encroachments or protrusions, or overlapping improvements." In plain terms: **anything a survey would have shown is not covered.**

The contract handles it as a checkbox. **Paragraph 6A(8)** gives exactly two choices: the standard printed exception "**will not be amended or deleted** from the title policy," or it "**will be amended to read, 'shortages in area'**" at the expense of the buyer or the seller ([TREC form 20-19, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). Amending it narrows the exception down to area shortages and restores coverage for the rest.

Getting there requires a survey the title company and lender will rely on, and **Paragraph 6C** is another **check one box only** election. The survey must be made by a **registered professional land surveyor** acceptable to the Title Company and the buyer's lender. The three boxes:

1. **Seller furnishes the existing survey plus a T-47 Affidavit or T-47.1 Declaration** within a stated number of days. If the seller fails to furnish **both** in time, "Buyer shall obtain a new survey **at Seller's expense** no later than 3 days prior to Closing Date." And if the Title Company or the buyer's lender **does not accept** the existing survey or the affidavit, a new survey is obtained at whichever party's expense the box says, on the same 3-days-before-closing outside date.
2. **Buyer obtains a new survey at Buyer's expense** within a stated number of days. The form adds a consequence: if the buyer fails to obtain it, the buyer "**may not terminate** the contract under Paragraph 2B of the **Third Party Financing Addendum** because the survey was not obtained."
3. **Seller furnishes a new survey at Seller's expense** within a stated number of days.

The underlying forms are the **T-47 Residential Real Property Affidavit**, which is notarized ([TDI](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/formT-47.pdf)), and the **T-47.1 Residential Real Property Declaration in Lieu of Affidavit**, seller-signed but **not notarized**, effective **November 1, 2024** ([TDI](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/form-t-47-1.pdf)). The contract names both by name.

The failure mode is specific: the seller added a deck, a pool, a fence or a barn after the old survey. The affidavit cannot truthfully say nothing changed, the existing survey is not acceptable, and a new survey has to be ordered — often late, and under box (1) potentially at the seller's expense. Identifying that on day two instead of day twenty is worth more than any other single thing on this page.

## Paragraph 6D: objections, the Cure Period, and the Schedule C carve-out

This is the machinery that decides whether a problem you found is a problem you can act on.

**The deadline.** The buyer must object in writing by "the earlier of (i) the Closing Date or (ii) [a stated number of] days after Buyer receives the Commitment, Exception Documents, and the survey." Whichever comes first.

**Waiver.** Failing to object in time "**will constitute a waiver** of Buyer's right to object." Then the carve-out that matters: "**except that the requirements in Schedule C of the Commitment are not waived by Buyer**." Schedule C requirements survive a missed objection deadline. Schedule B exceptions do not.

**The Cure Period.** Provided the seller is not obligated to incur any expense, the seller cures timely objections within a **15-day Cure Period**, and the Closing Date extends as necessary. Read that condition: the seller's cure obligation is bounded by "not obligated to incur any expense," which is why a seller can decline to cure a costly item without defaulting.

**The buyer's move after that.** If objections are not cured, the buyer has **5 days after the end of the Cure Period** to terminate — earnest money refunded — or to waive. Silence is a waiver.

**Restarts.** A revised Commitment, a revised survey, or a new Exception Document restarts the same objection window as to the new matter. A commitment that gets amended late in the deal is not just paperwork; it reopens a right.

The contract also tells the buyer, in the form's own words, to get help: **Paragraph 6E(1)** states that "Broker advises Buyer to have an abstract of title covering the Property examined by an attorney of Buyer's selection," and that if a Title Policy is furnished, the "**Commitment should be promptly reviewed by an attorney of Buyer's choice due to the time limitations on Buyer's right to object**." The word "promptly" is in the promulgated form for a reason.

## The sequence that works

1. Contract effective. Confirm the **title company actually received the contract** — the 20-day clock in 6B starts there.
2. Commitment arrives. Read Schedule A for accuracy and Schedule C for schedule risk the same day.
3. Request the Exception Documents and read the restrictions and easements, not just the one-line references.
4. Resolve the 6C survey box early enough that a "the lender won't accept it" answer still leaves time.
5. Object in writing inside the 6D window — the earlier of the Closing Date or the stated day count.
6. Calendar the 15-day Cure Period and the 5 days that follow it.

## Related questions

- [What is title insurance in Texas, and why is the price the same everywhere?](/answers/what-is-title-insurance-in-texas)
- [What is a T-47 affidavit?](/answers/what-is-a-t-47-affidavit)
- [Who pays for the survey in Texas?](/answers/who-pays-for-the-survey-in-texas)
- [What happens at a Texas closing?](/answers/what-happens-at-a-texas-closing)
- [Do I need a real estate attorney to buy a house in Texas?](/answers/do-i-need-a-real-estate-attorney-to-buy-a-house-in-texas)

## Questions about a specific property?

Call or text **[830-446-3847](tel:+1-830-446-3847)** · Email **[heath.shepard@kw.com](mailto:heath.shepard@kw.com)**

question: What is an ag exemption in Texas, and what are rollback taxes?
metaTitle: What is an ag exemption in Texas, and what are rollback taxes?
metaDescription: Texas ag exemption and rollback taxes explained: 1-d-1 open space, degree of intensity, the 5-of-7-years rule, wildlife management, and the three-year rollback.
shortAnswer: An ag exemption is not an exemption. It is a special appraisal that values qualifying land on its agricultural productivity instead of market value. Changing the use triggers a rollback: three years of additional tax equal to the difference between what was paid on ag value and what would have been paid on market value.
body:
## The name is wrong, and the wrong name causes real losses

Everyone says "ag exemption." What the Tax Code provides is **open-space special appraisal**, commonly called **1-d-1**. The land is still fully on the tax roll. It is simply valued on **productivity value** — what it can produce agriculturally — rather than on what it would sell for ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/ag-timber/index.php)).

That distinction matters because an exemption is something you either have or do not have, while a special appraisal is a **valuation method tied to how the land is currently being used**. Use changes, valuation changes, and a bill comes due for the years the land was valued the cheap way.

On Hill Country acreage the difference between productivity value and market value is frequently the majority of the tax bill. That is exactly the size of the exposure when it goes away.

## What qualifies for 1-d-1 open-space appraisal

Three requirements, per the [Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/ag-timber/index.php):

1. **Current principal use is agricultural.** Not incidental, not decorative. The agricultural use has to be the land's principal use.
2. **Degree of intensity generally accepted in the area.** This is the requirement that fails. The district compares your operation to what a typical prudent operator in that area does on similar land — stocking rates, acreage, management practices. Four goats on twelve acres is not a stocking rate. Whatever the local standard is, the appraisal district defines and applies it, and it varies county to county.
3. **History: agricultural or timber production in 5 of the preceding 7 years.** The land has to have been in qualifying use for five of the last seven years.

The history requirement means a buyer cannot create eligibility on raw land by starting an operation the day after closing. It also means a seller's lapse in use can break the chain for the buyer. What the land was actually doing in prior years is a question for the appraisal district, and it is one of the things worth asking before the option period ends rather than after.

## Wildlife management is a conversion, not a shortcut

Wildlife management valuation is widely misunderstood as an easier route for a buyer who does not want livestock. It is not a separate door. It is a change of use **from land that already qualified**.

To qualify, the land must have been **previously qualified as open-space or timber land**, and it must be used in **at least 3 of 7 specified ways** to propagate a sustaining breeding, migrating or wintering population of indigenous wild animals ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/ag-timber/index.php)).

So the sequence is: qualified ag land first, then a conversion to wildlife management. Land that never had the ag valuation cannot start at wildlife management. A buyer told "you can just put it in wildlife" needs to verify with the appraisal district that the parcel currently qualifies, because that claim is only true if it already does.

The three activities have to be real and documented. Districts ask for a management plan and annual reporting, and what satisfies them is a local determination.

## The rollback: three years, and no separate interest rate

Here is the part that most web pages get wrong.

When the use changes, **Tax Code §23.55** imposes an additional tax "equal to the difference between the taxes imposed on the land for **each of the three years preceding the year in which the change of use occurs**" and the taxes that would have been imposed had the land been taxed at market value ([Tax Code §23.55](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/tax-code/tax-sect-23-55/)).

**Three years.** The rollback period for 1-d-1 open-space land is three years of tax difference.

And on interest: **§23.55 does not impose a rollback interest rate.** The statute provides that the additional taxes incur **penalties and interest as provided by law for ad valorem taxes imposed by the taxing unit** only if they are **not paid by the delinquency deadline** for that additional tax ([Tax Code §23.55](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/tax-code/tax-sect-23-55/)). The Comptroller's ag and timber page likewise states no rollback interest rate ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/ag-timber/index.php)).

A great many real estate blogs, land listings and buyer handouts still publish a 5% or 7% annual rollback interest figure for 1-d-1 land. Do not plan around one. The rollback is three years of tax difference; ordinary delinquency penalties and interest attach only if the additional tax goes unpaid past its deadline.

The **amount** of a rollback on a specific parcel is calculated by the appraisal district, using its own market values and the adopted rates for those years. Ask them for the figure. Then take what it means for a deal to a CPA, because the tax treatment of a rollback payment in a transaction is a tax question, not a real estate one.

## What actually triggers a rollback

The trigger is a **change of use** away from qualifying agricultural use. Not a sale by itself. Not a change in ownership by itself.

Things that commonly cause the problem:

- **Development.** Platting, subdividing, building a subdivision, converting pasture to lots.
- **Stopping the operation.** The cattle leave and nothing replaces them. The buyer intends to run cows "eventually" and a year passes.
- **Carving out a homesite.** Building a house on part of a tract can change the use of that portion. How much acreage comes out and how the district treats the remainder is a district determination, and it is not uniform.
- **Failing the intensity standard.** Continuing to call it a ranch while operating below what the district accepts.

The most expensive version is a buyer who closes on ag-valued acreage, does nothing agricultural for a year because the house plans and the well and the septic took all the attention, and receives a rollback bill for three years of difference on land that has appreciated substantially.

## Buying ag-valued land: what to establish before you close

- **Does the parcel currently carry 1-d-1 open-space valuation, and for how long?** Confirm with the appraisal district, not from the listing.
- **What is the district's degree-of-intensity standard for this county and this land type?** Get it in writing if you can.
- **What is the market value the district would otherwise use?** That number, not the ag value, drives the rollback math.
- **What will the operation be on day one?** The gap between closing and a functioning ag use is where rollbacks are born.
- **Who pays a rollback if one is triggered?** This is a contract term, negotiated between buyer and seller. How it is written matters, and the wording is a job for a **Texas real estate attorney**, not something to improvise.
- **What is the tax consequence of the rollback payment itself?** CPA.

In Kendall County, the appraisal district that makes all of these determinations is **Kendall Appraisal District** ([kendallad.org](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)). Boerne is the county seat of Kendall County, not part of Bexar County or the City of San Antonio, so Bexar CAD's standards and schedules do not govern Kendall County land.

## Two adjacent points people conflate

**Ag valuation is not the homestead cap.** The 10% homestead cap applies to a residence homestead with a homestead exemption. Ag-valued land is a separate mechanism with separate rules.

**Ag land is excluded from the non-homestead circuit breaker.** The temporary **20% circuit breaker** under **Tax Code §23.231**, which covers tax years **2024, 2025 and 2026** and expires after the 2026 tax year unless renewed, **excludes land under agricultural-use special appraisal** ([Travis Central Appraisal District](https://traviscad.org/circuitbreaker)). Land that loses its ag valuation is landing in a world where that cap may no longer exist either.

If you disagree with a district's determination on qualification or on the rollback calculation, the protest deadline is **May 15, or 30 days after the district mails the notice of appraised value, whichever is later** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/protests/)).

Qualification, degree of intensity, wildlife management plans and rollback amounts are all determined by the appraisal district. Contract language allocating rollback liability is a matter for a Texas real estate attorney, and the tax consequences of a rollback belong with a CPA.

question: What is an ETJ in Texas?
metaTitle: What is an ETJ in Texas?
metaDescription: Extraterritorial jurisdiction under Local Government Code chapter 42: not on the city tax roll, but Boerne's STR ordinance still reaches the ETJ.
shortAnswer: An ETJ is a city's extraterritorial jurisdiction: unincorporated land just outside the city limits where the city keeps some regulatory authority under Texas Local Government Code chapter 42. Property there is not inside the city and not on the city's property tax roll, but some city rules still reach it. Boerne's short-term rental ordinance does.
body:
## The three-bucket picture

Texas property outside a city is not one thing. For a buyer in the Hill Country it is usually one of three:

1. **Inside the city limits.** The city's full set of powers applies. The property is on the city's tax roll.
2. **In the city's ETJ.** Unincorporated land adjacent to the city. The city retains **some** authority under [Texas Local Government Code chapter 42](https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/LG/htm/LG.42.htm) — subdivision platting is the classic one — but the parcel is not in the city.
3. **Unincorporated county, outside any city's ETJ.** Neither city limits nor ETJ. County authority applies, and Texas counties have narrower ordinance-making power than cities.

Buyers collapse buckets 2 and 3 constantly. "It's outside the city" is not an answer. A property can be outside the city, pay no city property tax, and still be subject to a city ordinance.

## What the ETJ is for

The ETJ exists so that a city has a say in how land right outside its edge gets subdivided and developed. Growth does not stop at a city limit line. Streets, drainage and lot layouts built to no standard on the city's doorstep become the city's problem eventually, and the ETJ gives the city a role in that before it happens.

The practical result is that in the ETJ, **subdividing land, platting lots and the development process typically run through the city**, even though the city does not collect property tax on the parcel.

Which specific powers reach a given city's ETJ is set by statute, and the details vary — including whether an owner's parcel is in the ETJ at all, since ETJ boundaries change as a city grows and as state law changes. Do not infer it from a map screenshot or a listing remark. **Confirm the jurisdiction for a specific address with the city's planning department.** In Boerne, that is the **Boerne Planning Department, (830) 248-1501**.

## The concrete Boerne example

Boerne's short-term rental regulation is the cleanest illustration of how an ETJ actually behaves, because it draws the line in two places at once.

Under **Ordinance No. 2023-09**, Boerne's short-term rental rules apply to **the city limits and the ETJ** ([City of Boerne](https://www.ci.boerne.tx.us/2444/Short-Term-Rentals)). An STR operator on an ETJ parcel is inside the ordinance: registration, permit term, insurance minimums, hotel occupancy tax.

But the **safety inspection requirement applies to properties inside the city limits and does not apply to ETJ properties** ([Short-Term Rental Ordinance 2023-09](https://www.ci.boerne.tx.us/DocumentCenter/View/23223/Short-Term-Rental-Ordinance-2023-09)).

That is the shape of the thing in one ordinance. The city's rule reaches into the ETJ. One specific piece of it stops at the city limit. You cannot predict which is which from first principles — you read the ordinance, or you call the department.

Two more Boerne-specific points that follow from the same logic:

- **Boerne is in Kendall County, not Bexar County, and Boerne is not San Antonio.** San Antonio's ordinances have no force in Boerne or Boerne's ETJ. Investors who research San Antonio rules and then buy near Boerne are reading the wrong rulebook.
- **Unincorporated Kendall County outside Boerne's city limits and ETJ is not covered by the Boerne ordinance at all.** What the county itself requires is a question for Kendall County, and Texas counties have limited ordinance-making power compared with cities.

## Taxes in the ETJ

An ETJ parcel is not in the city, so the city's property tax rate is not on its bill. The other entities still are — the county, the school district, and any special district covering the parcel.

The entity list for a Kendall County parcel comes from **Kendall Appraisal District**, which is the appraisal district for Boerne and Kendall County — **not Bexar CAD** ([Kendall AD](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)). Rate documents the county publishes are at [Kendall County tax rate information](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/184/Tax-Rate-Information).

Note that the **hotel occupancy tax question is separate from the property tax question**. Boerne's STR ordinance requires hotel occupancy tax for all STRs it covers, and the combined rate in Boerne is **13%** — state 6% plus city 7% ([City of Boerne current tax rates](https://www.ci.boerne.tx.us/646/Current-Tax-Rates)). Being outside the city property tax roll and being inside a city ordinance are two different facts about the same parcel.

## What to check before buying an ETJ property

- **Confirm the jurisdiction in writing** for the specific address: city limits, ETJ, or neither. Ask the City of Boerne Planning Department, not a neighbor.
- **Ask which city regulations apply out there** for what you actually intend to do — build, subdivide, add a second dwelling, operate a short-term rental.
- **Ask about platting.** If you plan to split the tract, the process likely runs through the city.
- **Confirm utilities.** Whether the parcel is on a city water or sewer connection, or on a private well and an on-site septic system, is a property-by-property fact, and it drives inspections and due diligence.
- **Ask the city about annexation** — whether the parcel could come into the city, and under what process. The rules around Texas annexation have changed over time, so get the current answer from the city rather than from an older article.
- **Check emergency services, address and school attendance** for the parcel rather than assuming they follow the city.

## Where the line is

An agent can tell you which bucket a property sits in and hand you the ordinance. Questions about how a regulation applies to your specific plan go to the **City of Boerne Planning Department**. Questions about deed restrictions, plat notes or enforceability go to a **Texas real estate attorney**. Tax consequences go to a **CPA**.

Ordinances change. Confirm current terms with the City of Boerne before you buy on the strength of what any page, including this one, says today.

## Related questions
