question: What is an HOA resale certificate in Texas?
metaTitle: What is an HOA resale certificate in Texas?
metaDescription: Texas Property Code chapter 207 sets what the resale certificate contains, a 10-business-day delivery deadline, a 60-day rule and a $375 fee cap.
shortAnswer: An HOA resale certificate is a Texas Property Code chapter 207 document the property owners' association prepares for a pending sale. It states assessments, unpaid amounts, known violations, insurance, pending lawsuits, reserves and transfer restrictions. The association must deliver it within 10 business days of a proper written request, prepared no earlier than 60 days before delivery.
body:
## What the certificate is for

A buyer purchasing into a mandatory-membership subdivision is buying two things: a house, and a contractual relationship with an association that can assess money against the house and restrict what is done with it. The resale certificate is how the association puts the current state of that relationship in writing before closing.

**Texas Property Code chapter 207** governs it. The statute calls the broader package **subdivision information**, and the resale certificate is the part of it the association fills in for this specific lot at this specific moment ([Texas Property Code 207.003](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-207-003/)).

## What is actually in it

Under section 207.003 the certificate covers, among other items:

- **Regular and special assessments** — the amount, and how often they are due
- **Unpaid amounts** owed on the property, including any assessment already levied but not yet due
- **Certain known violations** of the declaration or rules on that lot
- **Insurance** maintained by the association
- **Certain pending lawsuits** to which the association is a party
- **Reserves** and capital expenditure information
- **Budgets** and financial statements
- **Transfer restrictions** and the fees charged in connection with the transfer

Read the violations line and the special-assessment line first. An open violation — an unapproved fence, a shed in a setback, a paint color that was never submitted to the architectural committee — becomes the buyer's problem on the day the deed records. A special assessment already voted but not yet billed is a real number that does not appear anywhere on the MLS listing.

The certificate is the summary. It is not the governing documents. The declaration of covenants, conditions and restrictions is where the actual rules live, and it is usually far longer and far more consequential than the certificate. Ask for both.

## The two deadlines that matter

**Delivery:** section 207.003(a) requires the information **not later than the 10th business day after the date a written request for subdivision information is received** ([Texas Property Code 207.003](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-207-003/)).

**Freshness: the certificate must be prepared no earlier than 60 days before it is delivered.** A certificate pulled months ago for a different deal is not usable ([FirstService Residential — Texas HOA resale certificate](https://www.fsresidential.com/texas/news-events/articles/texas-hoa-resale-certificate/)).

Ten business days is up to two calendar weeks. That is longer than a lot of option periods. A buyer who wants to read the association documents before the termination right expires needs the request made immediately after the contract goes effective, not at the end of the week. When an association is self-managed by volunteers, or when a third-party management company routes the request through a payment portal, the clock is the full ten days more often than not.

If the documents arrive late and the buyer is out of option period, the buyer's leverage is gone. That sequencing failure is the single most common way a buyer ends up owning a covenant they never read.

## The fees

The statute caps the charge. Section 207.003(c) reads: a property owners' association "may charge a reasonable and necessary fee, not to exceed **$375**, to assemble, copy, and deliver the information required by this section" ([Texas Property Code 207.003](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-207-003/)).

Two things follow from the wording. The fee must be **reasonable and necessary** — $375 is a ceiling, not an entitlement. And it covers assembling, copying and delivering the subdivision information, which is a defined job, not an open-ended service charge.

Separately from the statutory resale certificate charge, associations and their management companies commonly bill **transfer fees** at closing. Those are a different item, they are disclosed on the certificate under transfer-related fees, and who pays them is negotiated in the contract, not set by law.

## What the contract itself warns you about

The association's obligation to produce documents comes from chapter 207. The buyer's exposure is spelled out in the contract.

**Paragraph 6E(2)** of the One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale) carries a check box for whether the property **is or is not** subject to mandatory membership in a property owners association, and where it is, the form prints the notice required by **section 5.012, Texas Property Code** ([TREC form 20-19, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). That notice tells the buyer they are obligated to be a member, that the restrictive covenants and dedicatory instruments have been or will be recorded in the county's Real Property Records and copies may be obtained from the county clerk, and then this:

> "**The amount of the assessments is subject to change. Your failure to pay the assessments could result in enforcement of the association's lien on and the foreclosure of the Property.**"

The same paragraph references **section 207.003** as the basis for an owner's entitlement to copies of the governing documents.

Read the two sentences together. The number on the resale certificate today is not fixed, and non-payment is secured by a lien on the house. That is the whole reason to read the reserves, the budget and the pending-litigation lines rather than just the current dues figure.

## The TREC forms involved

Two promulgated forms carry this ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)):

- **Addendum for Property Subject to Mandatory Membership in a Property Owners Association, form 36-11, effective 07/01/2026.** This is the addendum attached to the contract when the property is in a mandatory-membership subdivision. It is where the parties handle who orders the subdivision information, who pays for it, and the buyer's rights around receiving it.
- **Subdivision Information, Including Resale Certificate for Property in a Property Owners Association, form 37-5, effective 02/10/2014.** This is the certificate form itself.

For a condominium, the analogous document is different: the **Condominium Resale Certificate, form 32-5, effective 11/25/2024**, used with the condominium resale contract rather than the 1-4 family form. Condominium regimes are governed differently from ordinary subdivisions, and using the wrong form is a real error, not a formality.

## What buyers miss

**Short-term rental restrictions.** A declaration can be amended to restrict or prohibit short-term rentals, and deed restrictions are private contracts enforceable independently of any city ordinance. A property that qualifies for a city STR permit can still be barred by its HOA. That analysis belongs to a Texas real estate attorney reading the actual declaration and its amendments, not to a summary line on a certificate.

**Pending litigation.** An association in active litigation may be facing a cost that lands on owners later. The certificate discloses certain pending suits. Ask what it is about.

**Reserves.** An association with a large aging amenity and thin reserves is an assessment waiting to happen. The reserve figure is on the certificate. Almost nobody reads it.

**Architectural approval.** Most declarations require written approval before exterior changes. Buyers who plan to add a shop, a pool, a casita or a metal roof should confirm the approval process before the option period ends, not after closing.

## Where the line is

A real estate agent can order the documents, flag what is on them, and make sure the timeline works. Interpreting whether a specific covenant is enforceable against a specific intended use is legal work. That goes to a **Texas real estate attorney**. Questions about the association's finances and what a reserve shortfall implies are worth putting to a **CPA** if the purchase is an investment.

## Related questions

- [Can an HOA ban short-term rentals in Texas?](/answers/can-an-hoa-ban-short-term-rentals-in-texas)

question: What is earnest money in Texas, and is it refundable?
metaTitle: What is earnest money in Texas, and is it refundable?
metaDescription: Texas earnest money explained: how much, where it is held, when it is refundable, how it is credited at closing, and why escrow cannot release it unilaterally.
shortAnswer: Earnest money is a good-faith deposit the buyer delivers to the title company to be held in escrow. It is refundable if the buyer terminates during the option period or under a contract right such as the financing addendum. It is credited to the buyer at closing and cannot be released without mutual agreement or a court order.
body:
## What earnest money is

Earnest money is the buyer's money, deposited with a neutral third party, showing the seller the offer is real. It is not a fee and it is not paid to the seller. It sits in the escrow account of the title company from delivery until the deal either closes or dies.

Paragraph 5A of the current contract sets the mechanics: "**Within 3 days after the Effective Date**, Buyer must deliver to [blank] (**Escrow Agent**) at [blank] (address): $____ as earnest money and $____ as the option fee. The earnest money and option fee shall be made payable to Escrow Agent and may be paid separately or combined in a single payment" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶5A](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

At closing it is credited to the buyer — it counts toward the down payment and closing costs, so the wire the buyer sends at the end is reduced by that amount.

The critical structural fact: **earnest money in escrow cannot be released to either party without mutual agreement or a court order** ([Texas Real Estate Research Center](https://trerc.tamu.edu/article/option-period-basics-2360/)). Paragraph 18 of the contract is titled ESCROW and governs how the escrow agent handles and releases it. The title company is not a judge. It does not decide who was right. If the two sides disagree about who gets the money, the money stays where it is.

## How much earnest money

There is no statutory amount and TREC does not set one. It is a dollar blank in ¶5A that the buyer and seller negotiate ([TREC form 20-19](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

Paragraph 5A(1) adds an optional second layer: **additional earnest money**, delivered within a stated number of days after the effective date. It is a real negotiating tool — a buyer can deposit a modest amount up front and commit more once the option period expires, which signals seriousness without putting the full amount at risk during due diligence.

A stronger deposit is a signal — it tells the seller the buyer has cash and is not shopping around. A buyer competing on a well-priced listing may raise it deliberately. A buyer on a property with known complications may want it lower, because it is the amount at risk if the deal falls apart after the option period ends.

## When it is refundable

**During the option period.** Paragraph 5B: if the buyer gives notice of termination within the time prescribed, "(i) the option fee will not be refunded... and (ii) **any earnest money will be refunded to Buyer**." Notice must be given "by 5:00 p.m. (local time where the Property is located) by the date specified" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶5B](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). This is the clean exit and it requires no reason.

**Under a contract right that survives the option period.** The TREC promulgated addenda create their own termination rights with their own deadlines. The **Third Party Financing Addendum, form 40-11, effective 01/03/2025** governs the buyer's financing exit. The **Addendum Concerning Right to Terminate Due to Lender's Appraisal, form 49-1** addresses a low appraisal. The **Addendum for Sale of Other Property by Buyer, form 10-6** covers a buyer whose purchase depends on selling a home ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)). Each has its own notice requirement and its own clock.

**Under the seller's disclosure right.** Paragraph 7B(2) of the contract implements Texas Property Code §5.008. If the buyer has not received the seller's disclosure notice, "**Buyer may terminate this contract at any time prior to the closing** and the earnest money will be refunded to Buyer." If the seller then delivers it, "Buyer may terminate this contract for any reason **within 7 days after Buyer receives** the Seller's Disclosure Notice **or prior to the closing, whichever first occurs**, and the earnest money will be refunded to Buyer" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶7B(2)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf); [Texas Property Code §5.008](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-5-008/)).

**If the title commitment never arrives.** Paragraph 6B requires the seller to furnish the commitment within 20 days after the title company receives a copy of the contract, automatically extended up to 15 days or 3 days before the closing date, whichever is earlier. If it still is not delivered in time, "**Buyer may terminate this contract and the earnest money will be refunded to Buyer**."

**If title objections are not cured.** Under ¶6D, if the seller does not cure the buyer's timely objections within the 15-day cure period, the buyer has 5 days after the end of that period to terminate with the earnest money refunded — or waive. Silence is a waiver.

**Casualty loss.** Under ¶14, if the property is damaged after the effective date and the seller cannot restore it by the closing date due to factors beyond the seller's control, one of the buyer's three options is to terminate and have the earnest money refunded.

**If the seller defaults.** Paragraph 15: the buyer may enforce specific performance, seek other relief provided by law, or both, or terminate and receive the earnest money.

## When it is not

Once the option period expires and no other termination right applies, the earnest money is genuinely at risk. Paragraph 15 states the consequence plainly: if the buyer defaults, the seller may "(a) enforce **specific performance**, seek such other relief as may be provided by law, or both, or (b) terminate this contract and **receive the earnest money as liquidated damages**, thereby releasing both parties from this contract" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶15](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

"Liquidated damages" is the key phrase. The earnest money is the agreed measure of the seller's loss — the seller does not have to prove actual damages to keep it.

A buyer who changes their mind in week four, or cannot come up with funds that were never contingent, or simply does not show up to closing, is in default. "I got cold feet" is not a contract right. Neither is "the inspection worried me" once the option period is over — the inspection window and the unrestricted termination right are the same window, and it closes.

## The late-earnest-money rule with a timing catch

Paragraph 5C covers what happens when the buyer does not deliver the earnest money on time. The seller may terminate the contract, exercise the remedies under ¶15, or both.

The catch is the timing, and it cuts the buyer's way. The seller must give that notice **before the buyer delivers the earnest money** ([TREC form 20-19, ¶5C](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

So a buyer who is two days late but wires the money before the seller sends notice has cured the problem. A seller who waits to see whether something better comes along, then tries to terminate after the funds have landed, has missed the window. The remedy exists only in the gap between the missed deadline and the late delivery.

## Why "getting the money back" is a separate event from terminating

Terminating a contract and receiving escrowed funds are two distinct steps, and conflating them causes most of the frustration people have with Texas escrow.

Termination is unilateral when the contract gives you the right. You deliver notice, the contract ends.

Release of escrowed earnest money is **not** unilateral. It requires both parties to sign a release, or a court order ([Texas Real Estate Research Center](https://trerc.tamu.edu/article/option-period-basics-2360/)). A buyer who terminates perfectly and on time, and whose seller refuses to sign the release out of irritation, has a terminated contract and money still sitting in escrow.

That standoff is common and it is why a buyer's leverage is in the paperwork. A clean, timely, written termination delivered exactly the way the contract requires is what makes the seller's refusal indefensible. A sloppy one gives the seller an argument.

If a release stalls, the next conversation is with a Texas real estate attorney about the contract's dispute provisions. The title company will not break the tie.

## Earnest money versus the option fee

Different money, different rules.

The **option fee** buys the unrestricted right to terminate. It becomes the seller's money, ¶5B says it "will not be refunded" on termination, and under ¶5A(4) the buyer authorizes the escrow agent to release it to the seller "at any time without further notice to or consent from Buyer" ([TREC form 20-19](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

The **earnest money** stays the buyer's money in escrow, is refundable on a timely termination, and cannot move without mutual agreement or a court order.

## The delivery trap worth knowing

Paragraph 5A allows the option fee and earnest money to be paid separately or combined in a single payment. Paragraph 5A(3) then applies amounts received "**first to the option fee, then to the earnest money, and then to the additional earnest money**" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶5A(3)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

A combined payment that is short by any amount will fully fund the option fee and underfund the earnest money. Underfunded earnest money is a buyer default under the contract, and under ¶5C the seller can act on it — but only by notice given before the buyer delivers. Nothing alerts anyone at the time. Sending two separate payments eliminates the exposure and produces a clean escrow receipt for each.

Paragraph 5A(2) governs the calendar: if the last day to deliver the earnest money, option fee or additional earnest money falls on a **Saturday, Sunday or Legal Holiday** — defined by reference to Texas Government Code Sections 662.003(a) and 662.003(b)(4) and (6) — the time extends to the end of the next day that is none of those.

## Related questions

- [How does the option fee work in Texas?](/answers/how-does-the-option-fee-work-in-texas)
- [Is the option fee refundable in Texas?](/answers/is-the-option-fee-refundable-in-texas)

question: What is the 10 percent homestead cap in Texas?
metaTitle: What is the 10 percent homestead cap in Texas?
metaDescription: The 10 percent cap limits net appraised value once the homestead exemption is on, and resets to market value after a sale, which is why bills jump.
shortAnswer: Once a Texas home has a homestead exemption, the appraisal district cannot raise its net appraised value more than 10 percent per year, no matter how much the market moves. The cap does not transfer to a buyer. It resets to market value after a sale, which is why a new owner's tax bill often jumps.
body:
## What the cap actually limits

The cap is **10% per year on net appraised value**, and it applies to properties that already have a **homestead exemption** in place ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)).

It does not cap your tax bill. It does not cap the tax rate. It caps the growth of the value the taxing units are allowed to tax. Rates are still set every year by each taxing unit's own board, and a rate increase raises a bill with a fully capped value.

It also does not cap the district's **market value** conclusion. The district still appraises the home at what it believes the home is worth. The cap sits on top of that and limits what gets taxed.

## Read your notice: there are two values on it

This is the part that confuses people every spring. A notice of appraised value on a homesteaded property shows a **market value** and an **appraised (capped) value**, and after a few years of appreciation they are not close.

Market value is the district's opinion of what the property would sell for. Appraised value is the capped figure. Taxable value is that capped figure minus your exemptions. The bill is built off taxable value.

Two consequences follow:

- A homeowner whose capped value is far below market value may have little to gain from a protest that only argues market value down a little. The number that matters is whether the capped value is correct, and whether the market value has been driven low enough to actually pull the capped value with it.
- The **gap between the two** is stored-up increase. It does not vanish. It waits.

## The cap turns on when the exemption does

There is no cap without a homestead exemption. A property with no exemption on file has no cap, and the district can move its value to market in a single year.

The exemption requires that the owner **owned and occupied the home as a principal residence on January 1** of the tax year, and applications are due **before May 1** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)). In Boerne and anywhere else in Kendall County, that filing goes to the **Kendall Appraisal District** ([kendallad.org](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)), not Bexar CAD — Boerne is in Kendall County, not Bexar County, and not in the City of San Antonio.

So the practical sequence is: buy, qualify on a January 1, file the exemption, and the cap begins protecting you going forward. It does not reach backward and it does not apply in the interim.

## The reset: what happens when the house sells

The cap belongs to the property under a qualifying owner's exemption. It does not travel with the sale.

When a homesteaded property sells, the protection that built up over the seller's years of ownership ends. The new owner faces the district's market value — frequently informed by the price just paid — and must establish their own exemption and their own cap from that new baseline.

The practical version, and it is the most common tax surprise in Texas residential real estate:

**The seller's tax bill is not a forecast of the buyer's tax bill.** A seller who owned a Hill Country home through a run of appreciation might be paying on a capped value well below market. The listing shows that number. The county website shows that number. It is a record of what somebody else paid under their own exemption and their own cap, and it is not what the buyer will pay.

When taxes are escrowed, the correction shows up as a lender escrow analysis and a monthly payment increase, well after closing and long after the buyer stopped thinking about it. The number to budget from is an estimate built on the **purchase price**, the current adopted rates for the actual taxing units on that parcel, and the exemptions the buyer will personally qualify for — not the seller's bill.

For scale on the rates involved, Boerne ISD adopted **1.0109 per $100** of taxable value for 2025, after 0.9909 in 2024 ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/295/Boerne-ISD)).

## What the cap survives, and what it does not

The cap follows a qualifying owner's homestead on the property. Events that change ownership, occupancy or exemption status can end it — a sale, a move, a transfer into a trust or an entity, a change in who holds title after a death.

**New improvements** are treated separately. Added value from new construction — square footage, a casita, a shop, a pool — is generally taxed, rather than being absorbed under the cap. Ordinary repairs and maintenance are a different category. Where a specific project falls is a determination the appraisal district makes, and the time to ask is before the permit, not after the notice arrives.

Whether a specific transfer preserves or ends a homestead exemption and its cap is a legal and administrative question. The appraisal district decides exemption status; a **Texas real estate attorney** is the right person to look at the deed or trust before it is signed.

## Investors: the 10% cap is not yours, and the one that is expires

Non-homestead property gets no 10% cap. Rentals, second homes, land held for investment — the district can move those to market value in one year.

There has been a temporary substitute. Under **Tax Code §23.231**, a **20% circuit breaker** limits annual appraised value increases on qualifying **non-homestead** real property valued at or below a threshold. The threshold is **indexed annually**, and published figures for the current year do not agree with each other — confirm the number with your appraisal district rather than a blog.

The important part is the calendar. The circuit breaker was created by **SB 2 (2023)** as a pilot covering tax years **2024, 2025 and 2026**, and it **expires after the 2026 tax year** unless the Legislature renews it. There is no application; the appraisal district applies it automatically, and the owner must have held the property for **at least one full calendar year** to qualify ([Travis Central Appraisal District](https://traviscad.org/circuitbreaker)).

It also excludes land under agricultural-use special appraisal and homesteads already covered by the 10% cap.

Anyone underwriting a Texas rental or a piece of investment land past 2026 should run the numbers both ways: with the circuit breaker and without it. Its expiration is on the books, not speculative, and a proforma that quietly assumes a 20% ceiling in 2027 is assuming a law that currently sunsets.

## When the cap is the reason a protest is worth filing anyway

If the district's **market value** is materially wrong — wrong square footage, unrecorded condition problems, a comparison set that does not reflect your street — it is worth correcting even in a year when the capped value governs your bill. Market value feeds forward. A market value left too high keeps the capped value climbing 10% a year for as long as the gap lasts.

The protest deadline is **May 15, or 30 days after the district mails the notice of appraised value, whichever is later** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/protests/)).

Value determinations, exemption status and cap calculations are all made by the appraisal district. Take the tax consequences of a purchase, sale or ownership change to a CPA.

## Related questions

question: What is the Amendment to Contract in a Texas real estate deal?
metaTitle: What is the Amendment to Contract in a Texas real estate deal?
metaDescription: TREC form 39-11: check each applicable box, ten numbered items, and item 7 is how a Texas option period actually gets extended.
shortAnswer: The Amendment to Contract is the TREC form used to change the terms of a contract that is already in effect: price, closing date, repairs, option period. It takes effect only when every party signs and it is delivered. The current version is TREC form 39-11, effective 07/01/2026. It changes a contract. It does not end one.
body:
## What it is

Once a Texas contract is executed, its terms are the terms. There is no informal editing. If the parties want to change something — the price after an inspection, the closing date after an underwriting delay, a repair obligation, the length of the option period — they do it in writing with the **Amendment to Contract, TREC form 39-11** ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)). The form carries a footer date of **05-04-2026** and is **effective 07/01/2026** ([TREC form 39-11, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/39-11.pdf)).

It is a short form that does exactly one job: it restates the specific terms that are changing and leaves everything else intact. Anything the amendment does not touch still governs.

## "Check each applicable box" — this is not a one-thing-at-a-time form

The instruction printed at the top reads: "Seller and Buyer amend the contract as follows: (**check each applicable box**)" ([TREC form 39-11, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/39-11.pdf)).

Check **each** applicable box, not one. A single amendment can move the closing date, adjust the price and extend the option period at once, and in a real negotiation it usually should — one document, one round of signatures, one delivery, one version of the truth. Splitting three changes across three amendments is three chances for one of them to sit unsigned in an inbox.

The corollary: an unchecked box is not a change. A number written into item 3 with the item 3 box left blank is an argument, not an amendment.

## The ten items, walked

1. **The Sales Price in Paragraph 3.** Broken into A, the cash portion payable at closing; B, the sum of all financing described in the contract; and C, the Sales Price, which is the sum of A and B. All three lines get filled. A price change that adjusts C without reconciling A and B against the financing addendum produces a contract that does not add up.
2. **Repairs and treatments.** "In addition to any repairs and treatments otherwise required by the contract, Seller, at Seller's expense, shall complete the following repairs and treatments," followed by the printed notice: "(**Notice: Paragraph 7 of the contract governs the completion, delivery of documentation, and transfer of warranties of repairs and treatments.**)" The amendment creates the obligation; Paragraph 7 of the contract controls how it gets performed, documented and warranted. Writing a repair into item 2 does not rewrite Paragraph 7.
3. **The date in Paragraph 9** — the closing date. The most common amendment there is.
4. **The amount in Paragraph 12A(1)(b)** — the cap on the seller's contribution toward the buyer's expenses.
5. **The amounts in Paragraph 12B** — brokerage compensation contributions, with dollar or percentage-of-sales-price checkboxes for each party.
6. **Lender required repairs and treatment**, itemized on an attached list and split "$___ by Seller; $___ by Buyer." This is where a Property Approval problem under the Third Party Financing Addendum gets resolved instead of terminated.
7. **Option period extension.** Its own section below.
8. **Waiver of the option right.** "Buyer waives the unrestricted right to terminate the contract for which the option fee was paid." Checking this box ends the buyer's clean walk-away early, on purpose, usually to give a seller certainty in exchange for something.
9. **The Buyer Approval notice date** under the Third Party Financing Addendum: "The date for Buyer to give written notice to Seller that Buyer cannot obtain Buyer Approval as set forth in the Third Party Financing Addendum is changed to ___."
10. **Other Modifications**, with a printed warning that deserves its own section too.

## Item 7 is how a Texas option period actually gets extended

This is the part people handle by text message, and it does not work by text message.

Item 7 reads: "Buyer has paid Seller an **additional option fee of $___** for an extension of the unrestricted right to terminate the contract **on or before 5:00 p.m. on ___**. This additional option fee **will / will not** be credited to the Sales Price" ([TREC form 39-11, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/39-11.pdf)).

Three distinct things have to be decided, and all three are on the form:

- **An additional option fee**, stated as a dollar amount. The extension is bought, the same way the original option was bought.
- **A new expiration**, written as a date with **5:00 p.m.** already printed on the form. Not "another week." A date.
- **A separate election on whether that additional fee is credited to the Sales Price.** The original option fee is credited at closing under Paragraph 5A(4) of the contract. The additional fee under item 7 is credited only if the parties check that it is. This is the box that gets skipped, and it is real money.

The extension also has to be executed **before** the existing option period runs out. **Paragraph 5B** of the contract grants the unrestricted right to terminate only "within [ ] days after the Effective Date," with notice due by 5:00 p.m. local time, and **Paragraph 5E** adds: "**Time is of the essence** for this paragraph and strict compliance with the time for performance is required" ([TREC form 20-19, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). An amendment signed the morning after the option expired does not revive a right that already ended. There is nothing left to extend.

Delivery mechanics are worth confirming rather than assuming. The original option fee goes to the escrow agent — the title company — within three days after the effective date ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/article/changes-delivery-option-fee-0)). The additional option fee in item 7 is described on the form as paid to Seller. Who holds it, and when it actually moved, is something to confirm in the transaction rather than infer.

## Item 9 moves a financing deadline, and it points at a specific paragraph

Item 9 changes "the date for Buyer to give written notice to Seller that Buyer cannot obtain Buyer Approval as set forth in the Third Party Financing Addendum."

That is the **Paragraph 2A** deadline on the financing addendum — the borrower-side window, counted in days after the effective date. It matters because of what happens when it passes: under the addendum, if the buyer does not terminate under 2A, the contract is no longer subject to the buyer obtaining Buyer Approval at all. Item 9 is the only clean way to move that date, and like item 7 it has to be executed before the date it is moving.

Item 9 does **not** touch Property Approval under Paragraph 2B, which runs to the 3rd day before the Closing Date on its own terms.

## Item 10 exists, and the form itself warns you about it

Item 10 is **Other Modifications**, and TREC prints the warning right on it: "(**Real estate brokers and sales agents are prohibited from practicing law.**)" The form's footer repeats it: "**CONSULT AN ATTORNEY BEFORE SIGNING: TREC rules prohibit real estate brokers and sales agents from giving legal advice. READ THIS FORM CAREFULLY.**"

That warning is the hinge of this entire form. Items 1 through 9 are blanks a license holder fills in. Item 10 is a blank space, and blank space is where drafting happens.

A leaseback. A holdback for unfinished work. A contingency tied to the sale of another property. A carve-out on a fixture. A payment structure that does not exist anywhere in the promulgated forms. Every one of those is language somebody has to write, and a license holder writing it is practicing law. That is work for a **Texas real estate attorney**, and paying for a paragraph is cheaper than litigating one.

## The execution block, and the date of final acceptance

The form ends with "EXECUTED the ___ day of ___, 20___. (**BROKER: FILL IN THE DATE OF FINAL ACCEPTANCE.**)"

That instruction is directed at the broker for a reason. The date of final acceptance is the date the last party signed and that signature was delivered — not the date the first party signed, not the date somebody agreed on the phone. Every deadline the amendment creates or moves is measured against real dates, and a wrong date on an amendment propagates the same way a wrong effective date on a contract does.

## The two rules that make or break any amendment

**1. Every party signs.** A buyer-signed amendment sitting in an inbox is a proposal. An amendment on a contract with two sellers needs both sellers. An amendment on a property held by an entity needs whoever is authorized to bind the entity. A missing signature does not create a partially amended contract; it creates no amendment at all.

**2. It has to be delivered.** Signed and sitting on someone's desk is not delivered. The original contract's notice and delivery provisions apply to the amendment the same way they apply to everything else.

Both rules get broken constantly, usually under time pressure, and usually by someone assuming that a text-message agreement is the deal. A verbal "we agreed to extend closing a week" is not an extension. The closing date in the executed contract is still the closing date until an amendment says otherwise.

## Write repairs like someone will have to enforce them

The contract prints its own drafting warning on the repairs blank: "**Do not insert general phrases, such as 'subject to inspections' that do not identify specific repairs and treatments**" ([TREC form 20-19, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

Apply that to item 2 of the amendment. "Seller to complete repairs" without naming the repair, the standard of completion and who verifies it is an argument waiting to happen at the final walkthrough. Specific beats generous.

**Paragraph 7D** of the contract confirms the amendment is the right instrument for this: accepting the property As Is "does not preclude Buyer from inspecting the Property under Paragraph 7A, from **negotiating repairs or treatments in a subsequent amendment**, or from terminating this contract during the Option Period." That is the amendment's job in a deal — it is what turns an inspection report into an obligation.

## An amendment is not a termination

Different instruments, different outcomes.

- **Amendment to Contract, form 39-11** — changes terms; the contract continues.
- **Notice of Buyer's Termination of Contract, form 38-8, effective 04/01/2025** — the buyer ends the contract.
- **Notice of Seller's Termination of Contract, form 50-0, effective 08/13/2018** — the seller ends it under the circumstances the contract allows.

Using an amendment to try to end a deal, or a termination notice to try to change a term, does not produce the intended result.

Related point on money: earnest money is held by the title company and **cannot be released to either party without mutual agreement or a court order**. A contract that ends in disagreement leaves funds in escrow regardless of who believes they are right, and an amendment cannot unilaterally move that money either — it takes everyone's signature, which is the same rule as everything else on this page.

The underlying contract for an ordinary resale is **form 20-19, effective 07/01/2026** ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/forms/one-four-family-residential-contract-resale)). Condominiums, builder new construction and farm and ranch use different promulgated contracts, and the amendment attaches to whichever contract the parties actually signed.

## The practical version

Check every box that applies, fill the blanks with dates and dollar amounts instead of intentions, get every signature, deliver it, and execute it before the deadline it changes. Every amendment failure is one of those five steps missing.

question: What is the BRRRR method, and does it work in Texas?
metaTitle: What is the BRRRR method, and does it work in Texas?
metaDescription: If the BRRRR property is your homestead, the refinance is a Section 50(a)(6) loan capped at 80 percent LTV with a 12-day wait. A rental is not.
shortAnswer: BRRRR is buy, rehab, rent, refinance, repeat. It works in Texas, with one constitutional catch: if the property is the borrower's homestead, the refinance is a Section 50(a)(6) loan capped at 80 percent loan-to-value with a 12-day waiting period. A rental held as an investment is not the homestead and is not governed by 50(a)(6).
body:
## The five steps

**Buy** a property below its post-repair value, usually one that will not finance conventionally in its current condition. **Rehab** it. **Rent** it, so it produces income and an appraiser has something to value. **Refinance** to pull the invested capital back out. **Repeat** with the recycled capital.

The whole model lives or dies on the fourth step. Everything before it is ordinary renovation work. The refinance is what turns a one-time flip into a repeatable machine, and it is the step where Texas is genuinely different from every other state.

## Why the refinance step is different in Texas

Texas protects the homestead in its **Constitution**, not merely by statute. If the property being refinanced is the borrower's **homestead**, the cash-out is a home equity loan under **Article XVI, Section 50(a)(6)**, and it carries limits that do not exist elsewhere:

- **80 percent loan-to-value maximum.** All loans secured by the homestead, combined, cannot exceed 80 percent of fair market value at closing. At least 20 percent equity must remain.
- **A 12-day waiting period** — the loan cannot close until at least 12 days after the later of the application or the borrower's receipt of the required notice.
- **A 2 percent fee cap** on fees, excluding the appraisal fee, land survey fee, title insurance premium and title search or examination.
- **Generally non-recourse** — the lender cannot pursue the borrower personally for a deficiency.
- **One at a time**, and **12 months** must pass between home equity closings.

Sources: [Rocket Mortgage](https://www.rocketmortgage.com/learn/home-equity-loan-cash-out-refinance-texas), [Hurst Lending](https://hurstlending.com/texas-cash-out-refinance-rules-50a6-guidelines/). Full mechanics: [what is a Texas cash-out refinance under Section 50(a)(6)](/answers/what-is-a-texas-cash-out-refinance-50a6).

For a BRRRR strategy, the two that bite hardest are the 80 percent ceiling and the 12-month rule. The 80 percent ceiling means a fifth of the after-repair value stays trapped in the property permanently. The 12-month rule means a house-hacking investor who refinances their own residence cannot do it again the following quarter, no matter how good the next deal is.

## The investment property is a different animal

**A rental held in the investor's name as an investment property is not the homestead, and is not governed by Section 50(a)(6).** The Texas Constitution's home equity restrictions apply to the homestead. That is the whole reason a classic BRRRR sequence is workable here at all.

The limits that replace them come from the lender, not the constitution: the lender's own loan-to-value requirements, its seasoning requirement — how long the property must be owned or how long the current value must have existed before a cash-out is allowed — its reserve requirements, its debt service coverage test, and its cap on the number of financed properties.

Those vary by lender and by product, and they change. Any specific loan-to-value number or seasoning period on a blog is a number for someone else's loan program. **Get the current terms in writing from a lender before buying the property**, because the whole model is a bet on that refinance existing on those terms four to eight months later.

The failure mode is specific and common: the rehab runs long, the appraisal lands below the projected after-repair value, and the cash-out at the lender's loan-to-value leaves the investor short of the capital they needed to move on. Then the deal that was supposed to recycle capital has consumed it.

## Where the homestead question gets slippery

The clean version is easy: the investor lives in one house and rents four others. The four are investment property.

The version that trips people up is the house-hack. An investor who buys a duplex, lives in one side and rents the other has a homestead. An investor who lives in a property during the rehab and moves out to rent it has to pin down what that property is at the time of the refinance, and whether a homestead designation was ever filed or claimed. **Homestead character is a legal question with a tax consequence attached, and it belongs to a Texas real estate attorney and a CPA, not to an assumption.** Getting it wrong means applying for the wrong loan product and finding out at underwriting.

## The property tax side, which the pro forma usually ignores

Converting a property to a rental changes its property tax treatment in three ways.

**No homestead exemption.** The residence homestead exemptions — including the school district exemption of **$140,000**, raised from $100,000 by Proposition 13, approved by voters in November 2025 and implemented by SB 4 of the 89th Legislature for tax year 2026 — apply only to a **residence homestead** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)). A rental gets none of it.

**No 10 percent cap.** The 10 percent annual limit on increases in net appraised value applies to properties that already have a homestead exemption. A rental does not get it.

**The circuit breaker instead — for now.** Non-homestead real property valued at or below an annually indexed threshold is covered by a separate **20 percent** cap on appraised value under **Tax Code Section 23.231**, created by SB 2 (2023) as a pilot for tax years **2024, 2025 and 2026**. It **expires December 31, 2026 unless the Legislature renews it** ([Travis CAD](https://traviscad.org/circuitbreaker), [summary of 2023 Texas property tax law changes](https://resolutepts.com/texas-property-tax-law-changes/)). It excludes land under agricultural special appraisal and homesteads already under the 10 percent cap.

That expiration date is a live underwriting item for anyone buying a Texas rental in 2026 with a five-year hold. A pro forma that assumes 20 percent as a permanent appraisal ceiling is assuming a statute that sunsets. Model it both ways. Detail: [how rental properties are taxed differently in Texas](/answers/how-are-rental-properties-taxed-differently-in-texas).

For Boerne and the rest of Kendall County, the appraisal district is **Kendall Appraisal District (kendallad.org)** — not Bexar CAD. Boerne is in Kendall County, not the City of San Antonio.

## So does BRRRR work in Texas

Yes, with the refinance structured on the investment side rather than against a homestead, and with three things pinned down before the purchase rather than after the rehab:

1. **The lender's actual cash-out terms and seasoning requirement, in writing**, for the product the investor will use.
2. **Whether the property will be the homestead at the time of the refinance**, answered by a Texas real estate attorney and a CPA if there is any ambiguity.
3. **A property tax line that reflects no homestead exemption, no 10 percent cap, and the circuit breaker's December 31, 2026 expiration.**

A model that survives all three is a model. One that assumes national-average refinance terms and homestead tax treatment is a spreadsheet.

- [How are rental properties taxed differently in Texas?](/answers/how-are-rental-properties-taxed-differently-in-texas)
- [What is a 1031 exchange?](/answers/what-is-a-1031-exchange)
- [What is the 10 percent homestead cap in Texas?](/answers/what-is-the-10-percent-homestead-cap-in-texas)

question: What is the option period in a Texas real estate contract?
metaTitle: What is the option period in a Texas real estate contract?
metaDescription: The option fee goes to the title company within three days of the effective date, expires at 5:00 p.m. on the last day, and is credited at closing.
shortAnswer: The option period is a negotiated window in the TREC contract during which a Texas buyer can terminate for any reason and get their earnest money back. The buyer pays a separate option fee to the title company within three days of the effective date. The fee is credited at closing and is not refunded on termination.
body:
## What the option fee actually buys

The option fee buys an **unrestricted right to terminate**. Not a right to terminate if the inspection is bad, or if the appraisal comes in low, or if financing falls through — a right to terminate for any reason or no reason at all, as long as the buyer delivers written notice before the period ends ([Texas Real Estate Research Center](https://trerc.tamu.edu/article/option-period-basics-2360/)).

The contract says it in those words. **Paragraph 5B** of [TREC form 20-19](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf) reads: "For nominal consideration, the receipt of which Seller acknowledges, and Buyer's agreement to pay the option fee within the time required, Seller grants Buyer the unrestricted right to terminate this contract by giving notice of termination to Seller within ____ days after the Effective Date of this contract (Option Period). Notices under this paragraph must be given by 5:00 p.m. (local time where the Property is located) by the date specified." If the buyer terminates in time, "the option fee will not be refunded" and "any earnest money will be refunded to Buyer."

That is unusual. In most states a buyer's exits are tied to contingencies, and each one has to be justified. In Texas the buyer buys a clean walk-away.

The length of the option period and the size of the option fee are **negotiated between buyer and seller**. Neither is set by statute and neither is set by TREC. They are blanks on the contract. Practitioners commonly see seven to ten days and fees in the low hundreds, but in a competitive situation a buyer may shorten the period or raise the fee to strengthen an offer, and on a complicated property a buyer may need considerably longer.

## The three-day delivery deadline is the part that gets people

Since the rule change, the option fee is delivered to the **escrow agent — the title company — not to the seller**. **Paragraph 5A** requires the buyer to deliver both the earnest money and the option fee to the escrow agent "within 3 days after the Effective Date." **Paragraph 5A(2)** extends that deadline to the end of the next qualifying day if day three falls on "a Saturday, Sunday, or Legal Holiday," with "Legal Holiday" defined by reference to Sections 662.003(a) and 662.003(b)(4) and (6) of the Texas Government Code ([TREC form 20-19](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf); [TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/article/changes-delivery-option-fee-0)).

Miss that delivery and the buyer does not have a termination right, no matter what the contract says the option period is. **Paragraph 5D** is blunt about it: "If no dollar amount is stated as the option fee or if Buyer fails to deliver the option fee within the time required, Buyer shall not have the unrestricted right to terminate this contract under this paragraph 5."

Read that first clause again. **A blank option fee amount kills the termination right just as completely as a late wire does.** The buyer who negotiated a ten-day option period, scheduled the inspector and never noticed the empty blank on page two has no option at all. **Paragraph 5E** removes any argument about it: "Time is of the essence for this paragraph and strict compliance with the time for performance is required."

The option fee and the earnest money **may be paid separately or combined in one payment** (¶5A). If they are combined, **paragraph 5A(3)** applies the funds "first to the option fee, then to the earnest money, and then to the additional earnest money." A combined payment that is short by even a small amount therefore leaves the earnest money underfunded — and under **paragraph 5C** the seller may then terminate or pursue the ¶15 default remedies, though only by giving notice before the buyer delivers the earnest money. A quiet trap worth watching ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/article/changes-delivery-option-fee-0)).

**Paragraph 5A(4)** lets the escrow agent release the option fee to the seller "at any time without further notice to or consent from Buyer."

## How the days are counted

Calendar days, not business days. The **effective date is day zero**, and each following day is numbered in sequence. A ten-day option period on a contract with a November 1 effective date runs out at **5:00 p.m. local time on November 11** ([Texas Real Estate Research Center](https://trerc.tamu.edu/article/option-period-basics-2360/)).

The effective date is the date the last party signs and that signature is delivered — not the date the buyer wrote the offer, and not the date the seller verbally accepted. If the effective date on the contract is wrong, every deadline in the deal is wrong with it.

## How the buyer terminates

The buyer delivers **written notice** to the seller by 5:00 p.m. local time on the last day of the option period. TREC publishes a form for this: **Notice of Buyer's Termination of Contract, form 38-8, effective 04/01/2025** ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

On a timely termination the earnest money is released back to the buyer and the seller keeps the option fee. Earnest money itself is held by the title company and **cannot be released to either side without mutual agreement or a court order**, which is why a termination that the seller disputes can leave money sitting in escrow while the parties work it out.

## What happens to the option fee if the deal closes

It is **credited to the sales price at closing** — ¶5A(4) says so in those words. The buyer does not pay it twice. That is different from how buyers in some other states expect a "due diligence fee" to work, and it is worth saying out loud to a relocating buyer.

## Which contract this lives in

The current **One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale) is TREC form 20-19, effective 07/01/2026** ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/forms/one-four-family-residential-contract-resale)). It is the form used for single-family homes, duplexes, triplexes and four-plexes on resale. Condominiums, builder new construction, and farm and ranch each use a different promulgated contract, and the option mechanics look similar but the form number is different.

TREC promulgates these forms and license holders are required to use them. A license holder cannot draft contract language. If a deal needs custom terms, that is a job for a **Texas real estate attorney**.

## The practical version

An option period is time. What a buyer does with it is the whole point: inspections, a contractor walk, a survey review, an insurance quote, an HOA document read, a septic or well inspection on a Hill Country property. None of that happens automatically. The clock runs whether or not anything gets scheduled, and the termination right expires at 5:00 p.m. on the last day regardless of whether the inspector had an opening.

question: What is the Seller's Disclosure Notice in Texas?
metaTitle: What is the Seller's Disclosure Notice in Texas?
metaDescription: Property Code 5.008 and TREC form 55-1: the seven-day termination right, the Paragraph 7B box that must be checked once, and who is exempt.
shortAnswer: The Seller's Disclosure Notice is a written notice Texas Property Code section 5.008 requires from a seller of residential property with not more than one dwelling unit. It discloses known condition, defects and flood history. If the seller delivers it after the contract is signed, the buyer may terminate for any reason within seven days after receiving it.
body:
## Who owes the notice

The duty runs to a **seller of residential real property comprising not more than one dwelling unit**. That is the statutory phrase, and it is narrower than people assume — it captures the ordinary single-family house and does not, on its face, reach a fourplex. The seller must give the buyer a written notice in the form prescribed by section 5.008, or one that is substantially similar ([Texas Property Code 5.008](https://texas.public.law/statutes/tex._prop._code_section_5.008)).

The notice is the seller's. Not the agent's, not the inspector's, not the title company's. A license holder can hand a seller the form and can decline to pass along a notice they know to be false, but the answers on it are the seller's own statements about what the seller actually knows.

The current TREC version of the form is the **Seller's Disclosure Notice, form 55-1, effective 05/28/2026** ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)). Many brokerages and associations publish their own longer versions. Longer is common; shorter than the statute is not an option.

## The seven-day termination right

This is the enforcement mechanism, and it is the part that changes behavior.

If the contract is signed **without the seller having given the notice**, the buyer may terminate the contract **for any reason within seven days after receiving it** ([Texas Property Code 5.008](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-5-008/)). Not for cause. For any reason.

Practically, that means a late disclosure hands the buyer a second walk-away right that can outlive the option period. A seller who signs a contract on Monday and produces the disclosure on Friday has just extended the buyer's exit window past the day the contract was signed, on terms the seller does not control. The fix is boring and it works: the notice goes out with the listing, before anyone writes an offer.

## Paragraph 7B: the box almost nobody reads carefully

The statute creates the duty. The contract operationalizes it, and the contract's version has a limit the statute does not spell out.

**Paragraph 7B** of the One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale) is headed "SELLER'S DISCLOSURE NOTICE PURSUANT TO §5.008, TEXAS PROPERTY CODE," and it is a **check one box only** election with three options ([TREC form 20-19, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)):

- **(1)** Buyer **has received** the Seller's Disclosure Notice.
- **(2)** Buyer **has not received** it, and Seller delivers it within a stated number of days after the Effective Date.
- **(3)** Seller **is not required** to furnish the notice under the Texas Property Code — the exemption box.

Box (2) is the one to read word for word. The form says: if the buyer does not receive the notice, "**Buyer may terminate this contract at any time prior to the closing** and the earnest money will be refunded to Buyer. If Seller delivers the Seller's Disclosure Notice, **Buyer may terminate this contract for any reason within 7 days after Buyer receives** the Seller's Disclosure Notice **or prior to the closing, whichever first occurs**, and the earnest money will be refunded to Buyer."

Two things fall out of that language.

**The right is bigger than seven days until the notice arrives.** If the seller never delivers, the buyer can terminate at any time before closing with earnest money refunded. That is a live termination right sitting under the deal for its entire length.

**"Whichever first occurs" cuts the seven days short.** This is the detail most explanations of the Texas disclosure get wrong. The seven days do not extend past closing. A notice delivered five days before a closing date does not buy the buyer a week — it buys five days, because closing arrives first.

Leaving 7B blank is not a neutral act. It is an unchecked election on an executed contract, and which box should have been checked is exactly the kind of question that gets expensive later.

## The two paragraphs that sit next to it

**¶7C — lead-based paint.** The form states that lead-based paint disclosure "is required by Federal law for a residential dwelling constructed **prior to 1978**." That is a separate federal requirement with its own addendum, not something the §5.008 notice covers.

**¶7D — "As Is."** The contract defines it: "'**As Is**' means the present condition of the Property with any and all defects and without warranty except for the warranties of title and the warranties in this contract." Buying As Is "**does not preclude Buyer from inspecting the Property under Paragraph 7A, from negotiating repairs or treatments in a subsequent amendment, or from terminating this contract during the Option Period**."

So "As Is" is not the trap buyers think it is — it does not waive inspection or the option period. It is also a check one box only election: As Is, or As Is provided the seller completes **specific listed repairs**. The form prints its own warning on that blank: "**Do not insert general phrases, such as 'subject to inspections' that do not identify specific repairs and treatments.**" A repair line that does not name the repair is not an enforceable repair obligation, and that sentence is printed on the form because it kept happening.

## Who is exempt, and what exempt actually means

Section 5.008 lists transfers that are exempt from the notice requirement. They include transfers:

- pursuant to a court order
- by foreclosure
- by a trustee in bankruptcy
- between co-owners
- to a spouse or to a descendant
- by a fiduciary administering an estate
- of a new residence that has not previously been occupied

An executor selling a parent's house, a builder selling a never-occupied new home, a lender selling REO — all commonly land in an exemption.

Here is the part that gets misread. **The exemption is from the form, not from liability.** Being exempt from delivering a section 5.008 notice does not authorize misrepresentation, and it does not erase common-law duties around known material defects or fraud. An exempt seller who affirmatively lies about a foundation repair is not protected by the exemption. How that plays out in a specific dispute is a question for a Texas real estate attorney, not for a real estate agent.

For buyers, the practical read on an exempt sale is different: you are buying with less written history than usual, so the inspection and the option period carry more weight than they otherwise would.

## The death-on-the-property carve-out

Section 5.008 states that a seller or a seller's agent is **not required to disclose a death on the property by natural causes, suicide, or an accident unrelated to the property's condition** ([Texas Property Code 5.008](https://texas.public.law/statutes/tex._prop._code_section_5.008)).

Read the exception inside the exception. A death *related to the condition of the property* — a fall from a defective stair, a carbon monoxide event tied to a heater — is not covered by that carve-out, because the underlying condition is exactly what the notice is about.

If a buyer cares about this, the buyer should ask directly and in writing. A seller who chooses to answer must answer truthfully.

## The flood questions, and why they were added

The statutory notice was expanded by **SB 339, 86th Legislature**, mandatory for contracts executed on or after **September 1, 2019** ([SB 339 bill text](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/86R/billtext/pdf/SB00339F.pdf)). This came out of Hurricane Harvey, and it is the most useful block of questions on the form.

The flood-related items include whether the property is:

- in a **FEMA 100-year floodplain**
- in a **FEMA 500-year floodplain**
- in a **reservoir flood pool**
- whether the property has **flooded at least once in the past five years**
- whether it has been **repaired for flood damage**
- whether the seller has **received flood insurance proceeds**

The two floodplain terms have specific meanings:

- **100-year floodplain** is a Special Flood Hazard Area — FEMA Zones A, V, A99, AE, AO, AH, VE or AR — carrying a **1% annual chance** of flooding.
- **500-year floodplain** is a moderate flood hazard area, shaded Zone X, carrying a **0.2% annual chance**.

"100-year flood" is a bad name for a 1%-per-year event. Over a 30-year mortgage, a 1% annual chance is not a remote possibility. In the Hill Country, where a lot of the flood risk is flash flooding off creeks rather than a slow river rise, a property can flood without being mapped into a Special Flood Hazard Area at all. The disclosure answers the mapping question and the history question separately for a reason. Read both, and take the insurance question to an insurance agent rather than assuming the flood zone answers it.

## What a buyer should actually do with the notice

Treat it as a lead sheet, not a warranty. It tells you what the seller says they know. It does not tell you what is true.

- Cross-check every "yes" against the inspection report.
- Ask for repair invoices, permits and warranty documents named on the notice.
- Note every "unknown" on an item a long-term owner would normally know, and ask about it.
- Compare the disclosed flood answers to the actual FEMA map for the parcel and to the elevation of the structure relative to the nearest drainage.
- Do it inside the option period, while a clean exit still exists.

An inspection finds condition. The disclosure finds history. They are different tools, and the gap between them is usually where the real problem is.

## Related questions

question: What is the Texas homestead exemption in 2026?
metaTitle: What is the Texas homestead exemption in 2026?
metaDescription: School districts must exempt $140,000 for 2026, up from $100,000 after Proposition 13. You must own and occupy by January 1 and file before May 1.
shortAnswer: The Texas homestead exemption removes part of your home's value from property taxation. For 2026, school districts must exempt $140,000 of a residence homestead's value, up from $100,000 after voters approved Proposition 13 in November 2025. You must own and occupy the home as your principal residence on January 1.
body:
## The number changed, and it changed recently

The mandatory school district residence homestead exemption is **$140,000**. It was **$100,000** before. Texas voters approved **Proposition 13 in November 2025**, and the Legislature implemented it through **SB 4, 89th Legislature**, effective for tax year 2026 ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)).

That matters because most of what is written about Texas homestead exemptions online is older than the change. A page that says $100,000, or $40,000, or $25,000 is describing a prior version of the law. As of September 2026, the school district figure is $140,000.

The exemption is not a discount on your tax bill. It is a subtraction from the **taxable value** the school district uses. On a home appraised at $500,000 with a homestead exemption, the school district taxes $360,000 instead of $500,000. The dollar savings depend on the school district's rate, which is set locally and changes annually.

## The exemption is not one exemption — it is a stack

A Texas tax bill is not one tax. It is a separate tax from every taxing unit whose boundaries include your property: the school district, the county, the city if you are inside city limits, and any special districts. Each unit applies its own exemptions.

The pieces, per the [Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/):

- **School district: $140,000 mandatory.** Every school district in Texas must grant it on a qualifying residence homestead.
- **Local option, up to 20% of appraised value.** Any taxing unit may adopt a percentage exemption of up to 20% of appraised value, with a minimum of $5,000. This one is percentage-based, so it grows with your appraisal.
- **County farm-to-market or flood control: $3,000.** A county that collects a farm-to-market road or flood control tax must give a $3,000 residence homestead exemption.
- **Age 65 or older, or disabled: an additional $60,000** from the school district, on top of the $140,000. Other taxing units may adopt a local option of at least $3,000.

Whether your city, county or special district actually adopted a local option exemption is a local decision, and the answer differs by jurisdiction. For a Boerne or Kendall County property, the adopted exemptions by taxing unit are published by the [Kendall Appraisal District](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/).

## Who qualifies

Two conditions, both of them strict:

1. You **owned** the property on **January 1** of the tax year.
2. You **occupied it as your principal residence** on **January 1** of the tax year.

([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/))

January 1 is a snapshot date, not a rolling test. A buyer who closes in March does not meet the January 1 test for that year on that property under the general rule, and a seller who moved out in February was still the January 1 owner-occupant. This is a common source of surprise in a first-year tax bill, and it is one of the reasons a newly purchased home's tax bill often looks nothing like the prior owner's.

"Principal residence" means one home. Not a rental, not a second home, not a lot you are holding. One homestead, the one you actually live in.

## The deadline

Applications are due **before May 1** — commonly stated as April 30 ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)). You file with the **appraisal district** for the county where the property sits, not with the city, not with the school district, and not with the tax assessor-collector who mails the bill.

For a home in Boerne or anywhere else in Kendall County, that is the **Kendall Appraisal District** at [kendallad.org](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/). Not Bexar CAD. Boerne is the county seat of Kendall County and is not part of the City of San Antonio or Bexar County, and a Boerne homeowner who files with Bexar has filed with the wrong district.

There is no fee to file a homestead exemption application with an appraisal district. Companies that mail official-looking letters offering to file it for you for a fee are selling a service you can do yourself.

## What the exemption does besides lower value

Filing a homestead exemption also turns on the **10% appraisal cap**. Once a property has a homestead exemption in place, the appraisal district cannot increase its net appraised value by more than 10% per year, no matter what the market does ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)).

In a market that has moved the way the Hill Country has, the cap is often worth more over time than the exemption amount itself. A homeowner who has held a homesteaded property through several years of appreciation can be taxed on a value well below what the home would sell for. That gap disappears when the property sells and the cap resets, which is the single most common reason a new owner's tax bill jumps.

## What it does not do

The homestead exemption is a property tax exemption. It is separate from the **Texas homestead protection** in the Property Code and Constitution, which is a creditor-protection concept, and separate from the **Texas home equity rules** that limit borrowing against a homestead. People use the word "homestead" for all three. They are different bodies of law, and a Texas real estate attorney is the right person to sort out which one applies to a specific situation.

It also does not freeze your taxes. The exemption reduces value; the taxing units still set their rates every year, and a rate increase can raise your bill even with the exemption in place and the cap holding.

## What actually goes wrong

- **Never filing.** The exemption is not automatic. It has to be applied for once, and homeowners who moved several years ago and assumed it followed them are a recurring find.
- **Filing with the wrong district.** County lines, not mailing addresses, decide which appraisal district you file with.
- **Losing it in a transfer.** Moving a home into a trust or an LLC, adding or removing an owner, or a death in the family can affect exemption status. The appraisal district decides whether the exemption survives the change, and that question should go to them and to a Texas real estate attorney before the deed is signed, not after.
- **Assuming the prior owner's tax bill is yours.** It reflects their exemptions and their capped value, neither of which transfers to you.

Whether a specific property and a specific owner qualify, and what a given exemption is worth on a given bill, is determined by the appraisal district that appraises the property. For the tax consequences of an ownership change, talk to a CPA.

## Related questions

- [How do I file for a homestead exemption in Kendall County, Texas?](/answers/how-do-i-file-for-a-homestead-exemption-in-kendall-county)
- [What is the 10 percent homestead cap in Texas?](/answers/what-is-the-10-percent-homestead-cap-in-texas)
- [What is the Texas over-65 property tax exemption and school tax ceiling?](/answers/texas-over-65-property-tax-exemption-and-school-tax-ceiling)
