question: What is the Third Party Financing Addendum in Texas?
metaTitle: What is the Third Party Financing Addendum in Texas?
metaDescription: TREC form 40-11: Buyer Approval expires on a day count from the effective date, Property Approval runs to the 3rd day before the Closing Date.
shortAnswer: The Third Party Financing Addendum is the TREC form that makes a Texas contract conditional on the buyer's loan. It identifies the loan type and terms, and it gives the buyer a deadline to terminate if the lender will not approve the buyer. The current version is TREC form 40-11, effective 01/03/2025.
body:
## Why the addendum exists at all

The One to Four Family Residential Contract does not, by itself, care how the buyer pays. Strip the addenda off and you have a contract to buy a house for a price by a date. If the buyer's loan falls apart and there is no financing addendum attached, the buyer still owes performance, and the earnest money is exposed.

The Third Party Financing Addendum is what converts "I am getting a mortgage" from an assumption into a contract term. It is attached to the contract and checked as an addendum on the contract's addenda paragraph. If the box is not checked and the form is not attached, the financing condition does not exist ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

The form itself carries a footer date of **11-04-2024**, and TREC's contract list shows it **effective 01/03/2025** ([TREC form 40-11, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/40-11.pdf)). Both dates appear in the wild, and they describe the same two-page form. The contract it attaches to, for an ordinary resale, is **form 20-19, effective 07/01/2026** ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/forms/one-four-family-residential-contract-resale)).

## The whole form turns on one sentence: approval means two approvals

Almost every explanation of this addendum gets this wrong, and getting it wrong costs deals.

**Paragraph 2** reads: "Approval for the financing described above will be deemed to have been obtained when **Buyer Approval and Property Approval are obtained. Time is of the essence for this paragraph and strict compliance with the time for performance is required**" ([TREC form 40-11, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/40-11.pdf)).

Two separate approvals, two separate subjects, two separate deadlines. Buyer Approval is about the borrower. Property Approval is about the house. They are not the same test, they do not expire on the same day, and a buyer who thinks "my financing contingency" is one thing has misread the form.

The "time is of the essence" sentence is not decoration either. It means a deadline missed by a day is a deadline missed.

## Paragraph 2A, Buyer Approval: an election, and a hard cut-off

Paragraph 2A is a **check one box only** election. The parties choose whether the contract is subject to Buyer Approval at all.

If the box making the contract **subject to** Buyer Approval is checked, the form gives the buyer this: "If Buyer cannot obtain Buyer Approval, Buyer may terminate this contract **within ___ days after the Effective Date** of the contract by giving Seller: **(i) notice of termination; and (ii) a copy of a written statement from the lender setting forth the reason(s) for lender's determination.**" On a timely termination, "the earnest money will be refunded to Buyer."

Then comes the sentence that decides more outcomes than any other line in the addendum:

> "If Buyer does not terminate the contract under Paragraph 2A, **the contract shall no longer be subject to the Buyer obtaining Buyer Approval.**"

Read that literally, because it operates literally. The day count in that blank is not a reminder to check in with the lender. It is the entire life of the borrower-side contingency. Let it pass without a termination and the contingency is gone — not weakened, not extended while underwriting continues, gone. A buyer who is denied in week five, on a contract with a 21-day Buyer Approval window, has no exit under 2A. The earnest money is no longer protected by that paragraph.

The form also defines when the approval counts as obtained: Buyer Approval "will be deemed to have been obtained when (i) the terms of the loan(s) described above are available and (ii) lender determines that Buyer has satisfied all of lender's requirements related to **Buyer's assets, income and credit history**." Assets, income, credit history. That is the borrower. Nothing in that sentence is about the house.

The other box — "This contract **is not subject to** Buyer obtaining Buyer Approval" — is a real election that gets used in competitive offers. A buyer who checks it has agreed that a loan denial is their problem, not a contract exit.

## Paragraph 2B, Property Approval: the house, and a much later deadline

Paragraph 2B covers the other half: "If Buyer's lender determines that the **Property** does not satisfy lender's underwriting requirements for the loan (**including but not limited to appraisal, insurability, and lender required repairs**) Buyer may terminate this contract **on or before the 3rd day before the Closing Date**" by giving the seller notice of termination and a copy of the lender's written statement of reasons. The earnest money is refunded ([TREC form 40-11, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/40-11.pdf)).

Three things worth pulling out of that.

**Appraisal lives here.** A low appraisal is a property problem, not a borrower problem, and it is 2B that addresses it — not 2A. TREC also publishes a separate **Addendum Concerning Right to Terminate Due to Lender's Appraisal, form 49-1, effective 03/01/2019**, which is used to handle the appraisal outcome more specifically, and which is frequently waived or partially waived in a competitive offer. A buyer who waives appraisal protection is agreeing to cover a shortfall in cash.

**Insurability lives here too.** If a carrier will not write the policy the lender requires, that is a property approval failure. On older Hill Country properties, roof age, wildfire scoring and prior claims history all reach this paragraph.

**It runs almost to closing.** "On or before the 3rd day before the Closing Date" is a far later date than the 2A window. That asymmetry is deliberate: the borrower's file should be resolved early, but the appraisal, the insurance binder and any lender-required repairs are not finished until late.

## Both exits require the lender's letter

Under 2A and under 2B, termination takes two documents: the notice **and** "a copy of a written statement from the lender setting forth the reason(s) for lender's determination."

A phone call from a loan officer is not that. An email saying "we're not going to be able to do this" may or may not be that. A buyer who gives notice on the last day and cannot produce the lender's written statement of reasons has delivered half of a termination, and a seller with an aggressive position can say so. Ask the lender for the letter at the same moment the file turns, not on the deadline.

## Paragraph 1: what the buyer promised to do, and the blanks that cap the loan

Paragraph 1 opens with an affirmative duty: the buyer "shall apply **promptly** for all financing described below and make **every reasonable effort** to obtain approval for the financing, including but not limited to furnishing all information and documents required by Buyer's lender." A buyer who sits on a document request is not making every reasonable effort.

Below that duty, the financing types run lettered A through G, each its own checkbox with its own fill-in terms:

- **A. Conventional financing** — a first mortgage loan, plus an optional second mortgage loan, each with a principal amount stated "(excluding any financed PMI premium)," a term in years, an interest rate "not to exceed ___% per annum for the first ___ year(s) of the loan," and **Origination Charges as shown on Buyer's Loan Estimate not to exceed ___% of the loan**.
- **B. Texas Veterans loan** — a loan from the **Texas Veterans Land Board**, "at the interest rate established by the Texas Veterans Land Board."
- **C. FHA insured financing** — "A Section ___ FHA insured loan of not less than $___ (excluding any financed MIP)," with the same rate and origination caps.
- **D. VA guaranteed financing** — "of not less than $___ (excluding any financed Funding Fee)."
- **E. USDA guaranteed financing** — same structure, also excluding any financed funding fee.
- **F. Reverse mortgage financing** — "a reverse mortgage loan (also known as a **Home Equity Conversion Mortgage** loan)," with a box for whether it will or will not be FHA insured.
- **G. Other financing** — a named lender, amount, term and the same caps.

Two details in there are easy to skim past and expensive to miss.

**The stated amounts exclude financed PMI, MIP or Funding Fee.** The number in the blank is the base loan, not the number that shows up on the note after the premium is rolled in.

**The rate and origination caps are real terms.** They describe the loan the contract was conditioned on. A loan offered at a higher rate than the cap, or with origination charges above the stated percentage of the loan as shown on the buyer's Loan Estimate, is not the loan in the addendum. Those blanks should be filled from the buyer's **lender**, in writing, not estimated by an agent. Filled too tight, they create exits nobody intended. Filled too loose, the contingency is decorative.

## The survey trap the contract writes into 2B

The main contract reaches into this addendum in one specific place, and it converts a missed errand into a lost termination right.

**Paragraph 6C** of the One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale) is a check-one-box survey election. If box **(2)** is checked — the buyer obtains a new survey at the buyer's expense within a stated number of days — the form adds that if the buyer fails to obtain the survey, the buyer "**may not terminate** the contract under **Paragraph 2B of the Third Party Financing Addendum** because the survey was not obtained" ([TREC form 20-19, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

A buyer who agreed to order the survey and then did not order it cannot use Property Approval to exit on the grounds that the lender could not complete the file without one. The buyer's own inaction does not become a contingency failure.

Under box **(1)**, where the seller furnishes the existing survey plus a **T-47 Affidavit or T-47.1 Declaration**, the exposure flips: if the seller fails to furnish both in time, the buyer obtains a new survey **at the seller's expense** no later than 3 days prior to the Closing Date.

## It is not a substitute for the option period

The option period gives an unrestricted right to terminate for any reason, and it typically expires well before either financing deadline. The financing addendum gives two conditional rights, each tied to a specific failure and each requiring the lender's written statement.

They are not interchangeable. A buyer who is nervous about the loan should not assume 2A rescues a decision they could have made during the option period — and a buyer whose 2A window closes silently has given up the borrower-side protection they wrote into the contract while still holding the property-side one.

All of these deadlines count from the **effective date**. If the effective date is wrong, they are all wrong.

If a financing deadline needs to move, that is done on the **Amendment to Contract**, which has a dedicated item for changing the date the buyer must give notice under this addendum.

## Loan limits sit behind the blanks

The addendum states the loan amount. Whether that amount is available depends on program limits that change annually.

- The **2026 conforming one-unit baseline is $832,750**, up $26,250 from $806,500 in 2025, with a high-cost ceiling of $1,249,125 ([FHFA](https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/fhfa-announces-conforming-loan-limit-values-for-2026)).
- **FHA for 2026** runs a nationwide one-unit floor of $541,287 and a ceiling of $1,249,125, applied by county.
- **VA**: a veteran with **full entitlement has no VA loan limit**, and the VA guaranty does not exceed 25% ([VA](https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/loan-limits/)).

Credit score minimums are not something to publish as fact. Program floors exist, but lender overlays move them, and two lenders will quote the same borrower differently. Get the answer from a lender, in writing, before the financing blanks get filled in.

## How this goes wrong in practice

- **The 2A day count passes with no denial, no termination and no thought.** The contingency is gone by operation of the paragraph.
- **The buyer terminates with a phone call.** No lender letter, no valid termination under either 2A or 2B.
- **The addendum is attached but the addenda box on the contract is not checked.** Sloppy, and it creates an argument nobody needs.
- **The rate or origination cap does not match what the lender is actually offering**, so the contract is conditioned on a loan the buyer was never getting.
- **The loan amount in the blank includes financed MIP or Funding Fee**, which the form says it should not.
- **The buyer changes something mid-contract** — a new credit card, a job change, a large unexplained deposit — and underwriting re-pulls in week four, after 2A has already closed.
- **Appraisal comes in low with appraisal protection waived**, and the buyer covers the gap in cash.

None of these are exotic. They are the ordinary failure modes, and most of them are calendar problems as much as finance problems.

question: What is the TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract?
metaTitle: What is the TREC One to Four Family Residential Contract?
metaDescription: The TREC 1-4 Family Residential Contract (Resale), form 20-19 effective 07/01/2026: what it covers, what it does not, and how the addenda attach to it.
shortAnswer: The One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale) is the TREC promulgated form Texas license holders use to sell existing single-family homes, duplexes, triplexes and four-plexes. The current version is form 20-19, effective July 1, 2026. Condominiums, builder new construction and farm and ranch each use a different form.
body:
## What "promulgated" means and why it matters

The Texas Real Estate Commission writes and approves the contract forms that Texas license holders are required to use. A REALTOR does not draft your purchase contract. They fill in the blanks on a form the state wrote ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

This is not a technicality. Drafting contract language is the practice of law, and a real estate license does not authorize it. The promulgated forms exist precisely so that license holders can paper a transaction without practicing law. When a deal needs a term the form does not contemplate, the correct answer is not a creative paragraph typed into a blank — it is a Texas real estate attorney.

TREC describes the resale contract as its most frequently used form ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/forms/one-four-family-residential-contract-resale)). Most residential purchases in Texas run on this one document.

## What it covers

The form is for the resale of **single-family homes, duplexes, triplexes and four-plexes**. The current version is **12 pages** and carries a **05-04-2026** footer date ([TREC form 20-19 PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf), [TREC form page](https://www.trec.texas.gov/forms/one-four-family-residential-contract-resale)).

Twelve pages sounds like a lot until you try to find something in it. Here is the map of the paragraphs that actually control the deal.

| ¶ | Title | What it decides |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Earnest Money and Termination Option | The 3-day delivery deadline, the option fee, the unrestricted right to terminate |
| 6 | Title Policy and Survey | Who pays for the owner's policy, the 20-day commitment deadline, the survey election, the objection and cure process |
| 7 | Property Condition | Access and inspections, the seller's disclosure notice, as-is versus listed repairs |
| 12 | Settlement and Other Expenses | Each party's itemized expenses, brokerage compensation |
| 13 | Prorations | Taxes, interest, rents, dues through the closing date |
| 14 | Casualty Loss | What happens if the house is damaged before closing |
| 15 | Default | Specific performance, earnest money as liquidated damages |
| 18 | Escrow | How the escrow agent handles and releases the earnest money |
| 23 | Consult an Attorney Before Signing | TREC rules prohibit license holders from giving legal advice |

That is the spine. The deadlines that run the deal — the option fee delivery deadline, the option period expiration, the title commitment, the objection window, the financing deadlines, the closing date — all trace back to the **effective date** written on this form.

## The three "check one box only" elections

Three paragraphs carry a printed instruction to check exactly one box. A blank election or a double-checked one is a real defect in the contract, not a typo, and each of them has been the cause of a deal going sideways weeks later.

**¶6C — the survey.** Three mutually exclusive options: the seller furnishes the existing survey plus a **T-47 Affidavit or T-47.1 Declaration**; the buyer obtains a new survey at buyer's expense; or the seller furnishes a new survey at seller's expense ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6C](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). Option (1) contains a second, nested Seller/Buyer expense checkbox for the case where the title company or lender will not accept what was furnished. Option (2) carries a warning: a buyer who elects it and then fails to obtain the survey "may not terminate the contract under Paragraph 2B of the Third Party Financing Addendum because the survey was not obtained."

**¶7B — the seller's disclosure notice.** Three options: the buyer has received it; the buyer has not and the seller will deliver within a stated number of days; or the seller is not required to furnish it under the Texas Property Code. Option (2) is the consequential one — if the buyer does not receive the notice, the buyer "may terminate this contract **at any time prior to the closing**," and once the seller delivers it, the buyer may terminate for any reason "within **7 days** after Buyer receives" it "or prior to the closing, **whichever first occurs**," with earnest money refunded ([TREC form 20-19, ¶7B(2)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

**¶7D — as-is or listed repairs.** The contract defines "As Is" as "the present condition of the Property with any and all defects and without warranty except for the warranties of title and the warranties in this contract," and is careful to say that accepting as-is "does not preclude Buyer from inspecting the Property under Paragraph 7A, from negotiating repairs or treatments in a subsequent amendment, or from terminating this contract during the Option Period, if any."

The election is either (1) buyer accepts the property as-is, or (2) buyer accepts as-is provided the seller completes specific listed repairs and treatments at seller's expense. And the form prints its own warning next to the blanks:

> "**Do not insert general phrases, such as 'subject to inspections' that do not identify specific repairs and treatments.**"

TREC printed that because people do it anyway. "Subject to inspections" is not a repair obligation — it is a sentence that means nothing and binds nobody, and it is the reason inspection-driven repair fights end up unresolvable. Repairs belong in ¶7D as named items, or in a later amendment on form 39-11.

There is one more ¶7 detail worth carrying: under **¶7A**, inspectors must be "licensed by TREC or otherwise permitted by law," "any **hydrostatic testing must be separately authorized by Seller in writing**," and the seller "at Seller's expense shall immediately cause **existing utilities to be turned on** and shall keep the utilities on during the time this contract is in effect." A buyer whose inspector shows up to a house with the water off has a contract right, not a scheduling problem.

## Money and time: ¶12, ¶13, ¶14, ¶15

**¶12A(1) Seller's Expenses:** releases of existing liens including prepayment penalties and recording fees, release of seller's loan liability, tax statements or certificates, preparation of deed, one-half of escrow fee, plus an optional capped dollar contribution toward the buyer's expenses.

**¶12A(2) Buyer's Expenses:** the loan costs, the loan title policy with lender endorsements, one-half of escrow fee, all prepaid items including flood and hazard insurance premiums and reserves, and PMI, the VA Loan Funding Fee or FHA MIP as required by the lender.

**¶12B Brokerage Compensation** states outright: "**Brokerage compensation is not set by law and is fully negotiable.**" Each party pays their own broker under separate written agreements. Optional checkboxes let one side contribute toward the other's broker compensation, but those contributions "shall not change" either party's obligation under its own agreement ([TREC form 20-19, ¶12B](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

**¶13 Prorations:** taxes, interest, rents and regular periodic maintenance fees, assessments and dues are prorated through the closing date. The proration "may be calculated taking into consideration any change in exemptions," and if the actual taxes differ, "the parties shall adjust the prorations when tax statements for the current year are available."

**¶14 Casualty Loss:** if the property is damaged after the effective date and the seller cannot restore it by the closing date for reasons beyond the seller's control, the buyer may terminate with earnest money refunded, extend performance up to 15 days, or accept the property damaged with an assignment of insurance proceeds **plus a credit from the seller in the amount of the deductible**.

**¶15 Default:** if the buyer defaults the seller may enforce specific performance, seek other relief, or both, or terminate and "receive the earnest money as liquidated damages." If the seller defaults the buyer has the mirror-image remedies.

## What it does not cover

It is not a universal contract. Using the wrong promulgated form is a real error, not a formality.

| Situation | Correct promulgated form |
|---|---|
| Condominium resale | Residential Condominium Contract (Resale), 30-18 |
| Vacant land | Unimproved Property Contract, 9-18 |
| Acreage, ag land, rural tracts | Farm and Ranch Contract, 25-17 |
| Builder new home, construction complete | New Home Contract (Completed Construction), 24-20 |
| Builder new home, construction not complete | New Home Contract (Incomplete Construction), 23-20 |

All five of those, and the resale contract itself, carry a **07/01/2026 effective date** on the current versions ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

In the Hill Country this distinction comes up constantly. A house on ten acres outside Boerne with a well and a septic system may or may not belong on the resale form rather than the Farm and Ranch contract, and the answer depends on the property, not on habit.

## The addenda do the specialized work

The base contract is deliberately generic. The promulgated addenda handle everything specific, and each one attaches to the contract and is checked off on it.

The ones that appear most often:

- **Third Party Financing Addendum, 40-11, effective 01/03/2025** — the buyer's loan terms and financing termination right.
- **Addendum for Property Subject to Mandatory Membership in a Property Owners Association, 36-11, effective 07/01/2026** — the HOA addendum, which triggers the subdivision information and resale certificate.
- **Addendum Concerning Right to Terminate Due to Lender's Appraisal, 49-1** — the low-appraisal exit.
- **Addendum for Sale of Other Property by Buyer, 10-6** — the home-sale contingency.
- **Non-Realty Items Addendum, 57-0, effective 09/03/2025** — items that are not part of the real property.
- **Addendum Containing Notice of Obligation to Pay Improvement District Assessment, 53-0** — PID disclosure.
- **Addendum for Reservation of Oil, Gas, and Other Minerals, 44-3** — mineral reservations.
- **Seller's Disclosure about Groundwater and Surface Water Rights, 61-0, effective 07/01/2026** — water rights.
- **Seller Financing Addendum, 26-8**, and **Loan Assumption Addendum, 41-3**.

Full current list and effective dates are published by [TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts).

An addendum that was negotiated but never attached and checked is a frequent and expensive oversight. The contract is the document, not the conversation.

## The seller's disclosure is a separate document, governed inside the contract

The **Seller's Disclosure Notice, TREC form 55-1, effective 05/28/2026**, is its own document, not a page of the purchase contract. It is a statutory notice required under Texas Property Code §5.008 for residential property of not more than one dwelling unit ([Texas Property Code §5.008](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-5-008/)).

What ¶7B does is govern what happens when it has not been delivered. If the buyer has not received it, the buyer may terminate at any time prior to closing; once the seller delivers it, the buyer has **7 days after receipt, or until closing, whichever comes first** ([TREC form 20-19, ¶7B(2)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). That is a termination right independent of the option period, and it can outlive it by weeks.

Two neighboring items in ¶7: **¶7C** notes that lead-based paint disclosure "is required by Federal law for a residential dwelling constructed **prior to 1978**." And **¶6E(2)** carries the §5.012 Property Code notice for property subject to mandatory POA membership, warning that "the amount of the assessments is subject to change" and that failure to pay "could result in enforcement of the association's lien on and the foreclosure of the Property."

## Changing the contract after it is signed

Once both parties sign, changes go on the **Amendment to Contract, form 39-11, effective 07/01/2026** ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)). Price changes, repair agreements, closing-date moves and option-period extensions all belong there, signed by both parties.

Emails and texts between agents do not amend a contract. Neither does a verbal agreement between the parties.

## Where the form ends and a lawyer begins

The contract answers this itself. **Paragraph 23 is titled CONSULT AN ATTORNEY BEFORE SIGNING**, and its text reads: "**TREC rules prohibit real estate brokers and sales agents from giving legal advice. READ THIS CONTRACT CAREFULLY.**" The form provides printed fields for the buyer's attorney and the seller's attorney, with phone numbers ([TREC form 20-19, ¶23](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

**Paragraph 6E(1)** names the specific job: "Broker advises Buyer to have an abstract of title covering the Property examined by an attorney of Buyer's selection, or Buyer should be furnished with or obtain a Title Policy. If a Title Policy is furnished, the **Commitment should be promptly reviewed by an attorney of Buyer's choice due to the time limitations on Buyer's right to object**."

Those time limitations are ¶6D: objections are due by the earlier of the closing date or a stated number of days after the buyer receives the commitment, exception documents and survey, and failure to object in time "will constitute a waiver."

TREC forms cover the ordinary case very well. They do not cover everything. A Texas real estate attorney is the right call for custom contract language, an entity or trust taking title, a probate or estate sale, a property with a title defect or a boundary problem, seller financing structured beyond what the addendum contemplates, a 1031 exchange structure, deed restriction interpretation, or a partition. TREC does not write custom contracts, and license holders may not draft them.

- [What is the option period in a Texas real estate contract?](/answers/what-is-the-option-period-in-texas)
- [What is the Third Party Financing Addendum?](/answers/what-is-the-third-party-financing-addendum)

question: What is the VA funding fee, and who is exempt?
metaTitle: What is the VA funding fee, and who is exempt?
metaDescription: The VA funding fee: what it pays for, who is exempt including service-connected disability compensation, and the three documents the VA accepts as proof.
shortAnswer: The VA funding fee is a one-time fee paid to the VA on most VA-guaranteed home loans, charged as a percentage of the loan amount. Veterans receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability are exempt, as are several other groups. Exemption is documented with VA Form 26-8937, a current award letter, or a Veteran Service Center Manager letter.
body:
## What the fee is and why it exists

The VA does not lend money. It **guarantees** a portion of a loan made by a private lender, and that guaranty is what lets the program operate without mortgage insurance and, for a veteran with full entitlement, without a VA-imposed loan limit. The VA guaranty does not exceed **25%** of the loan ([U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs](https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/loan-limits/)).

The funding fee is what keeps that guaranty funded. It is charged as a **percentage of the loan amount**, paid once, and it goes to the VA rather than to the lender. It is the reason the program can run without the ongoing monthly mortgage insurance that conventional and FHA borrowers carry.

The percentage is not one number. It varies by the type of loan, whether the borrower has used the VA benefit before, and how much is put down. Because those percentages are periodically revised, get the figure that applies to your file from your lender at application rather than from an article.

## Who is exempt

The exemptions published by the VA include ([U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs](https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/funding-fee-and-closing-costs/)):

- **Veterans receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability.**
- **Veterans who are eligible to receive that compensation but are receiving retirement pay or active-duty pay instead.**
- **Certain recipients of Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC).**
- **Purple Heart recipients who are still serving on active duty.**

The second one is the category that gets missed. A veteran who has been found eligible for compensation but elected retirement pay in its place can still be exempt, even though no compensation check arrives each month. Borrowers in that position frequently assume the exemption does not apply to them and pay a fee they did not owe. Raise it with the loan officer at application and let the VA's records settle it.

The exemption is a meaningful number on a real purchase. On any loan large enough to be interesting, a percentage of the loan amount is not a rounding error, and it is cash or financed principal that an exempt borrower simply does not carry.

## How exemption is documented

The VA accepts any of the following as evidence:

- **VA Form 26-8937, Verification of VA Benefits.**
- A **current VA award letter, dated within the last 12 months.**
- A letter from a **Veteran Service Center Manager.**

([U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs](https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/funding-fee-and-closing-costs/))

The date requirement on the award letter is the practical trap. An award letter from four years ago in a filing cabinet does not satisfy it. A current letter can usually be generated through the VA's benefit letters portal, but do it at the start of the file rather than the week of closing — the closing disclosure has to reflect the exemption, and correcting it late means redrawing documents and can push the closing date.

## What to do if the fee was charged and you were exempt

Exemption status is sometimes established or corrected after the loan closes. A veteran whose disability rating is granted with an effective date preceding the loan closing may be entitled to a refund of a funding fee already paid. That is a VA and lender question, handled through the loan servicer and the VA, and the effective date of the rating is the fact that drives it. Bring the rating decision and the closing documents to both.

## The Texas layer worth knowing about separately

The VA funding fee exemption is federal and applies to the loan. Texas separately exempts part or all of a disabled veteran's **property taxes**, and the two are unrelated — being exempt from one does not automatically do anything about the other.

Under **Texas Tax Code §11.22**, a disabled veteran gets a fixed dollar exemption off the appraised value of one property, tiered by VA disability rating: **$5,000** for a rating of at least 10 percent but less than 30, **$7,500** for at least 30 but less than 50, **$10,000** for at least 50 but less than 70, and **$12,000** at 70 percent or more ([Texas Tax Code §11.22(a)](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/tax-code/tax-sect-11-22/)). It applies to one property the veteran designates. The partial exemption application is **Form 50-135**, filed with the appraisal district — Kendall Appraisal District for a Boerne property.

Under **Texas Tax Code §11.131**, a veteran with a **100% disability rating** or a determination of **individual unemployability** — either one qualifies, not both — may receive a **total exemption of the total appraised value** of the residence homestead. The application is **Form 50-114**, due April 30, though it may be filed up to **five years after the delinquency date**. A surviving spouse qualifies if they have not remarried, the property was their homestead at the veteran's death, and it remains their homestead; if the spouse later moves, the exemption is **capped at the dollar value of the last year's exemption on the prior home**, not carried over in full ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/disabledvet-100-faq.php)).

For a property in Boerne or anywhere in Kendall County, that filing goes to the **Kendall Appraisal District** — not Bexar CAD. Boerne is in Kendall County, not the City of San Antonio.

## Who to ask

Funding fee percentages, exemption status on your file, entitlement and refund requests are **lender** and **VA** questions, and the lender pulls the VA's records as part of the file. Property tax exemption amounts, applications and deadlines go to the **Kendall Appraisal District** for a Kendall County property. Anything involving how title is held, surviving spouse status or estate matters is for a **Texas real estate attorney**.

## Related questions

- [Conventional vs. FHA vs. VA loan in Texas: which one?](/answers/conventional-vs-fha-vs-va-loan-in-texas)
- [What are the 2026 conforming and FHA loan limits in Kendall County, Texas?](/answers/what-are-the-2026-loan-limits-in-kendall-county)
- [What is the Texas disabled veteran property tax exemption?](/answers/texas-disabled-veteran-property-tax-exemption)

question: What is title insurance in Texas, and why is the price the same everywhere?
metaTitle: What is title insurance in Texas, and why is the price the same everywhere?
metaDescription: The Texas Department of Insurance sets the premium, so it is identical everywhere. What is left to shop, and the 6A(8) survey exception on coverage.
shortAnswer: Texas title insurance premium rates are promulgated by the Texas Department of Insurance, so the premium for a given policy amount is identical at every title company in Texas. Shopping title companies is about service, escrow fees and closing experience, not premium price. The current rate schedule took effect March 1, 2026.
body:
## The promulgated-rate fact, stated plainly

Texas does not let title insurers set their own premium rates. The **Texas Department of Insurance sets them** and publishes the schedule. The current one is titled "Texas Title Insurance Premium Rates, Rates Effective March 1, 2026" ([TDI](https://tdi.texas.gov/title/titlerates2026.html), [full schedule, PDF](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/titlerates2026.pdf)).

The consequence is the part almost no consumer knows: **for a given policy amount, the title insurance premium is the same number at every title company in the state.** The big national underwriter, the regional independent, the small office in the town square — same premium. Not similar. The same.

So the advice buyers arrive with from other states — "call three title companies and compare quotes" — does not do what they think it does in Texas. You can call three. The premium line will match.

Look up the actual number for your price point on the TDI schedule rather than trusting a figure quoted in an article, including this one. The schedule is a rate table by policy amount and it is the authoritative source.

## What is actually left to shop

Plenty. The premium is fixed; the rest of the experience is not.

- **Escrow and closing fees.** These are the title company's own charges for acting as escrow agent, and they are not the promulgated premium. Ask for a written fee sheet.
- **Ancillary charges** — courier, wire, recording service, document prep, e-recording, tax certificates. Small individually, not zero together.
- **Competence on a hard file.** A file with probate, an unreleased lien, an out-of-state seller, an entity in the chain, or a metes-and-bounds description that does not match the survey is not a routine file. The difference between a title company that clears a Schedule C item in three days and one that clears it in three weeks is the whole deal.
- **Communication.** Whether the escrow officer answers, and whether they tell you a problem exists before it is a crisis.
- **Where they close, and how.** Location, after-hours availability, remote or mail-away closing capability for out-of-state parties.

That is a real list of differences worth choosing between. It is just not a price list.

## What the policy actually covers

Two policies, two different beneficiaries.

**The owner's policy** protects the buyer's ownership interest against covered title defects that existed before the policy date — a forged deed in the chain, an undisclosed heir, a missed lien, a recording error, a spousal interest that was never released. It is a one-time premium and it lasts as long as the insured holds an interest.

**The lender's policy** protects the lender's lien position, in the amount of the loan. It protects the lender. It does not protect the buyer's equity.

A cash buyer who skips the owner's policy has no title coverage at all. A financed buyer who assumes the lender's policy covers them has misunderstood what they paid for.

Title insurance is also backward-looking, not forward-looking. It covers defects that already existed as of the policy date. It is not a home warranty, it does not cover condition, and it does not cover things you agreed to exclude.

## Coverage is shaped by the exceptions, not the premium

This is where the money actually moves.

The policy issues subject to the exceptions on **Schedule B of the title commitment**, and the contract itself enumerates them. **Paragraph 6A** of the One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale) lists what the policy is subject to ([TREC form 20-19, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)):

- restrictive covenants common to the platted subdivision
- the standard printed exception for standby fees, taxes and assessments
- liens created as part of the financing under Paragraph 3
- utility easements created by the dedication deed or plat
- reservations otherwise permitted or approved by the buyer in writing
- the standard printed exception as to marital rights
- the standard printed exception as to waters, tidelands, beaches, streams and related matters
- the minerals exception approved by the Texas Department of Insurance
- the survey exception

**The survey exception is 6A(8), and it is a checkbox with exactly two positions.** The standard printed exception as to "discrepancies, conflicts, shortages in area or boundary lines, encroachments or protrusions, or overlapping improvements" either "**will not be amended or deleted** from the title policy," or "**will be amended to read, 'shortages in area'**" at the expense of the buyer or the seller.

Amending it does not delete the exception. It narrows it to area shortages, which restores coverage for the encroachment and boundary problems that actually generate claims. Which box is checked, and who pays, is negotiated in the offer like everything else.

Getting the amendment requires a survey the title company and lender will accept. That is either a **new survey**, or the **existing survey plus a T-47 Residential Real Property Affidavit**, notarized, stating nothing has changed since it was made ([TDI](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/formT-47.pdf)). There is also a **T-47.1 Declaration in Lieu of Affidavit**, seller-signed but not notarized, effective **November 1, 2024** ([TDI](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/form-t-47-1.pdf)). The contract names both forms by name.

If the seller built a deck, a pool or a fence after the old survey, the affidavit route closes. A new survey has to be ordered, and it needs to be ordered early.

**Endorsements** add or modify coverage on specific issues. Ask the title company which endorsements apply to your transaction, what each one does, and what it costs — the TDI schedule is the reference for what is regulated, and the escrow officer can tell you what is being added to your file.

## Who pays for it in Texas

Negotiated in the contract. Not fixed by law — and you do not have to take that on faith, because the promulgated form says so on its face.

**Paragraph 6A** reads: "Seller shall furnish to Buyer at [ ] **Seller's** [ ] **Buyer's** expense an owner policy of title insurance (Title Policy) issued by [Title Company] in the amount of the Sales Price, dated at or after closing" ([TREC form 20-19, PDF](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). It is a checkbox. A cost allocation that were fixed by law would not need one.

The long-running custom across much of Texas is that the **seller pays for the owner's title policy** and the buyer pays for the lender's policy — and the contract's expense paragraph puts the **loan title policy with endorsements required by lender** squarely in the Buyer's Expenses list, alongside **one-half of the escrow fee**, with the other half in the Seller's Expenses. But the owner's policy line is a checkbox, custom varies by market, and in a competitive situation it is one of the first things that moves. What matters is what the executed contract says.

That makes the owner's policy a negotiating item rather than a fixed cost, which is a more useful way to think about it than treating it as a line on a standard closing-cost list.

## The contract tells you to have a lawyer read it

Not an outside opinion — the form's own text. **Paragraph 6E(1)** states that "Broker advises Buyer to have an abstract of title covering the Property examined by an attorney of Buyer's selection," and that if a Title Policy is furnished instead, the "**Commitment should be promptly reviewed by an attorney of Buyer's choice due to the time limitations on Buyer's right to object**."

And **Paragraph 23** is headed CONSULT AN ATTORNEY BEFORE SIGNING, with the printed line: "**TREC rules prohibit real estate brokers and sales agents from giving legal advice. READ THIS CONTRACT CAREFULLY.**" The form provides fields for the buyer's and seller's attorneys.

Nobody is required to hire one. The promulgated contract advises it in two separate places, and the reason given is the clock on the objection right.

## The closing itself

**No attorney is required** to close a residential transaction in Texas. The title company acts as escrow agent, runs the title search, issues the commitment and the policy, prepares closing documents, and disburses funds. Hiring an attorney is optional and sometimes well worth it — complex title, entity purchases, seller financing, estate issues.

And the distinction that trips up out-of-state buyers: **signing is not closing.** The deal closes when the title company **funds and records**. Documents are not recorded and funds are not disbursed until every required item is in. A buyer who signs at 10 a.m. does not necessarily own anything at 10:15.

## Related questions

- [What is a title commitment in Texas?](/answers/what-is-a-title-commitment-in-texas)
- [Who pays closing costs in Texas?](/answers/who-pays-closing-costs-in-texas)
- [What happens at a Texas closing?](/answers/what-happens-at-a-texas-closing)
- [What is a T-47 affidavit?](/answers/what-is-a-t-47-affidavit)
- [Do I need a real estate attorney to buy a house in Texas?](/answers/do-i-need-a-real-estate-attorney-to-buy-a-house-in-texas)

## Questions about a specific property?

Call or text **[830-446-3847](tel:+1-830-446-3847)** · Email **[heath.shepard@kw.com](mailto:heath.shepard@kw.com)**

question: What should I know about septic systems and water wells in the Texas Hill Country?
metaTitle: What should I know about septic systems and water wells in the Texas Hill Country?
metaDescription: OSSF and private well diligence inside the option period: who inspects an aerobic system, which permits to request, and Cow Creek District rules.
shortAnswer: A Hill Country property on a septic system and a private well carries due diligence a city-connected house does not. The buyer is responsible for inspecting the on-site sewage facility, testing and evaluating the well, and gathering permits and maintenance records, all inside the option period. TREC form 61-0 covers groundwater and surface water rights.
body:
## The difference a city tap makes

Inside Boerne's city limits, water and wastewater are a utility account. Boerne's drinking water comes from three sources — **surface water from Canyon Lake purchased through the Guadalupe-Blanco River Authority, Boerne City Lake, and local wells in the Trinity Group aquifers** ([City of Boerne](https://www.ci.boerne.tx.us/FAQ.aspx?QID=315)). Somebody else owns that infrastructure, tests that water and fixes it when it breaks.

On an acreage property outside the system, you own both ends. The water comes out of a well you own, and the wastewater goes into a treatment system you own and are responsible for maintaining. Two pieces of private infrastructure, each with its own failure modes, neither one covered by a standard home inspection.

That is not an argument against buying acreage. It is an argument for treating septic and well as their own diligence items with their own specialists, on their own timeline, starting the day the contract goes effective.

## The septic side: on-site sewage facilities

Texas calls a septic system an **on-site sewage facility, or OSSF**. Two broad families show up around Boerne:

- **Conventional systems** — a tank and a drainfield, relying on soil to treat effluent. Thin soil over limestone, which is much of the Hill Country, limits where these work.
- **Aerobic treatment units** — an engineered system with an air pump, a treatment tank, chlorination, and usually spray heads distributing treated effluent over the yard. These are common where soil will not support a conventional drainfield, they use electricity, they have mechanical parts, and they generally carry an ongoing maintenance obligation.

That last point is the one buyers miss. An aerobic system is not install-and-forget. It typically requires a maintenance provider under contract and periodic service. A seller who let the contract lapse leaves the buyer inheriting a system that has not been serviced and may not be operating to its permit.

**What to inspect and ask about:**

- Tank condition, and whether it has been pumped — when, and by whom
- For an aerobic unit: the air pump, chlorinator, control panel, alarm, spray heads and their coverage
- The drainfield or spray area — surfacing effluent, soggy ground, odor, unusually green strips
- Whether the system as built matches the system that was permitted
- Whether the system is sized for the house as it exists now, particularly if bedrooms or a guest quarters were added after the original permit
- Where the components are, physically, and whether anything has been built or parked over them

**Who inspects it:** a septic or OSSF inspector, not a general home inspector. A general inspection under the TREC **Property Inspection Report, form REI 7-6, effective 02/01/2022** is not a septic inspection ([TREC forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)). Hire the specialist separately.

**Documents to request from the seller:** the OSSF permit, the as-built or site plan showing component locations, the maintenance contract and service records for an aerobic unit, and pumping records. On-site sewage facilities in Texas are permitted through a local authorized agent — ask **Kendall County** which office holds permit records for the address, and request the file rather than relying on the seller's memory.

## The well side

A private well is a mechanical system plus a water quality question plus a supply question. Three separate things.

**Mechanical.** Pump, pressure tank, wiring, pitless adapter, well cap and casing, plumbing back to the house. A well that produces water today can still have a pump near the end of its life.

**Quality.** A general home inspection does not test water. Testing is its own item, done by a lab or a qualified provider, and what gets tested is a choice — bacteriological is the baseline, and other analyses are worth discussing based on the area and the age of the well. Ask your **lender** early whether the loan program requires a water test and what result it requires, because that answer sets a deadline.

**Supply.** How the well performs over time is not visible from a single tap opening. Ask what the well has done historically, and ask the owner directly about any period when it did not keep up.

**Documents to request:** the well report or driller's log, any registration with the groundwater district, pump installation and service records, water test results, and — critically — **any shared well agreement**. A well serving more than one property is a legal arrangement, not a plumbing arrangement, and what it says about cost sharing, maintenance, access and what happens when the pump fails is a document for a **Texas real estate attorney** to read before closing, not after.

## Groundwater is regulated, and the rules change

Groundwater in Kendall County is regulated by the **Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District**. The district monitors conditions using data from roughly 42 monitor wells, stream gauges on Cibolo Creek and the Guadalupe River, and more than 100 rain gauge sites, and it sets drought stages that carry pumping restrictions ([Cow Creek GCD](https://ccgcd.org/)).

Drought stage is not a fixed fact and this page will not state one. It moves. **Check the current stage and the current rules at [ccgcd.org](https://ccgcd.org/) before you rely on any number, including anything you read in an article.** What matters to a buyer is the structure: there is a district, it has authority over groundwater use, and its rules can restrict what a well owner may pump.

Cow Creek also appears as a taxing entity on Kendall County tax bills, alongside the county, the school districts, the cities and the special districts ([Kendall AD](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)).

Boerne is in **Kendall County**, not Bexar County. The Edwards Aquifer Authority rules people read about in San Antonio are a different regulator over a different aquifer, and the appraisal district is **Kendall Appraisal District**, not Bexar CAD.

## The disclosure forms that touch this

Two forms matter here ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)):

- **Seller's Disclosure about Groundwater and Surface Water Rights, form 61-0, effective 07/01/2026.** Water rights on a rural Texas property are not automatically what a buyer assumes, and the form exists to put the seller's statements about them in writing.
- **Seller's Disclosure Notice, form 55-1, effective 05/28/2026**, the general disclosure, which is where a seller reports known condition issues including water and sewer.

Neither is a substitute for an inspection. A disclosure records what the seller says they know. An inspection records what a specialist finds.

## Sequence it against the option period

The option period is an unrestricted right to terminate, and it expires at 5:00 p.m. on its final day whether or not the septic inspector had an opening. On a well-and-septic property the buyer is scheduling two specialists and a water lab, and requesting records from a county office and possibly a groundwater district, on a clock that does not extend itself.

Order of operations that works:

1. Contract effective. Option fee delivered to the title company on time.
2. Same day: book the general inspection, the septic inspection and the water test. Do not wait for the general inspector's report to decide whether to book the others.
3. Same day: request the OSSF permit file from the county and the well records from the seller.
4. Ask the lender what the loan program requires for water and septic.
5. Read the shared well agreement, if there is one, with an attorney.
6. Decide before the option period ends.

## Where the line is

A real estate agent can sequence the work, pull the records and tell you what is normal for the area. Interpreting a shared well agreement or a water rights reservation is work for a **Texas real estate attorney**. The condition of the system is a **licensed inspector's** call. Current groundwater rules come from the **Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District**. Permit history comes from **Kendall County**. Loan requirements come from your **lender**.

## Related questions

- [Does Boerne have enough water?](/answers/does-boerne-have-enough-water)
- [Should I buy in Boerne city limits or unincorporated Kendall County?](/answers/should-i-buy-in-boerne-city-limits-or-unincorporated-kendall-county)
- [Is Hill Country land a good investment?](/answers/is-hill-country-land-a-good-investment)
- [What is the option period in a Texas real estate contract?](/answers/what-is-the-option-period-in-texas)
- [What is the Seller's Disclosure Notice in Texas?](/answers/what-is-the-sellers-disclosure-notice-in-texas)

## Questions about a specific property?

Call or text **[830-446-3847](tel:+1-830-446-3847)** · Email **[heath.shepard@kw.com](mailto:heath.shepard@kw.com)**

---

*This page explains the due diligence a septic-and-well property requires. It is not legal advice, and it is not an inspection. Condition questions go to a licensed inspector, shared well agreements and water rights go to a Texas real estate attorney, and current groundwater rules come from the Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District.*

question: What surprises out-of-state buyers about buying a house in Texas?
metaTitle: What surprises out-of-state buyers about buying a house in Texas?
metaDescription: Eleven things: the unrestricted option period, the three-day option fee, state-set title premiums, the T-47, and the January 1 homestead rule.
shortAnswer: The biggest surprises are the option period, which lets a Texas buyer terminate for any reason; that no attorney is required and the title company runs closing; that title insurance premiums are set by the state, so they are identical everywhere; and that annual reappraisal replaces a state income tax.
body:
Texas does a lot of things differently from the states most relocating buyers come from. None of it is hidden — it is all printed on promulgated forms — but a buyer who assumes their home state's process carries over will miss a deadline. Here is the full list of the mechanics that catch people, in the order they come up in a deal.

## 1. The option period is an unrestricted right to terminate

In most states a buyer's exits are tied to contingencies, and each one has to be justified. In Texas, the buyer pays a separate **option fee** and gets an **unrestricted right to terminate** the contract during the option period — for any reason or no reason at all ([Texas Real Estate Research Center](https://trerc.tamu.edu/article/option-period-basics-2360/)).

The length of the period and the size of the fee are negotiated blanks on the contract. Neither is set by statute and neither is set by TREC. Termination requires **written notice delivered to the seller by 5:00 p.m. local time on the last day**. Days are calendar days and the effective date is day zero.

See: [What is the option period in a Texas real estate contract?](/answers/what-is-the-option-period-in-texas)

## 2. The option fee goes to the title company within three days, not to the seller

This is the single most common way a Texas buyer loses the protection they paid for. The option fee is delivered to the **escrow agent — the title company — within three days after the effective date**. If the third day is a weekend or legal holiday, it rolls to the next business day ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/article/changes-delivery-option-fee-0)).

Miss that delivery and there is no termination right, regardless of what the option period says.

The option fee and earnest money may be paid separately or combined in one payment. Combined, funds apply **first to the option fee and then to earnest money** — so a combined payment that is short leaves earnest money underfunded, which is a contract default. The option fee is **credited to the sales price at closing** and is not refunded on termination.

See: [How does the option fee work in Texas?](/answers/how-does-the-option-fee-work-in-texas)

## 3. No attorney is required, and the title company runs the closing

Buyers from attorney-state closings expect to hire counsel. In Texas, **no attorney is required** to close a residential transaction. The title company acts as escrow agent, runs the title search, issues the title commitment and the policy, prepares the closing documents and disburses funds. Hiring an attorney is optional, not standard.

One consequence worth internalizing: **signing is not closing**. The deal closes when the title company funds and records. Documents are not recorded and money does not move until every required item is in.

TREC promulgates the contract forms and license holders are required to use them. A license holder **cannot draft contract language**. Anything requiring custom terms is a job for a Texas real estate attorney ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

See: [Do I need a real estate attorney to buy a house in Texas?](/answers/do-i-need-a-real-estate-attorney-to-buy-a-house-in-texas)

## 4. Title insurance costs the same at every title company in Texas

Texas title insurance premium rates are **promulgated — set — by the Texas Department of Insurance**, not by the title companies. The current schedule is the Texas Title Insurance Premium Rates, effective March 1, 2026 ([TDI](https://tdi.texas.gov/title/titlerates2026.html)).

Because the rates are promulgated, **the premium for a given policy amount is identical at every title company in the state**. Shopping title companies on premium price is not a thing in Texas. Shop them on service, on closer availability and on how well they handle a complicated file.

Who pays for what is negotiated in the contract, not fixed by law. In much of Texas the custom is that the seller pays the owner's title policy; in some markets the buyer does. Treat it as customary and negotiable, never as automatic.

See: [What is title insurance in Texas?](/answers/what-is-title-insurance-in-texas)

## 5. You may not need a new survey — the T-47 exists

If the lender and title company will accept the seller's existing survey, the buyer does not have to buy a new one, and the title policy's survey exception can be amended.

The document that makes this work is the **T-47 Residential Real Property Affidavit**, a **notarized** seller affidavit stating that nothing has changed on the property since that survey ([TDI](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/formT-47.pdf)). Since **November 1, 2024** there is also a **T-47.1 Residential Real Property Declaration in Lieu of Affidavit**, which the seller signs but does not have notarized ([TDI](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/form-t-47-1.pdf)).

The failure mode: a seller who added a deck, a pool, a shed or a fence since the survey cannot truthfully sign it, and the buyer is buying a new survey. Ask early, not the week of closing.

See: [What is a T-47 affidavit?](/answers/what-is-a-t-47-affidavit)

## 6. The seller's disclosure notice is statutory, and a late one buys you seven days

Texas Property Code **§5.008** requires a seller of residential property of not more than one dwelling unit to give the buyer a written notice in the prescribed form or substantially similar ([Texas Property Code §5.008](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/property-code/prop-sect-5-008/)).

The provision out-of-state buyers do not expect: if the contract is signed without the seller having delivered the notice, the **buyer may terminate for any reason within 7 days after receiving it**. That is a separate exit from the option period and it runs on its own clock.

Exemptions from the form include foreclosure, court-ordered transfers, transfers by a trustee in bankruptcy, transfers between co-owners, transfers to a spouse or descendant, transfers by a fiduciary administering an estate, and new residences not previously occupied. Exempt from the form is not exempt from fraud.

§5.008 also states that a seller or agent is **not required to disclose** a death on the property by natural causes, suicide, or an accident unrelated to the property's condition. Buyers from disclosure-heavy states are frequently surprised by that one.

The current TREC version of the form is **55-1, effective 05/28/2026**.

See: [What is the seller's disclosure notice in Texas?](/answers/what-is-the-sellers-disclosure-notice-in-texas)

## 7. Property taxes replace the income tax, and the value is reset every year

Texas has no state individual income tax. Local government is funded largely through property tax, and Texas property is **reappraised at market value annually**. Once a homestead exemption is in place there is a **10% per-year cap** on the increase in net appraised value ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)).

Buyers from states with assessment limits built into purchase price expect the tax to stay put. It does not. It tracks the market, and in a growing county it moves.

A tax bill is also not one rate. It is the sum of every entity whose boundary covers the parcel. In Kendall County, those can include Boerne ISD, Comfort ISD, the City of Boerne, Kendall County, Kendall County MUD, Miralomas MUD, the Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District, and Kendall County WCID #1 ([Kendall AD](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)).

See: [Does Texas really have no state income tax, and what do I pay instead?](/answers/does-texas-have-no-state-income-tax)

## 8. The homestead exemption turns on January 1, so a spring closing waits a year

To claim a residence homestead exemption for a tax year you must have **owned and occupied the home as your principal residence on January 1** of that year, and the application deadline is **before May 1** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)).

Close in February and the exemption starts the following year. The first year is the unexempted bill, and the 10% cap does not protect a property that does not yet carry the exemption.

The exemption is not automatic, does not transfer from the seller, and is not filed by the title company. In Boerne it is filed with **Kendall Appraisal District** — not Bexar CAD, because Boerne is in Kendall County, not Bexar County.

School districts must grant a **$140,000** residence homestead exemption as of tax year 2026, with an **additional $60,000** for owners 65 or older or disabled.

See: [How do I file for a homestead exemption in Kendall County?](/answers/how-do-i-file-for-a-homestead-exemption-in-kendall-county)

## 9. MUD and PID line items on a new-subdivision tax bill

A house in a newer Texas subdivision can carry a municipal utility district or a public improvement district assessment that is not part of the city or county rate and does not appear in a generic "what are taxes here" answer.

TREC publishes forms specifically for this: the **Addendum Containing Notice of Obligation to Pay Improvement District Assessment (form 53-0, effective 09/01/2021)** and the **Notice to Purchaser of Special Taxing or Assessment District (form 59-0, effective 02/12/2024)** ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

Read the actual tax bill for the actual parcel. Not the neighbor's, not the subdivision brochure's.

See: [What is a MUD or PID in a Texas subdivision?](/answers/what-is-a-mud-or-pid-in-a-texas-subdivision)

## 10. Outside city limits, water and sewer are your problem

In the Hill Country, plenty of property sits outside a city's limits on a private well and a septic system. Both are systems you own, maintain and eventually replace.

Groundwater in Kendall County is regulated by the **[Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District](https://ccgcd.org/)**, which sets drought stages that can restrict permitted well pumping. Drought stage changes, so check the district's current stage rather than relying on any article.

TREC also has a **Seller's Disclosure about Groundwater and Surface Water Rights, form 61-0, effective 07/01/2026** ([TREC](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)) — water rights on a rural Texas property are not assumed to convey the way a city buyer expects.

See: [What should I know about septic and wells in the Hill Country?](/answers/what-should-i-know-about-septic-and-wells-in-the-hill-country)

## 11. Texas is a community property state

Texas Family Code §3.002 defines it in one sentence: "Community property consists of the property, other than separate property, acquired by either spouse during marriage" ([Texas Family Code §3.002](https://codes.findlaw.com/tx/family-code/fam-sect-3-002/)). How a married couple takes title, and what happens to property acquired during marriage, works differently here than in a common-law property state. That is a legal question with real consequences for estate planning and for a spouse who is not on the loan.

A Texas real estate attorney is the right person to answer it for your situation. A license holder cannot.

## The short version for a relocating buyer

Three deadlines decide most Texas deals: the **three-day option fee delivery**, the **5:00 p.m. end of the option period**, and the **January 1 homestead date**. None of them are flexible and none of them care that you are new here.

## Related questions

- [What is the option period in a Texas real estate contract?](/answers/what-is-the-option-period-in-texas)
- [Do I need a real estate attorney to buy a house in Texas?](/answers/do-i-need-a-real-estate-attorney-to-buy-a-house-in-texas)
