question: Who pays closing costs in Texas?
metaTitle: Who pays closing costs in Texas?
metaDescription: It is a negotiated contract term, not Texas law. The paragraph 12A line items for each side, and where to get real numbers for your deal.
shortAnswer: Who pays closing costs in Texas is negotiated in the contract, not fixed by law. Custom in much of Texas is that the seller pays the owner's title policy and the buyer pays lender and loan-related costs, but every line is negotiable. Your lender's Loan Estimate and the title company's fee sheet give the actual numbers.
body:
## Start here: nothing in this is law

There is no Texas statute that says the seller pays for X and the buyer pays for Y at a residential closing. What exists is a promulgated contract with a paragraph that lists each side's expenses, plus checkboxes and blanks where the parties decide the rest.

The cleanest proof is the very first line of **Paragraph 6A**: "Seller shall furnish to Buyer at [ ] **Seller's** [ ] **Buyer's** expense an owner policy of title insurance (Title Policy)" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6A](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). The single largest title-side cost in the transaction is a checkbox. If it were law, there would be no box to check.

Custom is real and it matters — an offer that ignores local custom reads as unserious — but custom is not binding. Anything on the settlement statement can be shifted if both parties agree, and the agreement goes in the contract or on the Amendment to Contract, form 39-11 ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

## What the contract actually assigns: Paragraph 12

**Paragraph 12A(1), Seller's Expenses**, lists: releases of existing liens, including prepayment penalties and recording fees; release of Seller's loan liability; **tax statements or certificates**; **preparation of deed**; **one-half of escrow fee**; and other expenses payable by Seller under the contract ([TREC form 20-19, ¶12A(1)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

It is a short list, and that surprises sellers who assume closing costs are mostly theirs. The seller's real money is elsewhere — the mortgage payoff and the brokerage compensation, neither of which is a ¶12A(1) expense.

¶12A(1) also contains an optional capped dollar contribution from the seller "to be applied to Buyer's Expenses other than brokerage compensation or contributions under Paragraph 12B." That is the seller-paid closing cost concession, and it lives right there in the same subparagraph.

**Paragraph 12A(2), Buyer's Expenses**, is the long one: "Appraisal fees; loan application fees; origination charges; credit reports; preparation of loan documents; interest on the notes from date of disbursement to one month prior to dates of first monthly payments; recording fees; copies of easements and restrictions; **loan title policy with endorsements required by lender**; loan-related inspection fees; photos; amortization schedules; **one-half of escrow fee**; all prepaid items, including required premiums for **flood and hazard insurance**, reserve deposits for insurance, ad valorem taxes and special governmental assessments; final compliance inspection; courier fee; repair inspection; underwriting fee; wire transfer fee; expenses incident to any loan; **Private Mortgage Insurance Premium (PMI), VA Loan Funding Fee, or FHA Mortgage Insurance Premium (MIP)** as required by the lender; and other expenses payable by Buyer under this contract."

Three things worth pulling out of that list.

**The escrow fee is split by default.** One-half appears on each side. It is one of the few genuinely shared line items.

**"Flood and hazard insurance" is named explicitly.** In the Hill Country that is not boilerplate. A property near Cibolo Creek or in a mapped flood zone can carry a flood premium that materially changes the cash to close, and it is prepaid at closing.

**PMI, the VA funding fee and FHA MIP are buyer expenses "as required by the lender."** The contract does not decide whether you owe one — the loan program does. Veterans receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability are among those exempt from the VA funding fee ([VA](https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/funding-fee-and-closing-costs/)), which is worth confirming with the lender before it lands on a settlement statement.

**Paragraph 12C** adds a protection: if a governmental loan program prohibits the buyer from paying certain charges, the seller's ¶12A(1) concession is applied first to those prohibited expenses, then to other buyer expenses — but never to brokerage compensation.

## Title and escrow, and why shopping on premium is pointless

Texas title insurance premium rates are **promulgated by the Texas Department of Insurance**, not set by the title company. The premium for a given policy amount is the same at every title company in Texas. Shop title companies on service, escrow fee and responsiveness; there is nothing to shop on premium. The current schedule is "Texas Title Insurance Premium Rates, Rates Effective March 1, 2026" ([TDI](https://tdi.texas.gov/title/titlerates2026.html), [rate table PDF](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/titlerates2026.pdf)).

The owner's policy is the ¶6A checkbox. The **loan title policy with lender endorsements** is a ¶12A(2) buyer expense. Amending the survey exception is its own election under ¶6A(8), at Buyer's or Seller's expense.

## Prorations — Paragraph 13

Quoted in full, because it is short and it governs a line people argue about:

> "**Taxes for the current year, interest, rents, and regular periodic maintenance fees, assessments, and dues (including prepaid items) will be prorated through the Closing Date. The tax proration may be calculated taking into consideration any change in exemptions that will affect the current year's taxes. If taxes for the current year vary from the amount prorated at closing, the parties shall adjust the prorations when tax statements for the current year are available. If taxes are not paid at or prior to closing, Buyer shall pay taxes for the current year.**"

([TREC form 20-19, ¶13](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf))

Two sentences in there matter more than the rest. The proration **may** account for a change in exemptions — relevant when a seller had a homestead or over-65 exemption the buyer will not have, or vice versa. And the parties **shall adjust** when the actual tax statements arrive, which means the number on your settlement statement is an estimate that can be trued up later.

## Brokerage compensation — Paragraph 12B

The contract states it directly: "**Brokerage compensation is not set by law and is fully negotiable.** Each party shall pay their respective brokers pursuant to the terms of the parties' obligations to compensate their brokers contained in **separate written agreements**" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶12B](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

Compensation lives in separate written agreements, not in the purchase contract. Paragraph 12B does include optional checkboxes letting the seller pay a dollar amount or percentage toward what the buyer owes the buyer's broker, and vice versa — but those contributions "shall be applied to and **shall not change** the parties' obligations to pay compensation pursuant to those agreements."

That last clause is the one to understand. A seller contribution toward the buyer's broker is a payment mechanism, not a transfer of the obligation. The buyer still owes their broker whatever their representation agreement says; the contribution just covers part of it at closing.

## Why this page does not give you a percentage

Every "closing costs are X percent of the sales price" number you will find online is a marketing estimate, and the components move independently of the price. A cash buyer has no lender costs at all. A VA buyer may have no funding fee — veterans receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability are among those exempt ([VA](https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/funding-fee-and-closing-costs/)). Two identical houses in Boerne can produce very different settlement statements depending on the loan, the insurance premium, the tax proration date and whether a new survey was ordered.

There are two documents that give you real numbers, and both are free:

**The Loan Estimate from your lender.** A standardized federal disclosure that itemizes the loan costs and the other costs, including the estimated cash to close. Request one from every lender you are considering and compare them side by side. If you want an early read before you have a property under contract, ask a lender for a cost worksheet on a target price.

**The title company's fee sheet.** The title company handling the transaction will produce an estimated settlement statement on request, using the actual sales price, the actual tax rates for the property, and the actual policy amount. That is the closest thing to a real number that exists before closing.

Ask for both. Do not budget off a blog percentage.

## The seller contribution, and its limit

A buyer can ask the seller to pay some of the buyer's closing costs. In the contract it is the capped dollar amount in **¶12A(1)**, applied to buyer's expenses other than brokerage compensation or ¶12B contributions, and it shows on the settlement statement as a seller credit. It is one of the most useful tools available to a buyer who is cash-tight but income-qualified, because the buyer effectively finances the closing costs into the price.

The ceiling is not set by the contract. **The lender caps how much seller contribution the loan program allows**, and the cap varies by loan type, occupancy and down payment. Exceeding it means the excess is simply disallowed at underwriting. Your lender is the only person who can tell you the number for your specific loan — ask before you write the offer, not after.

Paragraph 12C routes that concession intelligently if a governmental loan program bars the buyer from paying certain charges: the contribution is applied first to the prohibited expenses, then to the buyer's other expenses.

## Boerne and Kendall County specifics

Boerne is the county seat of **Kendall County**. It is not in Bexar County and not in the City of San Antonio, so the tax entities appearing on the proration line are Kendall County entities — Boerne ISD, the City of Boerne for property inside city limits, Kendall County, and potentially a MUD or a groundwater conservation district depending on the property ([Kendall Appraisal District](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)).

The tax proration on the settlement statement uses those rates, prorated through the closing date under ¶13. A buyer who compared a Boerne closing to a San Antonio closing and expected the same numbers is comparing different taxing jurisdictions.

The ¶13 exemption language matters here too. If the seller was carrying a homestead or an over-65 exemption that the buyer will not qualify for in the same year, the proration may be calculated taking that change into account — and the parties adjust when the actual statements arrive. Exemption questions for a specific Kendall County property go to Kendall Appraisal District, not to the title company.

## What actually determines your number

Loan type. Whether there is a loan at all. The sales price, which drives the title premium. The closing date, which drives the tax proration and prepaid interest. Whether a new survey was ordered. Whether the property has an HOA and what it charges to transfer. Whether the seller agreed to a contribution or a home warranty. Whether repairs were credited.

Change any one of those and the bottom line moves.

question: Who pays for the survey in a Texas real estate transaction?
metaTitle: Who pays for the survey in a Texas real estate transaction?
metaDescription: Who pays for the survey in Texas: it is a negotiated contract term, not law. How the TREC survey paragraph works, the T-47 route, and what happens on acreage.
shortAnswer: Who pays for the survey is negotiated in the contract, not set by Texas law. The TREC contract has a paragraph where the parties choose. Custom in much of Texas is that the seller furnishes an existing survey with a T-47 affidavit, and the buyer pays for a new one if the existing survey is not acceptable.
body:
## It is a contract term, not a rule

No Texas statute assigns the survey cost to either party. Anyone who tells you "the seller always pays for the survey in Texas" is describing a local habit, not the law.

It lives in **Paragraph 6C** of the One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), TREC form 20-19. The paragraph opens by requiring that "the survey must be made by a **registered professional land surveyor** acceptable to the Title Company and Buyer's lender(s)," and then gives three options under the printed instruction "**Check one box only**" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6C](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

One box. Not two, not zero. A contract that arrives with ¶6C blank, or with two boxes marked, has a defect in it — and it is the kind that surfaces three weeks later when the title company asks whose survey it is waiting on. This is negotiable in the offer, negotiable in a counter, and changeable afterward on the Amendment to Contract, form 39-11 ([TREC contract forms](https://www.trec.texas.gov/agency-information/contracts)).

## The three boxes, and what each one commits you to

### Box (1): seller furnishes the existing survey plus a T-47

The common one. The seller delivers, within a stated number of days, the survey they already have along with a **T-47 Affidavit or T-47.1 Declaration** — the contract names both forms by name ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6C(1)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)). The T-47 is notarized; the T-47.1 is signed but not notarized. Both are effective November 1, 2024 ([TDI T-47](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/formT-47.pdf), [TDI T-47.1](https://www.tdi.texas.gov/title/documents/form-t-47-1.pdf)).

Box (1) then splits into two separate failure branches, and they are not paid for the same way. This is the part nobody reads until it matters.

**Branch A — the seller fails to furnish them.** If the seller does not deliver **both** the existing survey and the affidavit or declaration within the time required, "Buyer shall obtain a new survey **at Seller's expense** no later than 3 days prior to Closing Date."

Note the word *both*. A seller who sends the survey but never signs the T-47 has failed the paragraph and is buying a new survey. There is no checkbox on this branch and nothing left to negotiate — the contract already allocated it.

**Branch B — the title company or lender will not accept what was furnished.** Different outcome entirely: "If the Title Company or Buyer's lender **does not accept** the existing survey, or the affidavit or declaration, Buyer shall obtain a new survey at [ ] **Seller's** [ ] **Buyer's** expense no later than 3 days prior to Closing Date."

That is a second checkbox, nested inside box (1), and it decides who pays when the seller did everything right but the survey was simply too old or too incomplete for the title company. It is easy to leave blank because it looks like fine print. It is the most commonly overlooked election in the paragraph, and on a rural tract it is worth real money.

So: seller's fault, seller pays. Nobody's fault, whichever box you checked.

### Box (2): buyer obtains a new survey at buyer's expense

The buyer orders and pays for a new survey within a stated number of days. Chosen when the seller has no survey, when the existing one is hopeless, or when the buyer wants current boundaries regardless.

It carries a trap the contract states outright: "If Buyer fails to obtain the survey, Buyer **may not terminate** the contract under **Paragraph 2B of the Third Party Financing Addendum** because the survey was not obtained" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6C(2)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

Read that twice. A buyer who checks box (2), forgets to order the survey, and then has the lender decline the loan for lack of one has forfeited the financing termination right — because the reason the loan died is the buyer's own failure. That buyer is now in a contract with no financing exit and earnest money exposed under ¶15. Electing box (2) means owning a deadline, and it belongs on a calendar the day the contract is executed.

### Box (3): seller furnishes a new survey at seller's expense

The seller orders and pays for a new survey within a stated number of days. Less common, but a seller on a rural tract may do this before listing precisely so the question never delays a contract.

## The other survey checkbox: ¶6A(8)

The one most buyers never notice, and it decides whether the title policy actually covers boundary problems.

Paragraph 6A(8) governs the standard printed exception "as to discrepancies, conflicts, shortages in area or boundary lines, encroachments or protrusions, or overlapping improvements." The election: "(i) **will not be amended or deleted** from the title policy; or (ii) **will be amended to read, 'shortages in area'** at the expense of [ ] Buyer [ ] Seller" ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6A(8)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

Option (i) means the policy excludes every one of those matters. A fence three feet over the line, a neighbor's driveway crossing a corner, a shed built past the setback — none of it is covered.

Option (ii) narrows the exception down to "shortages in area" alone, so encroachments, conflicts, protrusions and overlapping improvements become covered instead of excluded. That is what an acceptable survey plus the T-47 makes possible, and it is the entire point of the exercise.

A buyer who "saved money" by leaving ¶6A(8) on option (i) did not save anything. They absorbed the risk and bought a policy that excludes the thing a survey exists to find.

Texas title insurance premiums are promulgated by the Texas Department of Insurance, so the rate for a given policy amount is the same at every title company in the state; the current schedule is "Texas Title Insurance Premium Rates, Rates Effective March 1, 2026" ([TDI](https://tdi.texas.gov/title/titlerates2026.html)). Ask the title company handling your file what amending the survey exception costs.

## Whatever the survey shows, the objection clock is already running

Under ¶6D the buyer must object in writing to defects, exceptions or encumbrances disclosed on the survey by the earlier of the closing date or a stated number of days after receiving the commitment, exception documents and the survey. "Failure to object within the time allowed **will constitute a waiver** of Buyer's right to object," except that the requirements in Schedule C of the commitment are not waived ([TREC form 20-19, ¶6D](https://www.trec.texas.gov/sites/default/files/pdf-forms/20-19_4.pdf)).

If the buyer does object in time and the seller does not cure within the **15-day cure period**, the buyer has **5 days after the end of that period** to terminate with the earnest money refunded, or waive. Silence is a waiver.

A survey that finally arrives two days before closing, on a contract where the objection deadline has already run, is a survey the buyer can look at and not much else. That is the real argument for choosing a survey option with a short deadline rather than one that lets the document land at the end.

## What a new survey costs

Survey pricing is set by the individual surveyor and varies with acreage, terrain, how well the existing corners are marked, and how much record research the tract requires. A quarter-acre lot in a platted subdivision and a twenty-acre tract with a creek and an old fence line are not comparable jobs. Get a quote from a licensed Texas surveyor for the specific property.

## Where this matters most: acreage and the Hill Country

On a subdivision lot inside a city, the survey question is usually routine. On acreage in Kendall County and the rest of the Hill Country, it is where deals actually get complicated.

The recurring issues:

- **Fence lines that never matched deed lines.** A fence built for convenience decades ago, now treated by everyone as the boundary.
- **Shared drives and access easements.** Whether the easement is recorded, and whether it covers what people assume it covers.
- **Well and septic locations.** Setbacks from property lines and from each other matter, and the survey is where you see them.
- **Informal splits.** A parent tract divided among family without a new plat, leaving a legal description that does not match what is on the ground.
- **Old surveys.** A twenty-year-old survey on a rural tract is more likely to be genuinely out of date than a twenty-year-old survey on a city lot.

Boerne is in **Kendall County**, not Bexar County and not the City of San Antonio, so platting and subdivision requirements are Kendall County's and the City of Boerne's, not San Antonio's. Property inside Boerne's extraterritorial jurisdiction can be subject to city subdivision rules even though it is outside the city limits. The City of Boerne Planning Department is the right place to confirm what applies to a specific tract.

## The practical negotiation

The survey question is a legitimate lever in an offer, and buyers routinely leave it unused.

A buyer with a strong offer can check box (3) and ask the seller to furnish a new survey. A buyer competing against other offers can take the survey cost off the seller's plate as a concession that costs less than a price reduction. A seller with a clean recent survey and a signed T-47 ready to go has removed a source of friction from every offer they will receive, which is worth something on a rural listing.

Three elections decide the whole question and all three are easy to skip: which ¶6C box, the Seller/Buyer expense box inside ¶6C(1) Branch B, and the ¶6A(8) survey-exception amendment. None of it is automatic. It is whatever gets written into the contract.

question: Why are homes in Boerne, Texas so expensive?
metaTitle: Why are homes in Boerne, Texas so expensive?
metaDescription: A $554,983 median as of September 2026, 20.3 percent Kendall County growth, A-rated schools, groundwater limits on supply, and I-10 to San Antonio.
shortAnswer: Boerne prices are driven by structural scarcity, not hype. Kendall County grew 20.3 percent from 2020 to 2025 on domestic migration, Boerne ISD has six straight A ratings, Hill Country terrain and groundwater regulation limit how densely land can be developed, and I-10 puts San Antonio jobs 31 miles away.
body:
## About the price number itself

Public median and average price figures for Boerne vary widely by source, by ZIP code and by month. Zillow's reported average home value for Boerne was roughly **$554,983 as of September 2026** ([Zillow, Boerne home values](https://www.zillow.com/home-values/8154/boerne-tx/)). That is a third-party estimate produced by a model, not a closed-sale statistic, and it moves. Anyone quoting you a single Boerne median as settled fact is quoting a snapshot. Ask a local agent to pull current MLS sold data for the specific ZIP, price band and property type you are actually shopping.

What does not move month to month is the set of reasons the number is high. Those are below.

## Cause 1: demand is real and it is measurable

**Kendall County grew 20.3 percent between 2020 and 2025**, from an estimated 44,568 to 53,289 residents, and most of that growth came from **domestic migration** — households moving in from elsewhere in the country ([Community Impact](https://communityimpact.com/san-antonio/boerne-fair-oaks-ranch/government/2026/03/30/kendall-county-population-increases-by-203-from-2020-2025/)).

Domestic in-migration is the specific kind of demand that lifts prices fastest, because in-migrating buyers arrive with equity from a prior sale and are pricing against what they left, not against local wage data. The **City of Boerne's 2020 census count was 18,084**; current city-level figures are estimates ([World Population Review](https://worldpopulationreview.com/us-cities/texas/boerne)).

## Cause 2: the school district is a price input

**Boerne ISD has earned an "A" rating from the Texas Education Agency for six consecutive years**, including the 2024 and 2025 rating years, scoring **92 points** in 2024–2025 with **20 distinction designations** ([Boerne Star](https://www.boernestar.com/article/11432,boerne-isd-six-straight-years-of-a-ratings); [TEA](https://tea.texas.gov/texas-schools/accountability/academic-accountability/performance-reporting/2025-accountability-rating-system)).

A rating record that long is not a marketing line; it is the thing relocating families sort on before they look at a single listing. It concentrates demand inside district boundaries and pulls price with it. Note that the district rating is not the campus rating — the Boerne Star reported lower grades for Viola Wilson, Currington, Herff and Kendall elementaries in the same cycle.

## Cause 3: supply is constrained by terrain and by water

This is the part that outsiders miss. Hill Country land does not subdivide like flat coastal prairie. Slope, rock, floodplain along the creeks, and the cost of running utilities up and across grade all cut the number of finished lots you get out of a given tract.

Water compounds it. Boerne's drinking water comes from three sources — **Canyon Lake surface water purchased through the Guadalupe-Blanco River Authority, Boerne City Lake, and local wells in the Trinity Group aquifers** ([City of Boerne](https://www.ci.boerne.tx.us/FAQ.aspx?QID=315)). Groundwater across Kendall County is regulated by the **Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District**, which sets drought stages and pumping rules using roughly 42 monitor wells, stream gauges on Cibolo Creek and the Guadalupe River, and more than 100 rain gauge sites ([Cow Creek GCD](https://ccgcd.org/)).

A development that cannot document water cannot get built at the density its pro forma assumed. Constrained new supply plus measurable in-migration is the whole price story in one sentence.

## Cause 4: I-10 makes it commutable

Boerne sits roughly **31 miles northwest of San Antonio on Interstate 10**, a 30-to-45-minute drive to downtown depending on traffic ([City-Data](https://www.city-data.com/city/Boerne-Texas.html)). That is close enough to hold a San Antonio job and far enough to be a genuinely different place. Towns with that combination — real separation, real access — price at a premium over towns with only one of the two.

## What the price does not include: the tax bill

The 2025 adopted rates for a home inside the city limits in Boerne ISD, per $100 of taxable value:

- **Boerne ISD: 1.0109** — 0.6969 M&O plus 0.3140 debt ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/295/Boerne-ISD))
- **City of Boerne: 0.4716** ([Kendall County](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/297/Boerne-City-of))
- **Kendall County: 0.377** — 0.317976 M&O plus 0.059024 debt ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/306/Kendall-County))

Any special district on the parcel — a MUD, the WCID, the groundwater district — adds its own line; pull the entity list for your specific parcel from [Kendall Appraisal District](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/). Texas reappraises at market value annually, so a rising Boerne market raises your bill, not just your equity — the 10 percent homestead cap limits the annual increase in net appraised value only after a homestead exemption is in place.

The failure mode: a buyer qualifies on a payment built from the seller's current tax bill, which may reflect an exemption the buyer does not yet have, or a valuation set before the last run-up. Ask a **lender** to underwrite the payment using a full, unexempted valuation, and ask **Kendall Appraisal District** what will apply to you.

## Is it overpriced, or just priced?

Those are different questions. Overpriced means the number is unsupported by fundamentals. Boerne's number is supported by fundamentals — in-migration, schools, constrained buildable supply, highway access — that would each take years to reverse. That does not make any individual listing correctly priced. Individual houses are mispriced in both directions every week, and that is what comparable sales analysis is for.

## Related questions

question: Why did my Texas property taxes go up?
metaTitle: Why did my Texas property taxes go up?
metaDescription: Four causes: a higher appraisal, one entity's rate change in a 1.8595 combined stack, a missing exemption, or the homestead cap resetting after a sale.
shortAnswer: Your tax bill is appraised value times the combined rate of every taxing unit that covers your property, minus exemptions. It rises when the appraisal rises, when any single entity raises its rate, when an exemption is lost or was never filed, or when the 10 percent homestead cap resets to market value after a sale.
body:
## The formula, and why it matters that there are two sides

A Texas property tax bill is:

**(appraised value − exemptions) ÷ 100 × tax rate**, calculated separately for every taxing unit that covers the parcel, then added up.

Two different sets of people control the two halves. The **appraisal district** sets value and administers exemptions. **Each taxing unit's own elected board** sets its rate — the school board, the city council, the commissioners court, the MUD board. Neither one sees the whole bill before it goes out.

That is why a bill can rise in a year when everyone involved says they did not raise taxes. The district raised the value. The entities kept their rates flat. The bill went up anyway.

## Your bill is not one tax — it is a stack

Here is what that stack actually looks like for a home inside Boerne city limits, using adopted rates per $100 of taxable value:

| Taxing unit | 2025 rate | Prior years |
|---|---|---|
| Boerne ISD | **1.0109** (M&O 0.6969 + debt 0.3140) | 0.9909 (2024), 0.9932 (2023), 1.1786 (2022), 1.2046 (2021) |
| City of Boerne | **0.4716** | 0.4716 (2024), 0.4766 (2023), 0.4510 (2022) |
| Kendall County | **0.377** (M&O 0.317976 + debt 0.059024) | 0.3827 (2024), 0.38270 (2023), 0.38770 (2022), 0.412700 (2021) |

Sources: [Boerne ISD rates](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/295/Boerne-ISD), [City of Boerne rates](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/297/Boerne-City-of), [Kendall County rates](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/306/Kendall-County).

That is **1.8595 per $100** for 2025 across those three entities, before any MUD, water district or groundwater district that may also appear on a given parcel's bill. Kendall Appraisal District lists **Kendall County MUD, Miralomas MUD, Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District and Kendall County WCID #1** among the entities that show up on bills in the county ([Kendall AD](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/)).

Two things to read out of that table. First, the school district is more than half the bill, which is why the state's school exemption changes move more money than anything a city does. Second, **rates have generally been flat or falling** here in recent years. Kendall County adopted **0.373 for 2026**, down from 0.377 ([Kendall County](https://www.co.kendall.tx.us/306/Kendall-County)), and the 2025 rate of 0.377 was itself adopted against a posted no-new-revenue rate of 0.373981 and was a decrease from 2024, approved at the August 26, 2025 Commissioners Court meeting ([Community Impact](https://communityimpact.com/san-antonio/boerne-fair-oaks-ranch/government/2025/08/27/kendall-county-commissioners-approve-tax-rate-decrease/)).

Falling rates and rising bills are not a contradiction. They are what happens when value climbs faster than rates fall.

Property in **unincorporated Kendall County** does not pay the City of Boerne line at all, and property in the **Comfort ISD** boundary pays that district instead of Boerne ISD — **0.9328 for 2025** ([Kendall County](https://www.kendallcountytx.gov/300/Kendall-County)). Which lines are on your bill is a function of where the parcel sits, not what your mailing address says.

## Reason 1: the appraisal went up

The most common cause. Texas property is reappraised at market value, and Kendall County grew **20.3% between 2020 and 2025**. Rising sale prices in a neighborhood become rising appraised values on the tax roll.

If you think the district got your value wrong, the remedy is a protest — due **May 15, or 30 days after the district mails your notice of appraised value, whichever is later** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/protests/)).

## Reason 2: one entity raised its rate

You do not need every entity to raise rates to feel it. The school district is the largest share, so a swing there dominates. But a MUD, a water control and improvement district, or a bond issue with new debt service can add a line that was not there before or grow one that was small.

Read the bill line by line and find which entity actually changed. Then take the complaint to that entity's board, not to the appraisal district — the review board cannot lower a rate.

## Reason 3: an exemption is missing

This one is quiet and expensive. Check the notice of appraised value for the exemptions you expect to see.

Exemptions that commonly fail to post:

- A **homestead exemption that was never filed** after a purchase or a move. It is not automatic.
- A homestead exemption **lost in a transfer** — into a trust or an LLC, after a death, after adding or removing an owner.
- An **age-65 or disability exemption** the owner became eligible for and never applied for. That is an additional **$60,000** from the school district on top of the general exemption, plus a school tax ceiling ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)).
- A **disabled veteran exemption** after a rating change the district was never told about.

For 2026 the mandatory school district homestead exemption is **$140,000**, raised from $100,000 by **Proposition 13**, approved by voters in **November 2025** and implemented through **SB 4, 89th Legislature** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)). A homesteaded property in Boerne ISD gets $140,000 off the value the school district taxes. On a $500,000 appraisal, that is $360,000 taxable, and at the 2025 Boerne ISD rate of 1.0109 the school line runs roughly **$3,639**. Without the exemption on that same appraisal, the school line is about **$5,055**. The city and county lines depend on what local option exemptions those entities adopted, which is published by the [appraisal district](https://kendallad.org/adopted-tax-rates-and-exemptions/).

## Reason 4: you just bought the house, and the cap reset

This is the biggest shock, and it is completely predictable.

A property with a homestead exemption is protected by the **10% cap** on annual increases in net appraised value. An owner who held a home through several years of Hill Country appreciation can be taxed on a value far below what the home would sell for. The gap builds quietly.

When the property sells, that protection does not transfer with it. The new owner is looking at a fresh appraisal at market value — often the price just paid — and has to file their own homestead exemption, which requires having **owned and occupied the home as a principal residence on January 1** ([Texas Comptroller](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/property-tax/exemptions/)).

So the prior owner's tax bill, the one shown in the listing or on the county site, is not a forecast of yours. It is a record of somebody else's capped value and somebody else's exemptions. A buyer budgeting from it will be short, and if taxes are escrowed, the shortfall arrives later as a lender escrow analysis and a payment increase. That call is one of the most common post-closing surprises in Texas.

## Reason 5 (investors): the circuit breaker is temporary

Non-homestead real property has its own limit. Under **Tax Code §23.231**, appraised value increases on qualifying non-homestead real property at or below a threshold are capped at **20%** per year. The threshold is **indexed annually** — confirm the current figure with your appraisal district rather than relying on a published number.

It was created by **SB 2 (2023)** as a pilot for tax years **2024, 2025 and 2026**, and it **expires after the 2026 tax year** unless the Legislature renews it. No application is required; the appraisal district applies it automatically, and the owner must have held the property for at least one full calendar year to qualify ([Travis Central Appraisal District](https://traviscad.org/circuitbreaker)).

Any investor underwriting a Texas rental past 2026 should model the possibility that this cap is not there. It is a scheduled expiration, not a rumor.

## Boerne is in Kendall County

Worth stating because it changes every answer above: Boerne is the county seat of **Kendall County**. It is not in Bexar County and not in the City of San Antonio. Your rates are Kendall County's, your appraisal district is **Kendall Appraisal District**, and San Antonio and Bexar County figures do not describe your bill.

## What to do with a bill that jumped

1. Pull the bill and identify **which line** moved. Value, rate, or exemption.
2. Compare the notice of appraised value with last year's. Look at both market value and net appraised value — they can move differently when the cap is holding.
3. Confirm every exemption you are entitled to is showing.
4. If the value is wrong, protest by the deadline.
5. If a rate moved, take it to that entity's board and its budget hearings.

Values and exemptions are determined by the appraisal district. Rates are set by each taxing unit. For the tax consequences of any of it, talk with a CPA, and take deed, trust or ownership-structure questions to a Texas real estate attorney.
